The theory of computation and complexity deals with combinatorial problems set on finite combinatorial structures, and the algorithm complexity is measured with respect to an appropriate defined input length. At the same time, many problems can be defined on infinite structures (as infinite graphs, sets, etc.), presentable by infinite inputs. In such case the classical complexity theory becomes impracticable.

The paper proposes an approach to treatment of questions concerning the complexity of algorithms and corresponding problems, defined on infinite combinatorial structures. The introduced model can be also considered as natural framework for problems providing incremental search, where the information comes online, during the process of solving.

The main ideas are illustrated on some concrete examples. Algorithms for solving some of the problems are sketched, unsolvability of others is commented, and a comparison to the problems in the finite case is given.
MODEL

We will consider problems in the following general setting. The search problem $\Pi =$ $( I _ { \Pi } , S _ { \Pi } )$ is supposed to be defined on a combinatorial structure $s$ of arbitrary nature, presented by an input $I _ { \Pi }$ and having a set of solutions $S _ { \Pi }$ . $s$ could be a graph, a family of subsets of some ground set, etc. We assume that the problem has to be solved by some Solver $\mathcal { M }$ , that is in a position to perform various types of operations $t _ { 1 } , \ldots , t _ { k } .$ depending on the problem nature.

$\mathcal { M }$ must realize some aim a priori defined (to find some special subgraph of a graph, or a special subset in a given family of sets). In addition we suppose that $\mathcal { M }$ disposes of incomplete, local information about the ground structure, i.e. in general $\mathcal { M }$ does not know $s$ a priori, but completes the knowlege about it dynamically, during solving the problem, following some local-search-type algorithm.

This model generalizes the traditional one, where we could think that at the initial moment the known data (neighbourhood of $s$ ) includes all the structure. Such approach also allows to consider problems where $s$ is given by infinite input.

We presented the model on informal level because of its generality, but it could be precised in any concrete case, as it will be done in the next section. In some cases it would be convinient to think that the input data is received from some oracle, which has to be asked for additional information.

Supposing $\mathcal { M }$ can perform different operations, different types of complexity (eventually uncomparable each to other) correspond to them. In the classical complexity theory the most important type of complexity - the computational one, is measured with respect to the input size of the problem, but for problems with infinite inputs this is impossible. Our approach to the complexity in infinite structures is the following.

First, let us note that in the finite case, in generally, the algorithms use all the input in order to produce a solution, so that it could be said that the algorithm complexity (and correspondingly the problems' ones) is measured with respect to the volume of the data used. At the same time, it is possible for many individual problems to find the solution applying some local-search-type algorithm that manipulates only a part of the input (it is typical in cases when superfluous information is given). About the infinite case, it is clear that the problem has to be solved by algorithm using only a finite part of the infinite input. So, there are reasons to consider some data subset as an adequate characteristic of the input, if the knowlege of this subset allows to solve the problem in finite time.

Let $A _ { \Pi }$ be an algorithm such that if $\mathcal { M }$ follows it, a search problem $\Pi$ will be solved $i \pi \in I _ { \Pi }$ , $i _ { \Pi } ^ { A _ { \Pi } }$ denotes the data really used by $A _ { \Pi }$ to solve the problem (again the notion "really used" is to be precised in dependance on the concrete problem). According to our assumption about the different abilities of the Solver $\mathcal { M }$ , $A _ { \Pi }$ can be considered as a multyalgorithm, consisting of $\pmb { k }$ different algoritms $A _ { \Pi } ^ { 1 } , \dotsc , A _ { \Pi } ^ { k }$ corresponding to the various types of operations, and different types of complexity - one per each of the algorithms - can be examined. All these complexities will be measured with respect to a basic one - data complexity $\mu ( i _ { \Pi } ^ { A _ { \Pi } } )$ , that reflects in some appropriate way the volume of the used data $i _ { \Pi } ^ { A _ { \Pi } }$ defined above (in many cases it is most naturally function $\mu$ to give the number of elementary data units as numbers, graph vertices, elements of sets, etc., which are manipulated by the algorithm during its work). The complexity $\pmb { c _ { i } }$ of $A _ { \Pi } ^ { i }$ reflects the loss of operations during the work of $A _ { \Pi } ^ { i }$ It is a function that to every (natural) number $\pmb { n }$ juxtaposes the maximal (over all individual problems $\Pi _ { n }$ for which $A _ { \Pi } ^ { i }$ needs data complexity $n = \mu ( i _ { \Pi } ^ { A _ { \Pi } } ) )$ number of operations of type $\mathbf { \Delta } _ { t _ { i } } .$ , spent for solving the individual problems of $\Pi _ { n }$ .

We say that the (sub)algorithm $A _ { \Pi } ^ { i } ( 1 \leq i \leq k )$ is a polynomial one if for every individual problem $i _ { \Pi }$ the number of steps performed till obtaining the solution is bounded by a polynomial of the corresponding data complexity $\mu ( i _ { \Pi } ^ { A _ { \Pi } } )$ .The algorithm $A _ { \Pi }$ is polynomial if every $A _ { \Pi } ^ { i }$ is polynomial for $i = 1 , \ldots , k$ ,and $A _ { \Pi }$ is exponential if some of its complexities are exponential functions of the data complexity. The problem $\Pi$ is called polynomially solvable if there exists a polynomial algorithm $A _ { \Pi }$ such that the Solver $\mathcal { M }$ , performing $A _ { \Pi }$ , will realize the aim a priori set.

Such approach allows to evaluate the algorithms and problems complexity in infinite structures. Let us, however, note that if it is necessary to compare the complexities of two algorithms for one problem, it would be needed first to receive a relation for their data complexities, after to compare the corresponding complexity functions, and finally to obtain the relation between the algorithm complexities as a superposition of the above two relations.
EXAMPLES

We consider graph problems, supposing for simplicity that graphs are displaced on the plane, that the Solver $\mathcal { M }$ is able to move along the edges of the graph which are streight line segments, and that it possesses a "vision" in radius $\pmb { r }$ , can make computations, can store some data, as well as to measure passed distances. So we can talk about computational complexity, moving complexity (passed distance or number of passed edges), measuring complexity (number of performed measurings), memory complexity (the necessary memory volume). In the case of infinite graphs, we will suppose that $V$ (being an infinite set) does not contain cluster points, and that for every fixed node $v \in V$ its degree is finite. First we will consider the well known

Path Problem (PP). Given a graph G with positive weights of its edges and two fixed vertices s and $\pmb { t }$ (with known coordinates with respect to some fixed coordinate system), find a (Shortest, Longest) simple path (SPP, LPP) from $\pmb { s }$ to $\pmb { t }$ .

It is well known that on finite graphs the PP and SPP are polynomially solvable, for example by the Dijkstra's algorithm (DA) [3]; even if $G$ is a disjoint graph and s and $\pmb { t }$ belong to different connective components and there is no path between them, this can be checked in polynomial time [5]. It is known also that the LPP is NP-hard [4].

On connected infinite graphs, the PP and SPP are polynomially solvable, too. Really, DA could be applied, and in finite number of steps the target vertex will be reached. It is easy to see that the number of calculations, movings from one vertex to another, measurings (of angles or passed distances), and used memory are restricted by a polynomial of the data complexity, measured, for example, in number of visited edges.
At the same time, the LPP is unsolvable, as it easily follows from the infinity of the graph.
The SPP and LPP are both unsolvable if the weights can be positive and negative numbers, as well as if $G$ is disjoint and s and $\pmb { t }$ belong to different connective components.

Spanning Tree Problem (STP). Given a graph G with positive weights of its edges and a set $W \subseteq V$ of $k$ fixed vertices of $G$ (with known coordinates), find a (Shortest, Longest) Spanning Tree (SSTP, LSTP) for these vertices.

1 Introduction

Many problems arising in various branches of computational mathematics (in particular numerical analysis and scientific computations) have as natural domains real or complex numbers. This has motivated research derected to developing of extention of the classical theory of computation and complexity, dealing with combinatorial problems presentable over integers. The basic new conceptions, definitions and results can be found, for example, in [1]. We will mention here only that, according the new computational model, every arithmetic operation $( + , - , * , / )$ is assumed to be underlying one, performable in unique time.

A main theme in the initial research is the comparison of the results over the integers with ones over the reals, that gives deeper understanding to the basic concepts of decidability, computability, complexity, etc.

The present paper is an additional step in this direction.We consider the well known Knapsack Problem (KP) with two variables (1) $\operatorname* { m a x } \{ c _ { 1 } x + c _ { 2 } y ~ : ~ a _ { 1 } x + a _ { 2 } y \leq b .$ $x , y \in Z _ { + } \mathrm { ~ } \}$ , where $c _ { 1 } , c _ { 2 } , a _ { 1 } , a _ { 2 } , b \in R _ { + }$ . It is well known that if the coefficients are rational, the problem can be solved in polynomial time in the sense of the complexity theory over the integers [3]. The same is the case if at least one of $_ { \pmb { x } }$ and $\pmb { y }$ is not required to be nonnegative. In contrast, we have obtained that in the real data case there is no algorithm solving (1) if $\pmb { x }$ and/or $_ { y }$ may be negative (section 2). It is true also that, in terms of the new computational model, the problem (1) is intractable. The Job-Shop Problem and Immediate Selection
Peter Brucker, Bernd Jurisch, Andreas Krämer Universität Osnabrück Fachbereich Mathematik/Informatik Postfach 44 69 D-49069 Osnabrück Germany

In a job-shop scheduling problem we have $\pmb { n }$ jobs $J _ { 1 } , \ldots , J _ { n }$ to be processed on $_ m$ different machines $M _ { 1 } , \ldots , M _ { m }$ . Each job $J _ { i }$ consists of a number $\pmb { n _ { i } }$ of operations $O _ { i 1 } , \ldots , O _ { i n _ { i } }$ which have to be processed in this order. Operations $O _ { i j }$ can be processed only by one machine $\mu _ { i j } ( i = 1 , \ldots , n ; j = 1 , \ldots , n _ { i } )$ . Denote by $\pmb { p _ { i j } }$ the corresponding processing time. We assume that all processing times are integer numbers. There is only one machine of each type which can only process one operation at a time. Operations must be processed without preemption. Moreover, a job cannot be processed by two machines at the same time. For each machine $M _ { k }$ we have to find an ordering of all operations to be processed on $M _ { k }$ such that the maximal completion time $C _ { \bf m a x }$ of all jobs is minimal.

This problem is one of the most difficult NP-hard scheduling problems. A 10-job, $1 0 \mathrm { \ m a }$ chine problem formulated in 1963 (Muth & Thompson[1963]) has been solved only recently (Carlier & Pinson [1989]). The algorithm developed by Carlier and Pinson is a branch and bound method which is based on the disjunctive graph formulation of the job-shop problem. Other branch and bound algorithms have been developed recently (Applegate & Cook [1990], Brucker et al. [1991]).

The efficiency of all these branch and bound methods relies on the concept of immediate selection introduced by Carlier and Pinson. By immediate selection disjunctions, i.e. order relations between operations which have to be processed on the same machine, are fixed before branching. An order relation can be fixed if the reverse order relation yields a solution which does not improve the best solution found so far.

In Carlier & Pinson [1990] presented an $O ( n ^ { 2 } )$ -algorithm which usually fixes a large number of disjunctions. Recently they proposed an $O ( \operatorname* { m a x } \{ n \log n , d \} )$ -version of their algorithm (Carlier & Pinson [1993]). Here $\pmb { n }$ is the number of operations to be scheduled on the same machine and $\pmb { d }$ denotes the number of disjunctions to be fixed. The algorithm considers all pairs $( O _ { i } , O _ { j } )$ of operations to be processed on this machine and decides whether a disjunction between $O _ { i }$ and $O _ { j }$ can be fixed. Besides these conditions for pairs of operations Dewe® [1991] derived conditions for triples of operations which allow to fix additional disjunctions. We will generalize both concepts by

deriving conditions for fixing disjunctions which are based on $\pmb { r }$ -sets of operations to be processed on the same machine where $r \geq 2$ is an arbitrary integer   
simplifying the conditions given by DeweB   
describing algorithms for checking these conditions.

We will present an $O ( \operatorname* { m a x } \{ n \log n , d \} )$ -algorithm which fixes all disjunctions derived by so called cliques as the algorithm of Carlier and Pinson does. Our algorithm is based on alternative concepts. Due to these concepts the correctness proof is much simpler than the correctness proof in Carlier $\&$ Pinson [1990].

For checking 3-set conditions we present an $O ( n ^ { 2 } )$ -algorithm improving the approach of Dewe for checking 3-sets considerably. Finally we will report on the computational results we got by replacing the algorithm of Carlier and Pinson by these new algorithms in a branch and bound method presented in Brucker et al. [1991].

In our paper we will first introduce the job-shop problem. Then the typical situation in a node of the search tree of a branch and bound method is described. The method is based on the disjunctive graph formulation of this problem. There we have a set of already fixed order relations between operations to be scheduled on the same machine. Using these relations a head $\boldsymbol { r } _ { i }$ and a tail $\pmb q _ { \hat { \imath } }$ may be calculated for each operation i. Furthermore let $\pmb { U } \pmb { B }$ be an integer upper bound for the optimal solution value of the problem. Usually $\pmb { U } \pmb { B }$ is the value of the best solution found so far. If we want to improve this best solution each operation i must be finished not later than the due date $d _ { i } : = U B - q _ { i } - 1$ . Thus, operation i must be processed within the time window specified by the interval $[ r _ { i } , d _ { i } ]$ .

Then we will present two concepts for immediate selection. They use the time windows of the operations. The first concept based on so called cliques was introduced by Carlier and Pinson [1989]. Roughly speaking a clique $( J , c )$ consists of a set of operations $\pmb { J }$ (to be processed on the same machine) which must be scheduled within a certain time interval because of the operations' heads and due dates. Hence the capacity of the machine to process other operations during this interval is bounded. Thus, if the processing time of an operation $^ { c }$ exceeds this bound, it must be scheduled either before or after all operations of $\pmb { J }$ .

The second concept was introduced by DeweB [1991]. It uses so called $\pmb { r }$ -set conditions. This means that an operation $_ i$ must be scheduled before an operation $j$ if there exists a set $\pmb { J }$ of operations with $\pmb { r }$ elements $( i , j \in J )$ such that every sequence of operations of $\pmb { J }$ in which $j$ is scheduled before $_ i$ does not respect the time windows given by the heads and due dates.

Next we will describe algorithms to check the conditions induced by the two concepts. The first algorithm fixes disjunctions which may be derived from cliques. It has complexity $O ( \operatorname* { m a x } \{ n \log n , d \} )$ where $d$ is the number of disjunctions which will be fixed. This algorithm consists of two steps:

First heads and due dates of all operations to be scheduled on the same machine are improved. Therefore we calculate the earliest possible completion time $\scriptstyle { \pmb { s } } _ { c }$ of operation $^ { c }$ under the assumption that all operations respect their time windows and preemption is allowed. Then we can improve the head of operation $^ c$ to $\pmb { s _ { c } } - \pmb { p _ { c } }$ for the schedules without preemption. This needs $O ( n ^ { 2 } )$ (respectively $O ( n \log n ) )$ time for all operations to be scheduled on the same machine. The $O ( n \log n )$ -version is based on a sophisticated datastructure which enables to decrease $\pmb { n }$ different values by a constant amount in $O ( \log n )$ steps.
Then using the improved heads and tails we may fix all disjunctions induced by cliques in $O ( \operatorname* { m a x } \{ n \log n , d \} )$ time.

The second algorithm checks the conditions induced by triples, i.e. 3-sets. The idea is to calculate a lower bound for the total length of all parts of operations which must be scheduled between the head of operation $j$ and the due date of operation $_ i$ if we assume that $j$ is scheduled before i. Hence $_ i$ must be scheduled before $j$ if this lower bound exceeds the length of the interval. E.g. a very simple lower bound is ${ p } _ { \mathrm { { i } } } + { p } _ { \mathrm { { j } } }$ .We will give an $O ( n ^ { 2 } ) \cdot$ . algorithm for calculating such a bound for all pairs of operations $( O _ { i } , O _ { j } )$ to be processed on the same machine.

Finally we will report on the computational results. We implemented the different algorithms for immediate selection in a branch and bound algorithm (Brucker et al. [1991]) for solving the job-shop problem.

Of course, the number of search tree nodes did not change when we used our clique algorithm instead of Carlier and Pinson's one. But the running time was always improved by approx. $3 . 4 \%$ using our $O ( n ^ { 2 } )$ algorithm.

We also implemented the $O ( \operatorname* { m a x } \{ n \log n , d \} )$ -version to check clique conditions. We got an increase in the running time of approx. $3 5 { - } 4 0 \%$ for problems with 10 jobs, approx. $2 0 - 2 5 \%$ with 15 jobs, approx. $1 5 \mathrm { - } 2 0 \%$ with 20 jobs and approx. $1 5 \%$ with 30 jobs. Hence we may expect a better running time performance for problems with more jobs. The triple algorithm provided quite surprising results. In general it needed approx. $1 0 \mathrm { - } 1 5 \%$ search tree node less than the clique algorithm. The running time varied in a range of $\pm 1 0 \%$ of the amount given by the clique algorithm. We also found out that the triple algorithm fixes considerably more arcs than only the arcs induced by triples.

1 Introduction

Banking and insurance companies are both facing the problem of losing market shares with their core products sold via traditional marketing channels. In Germany the share of banking products sold in branches dropped from $98 \%$ in 1970 to $85 \%$ in 1987; the share of insurance products sold by the traditional exclusive agents dropped from roughly $90 \%$ to $70 \%$ in the same period and is expected to fall far below $50 \%$ at the end of the century (Krupp (1993); Schweickert (1993)). The bankassurance strategies in the financial services markets combine efforts to integrate insurance and banking products as well as the corresponding marketing channels. Suitable combined bankassurance products with provable customer advantages are one key for the success of these strategies; this is the topic of Chapter 2. The second key for success is to provide customer benefits by enabling the stationary and mobile marketing channels with the knowledge and capacity to offer and contract bankassurance products in an efficient way. Chapter 3 deals with the system support necessary for spreading knowledge and capacity in these channels; furtheron, first experiences from a prototype developed within the ALLFIWIB-project funded by the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft are sketched.
2 The Advantage of Combined Bankassurance Products

For customer decision support in the financial services field comparisons of e.g. loan interest rates offered by different banks or premiums for life policies offered from insurance companies are usual and widespread. The success of independent agents working together with a variety of financial services companies is largely based on such, often "computer-supported", comparisons of given, standardized offerings. Optimization of such offerings resulting in individual, tailored solutions for the special customer problem, however, is - due to complexity - hardly observable. In contrast to that, it turns out that such "local" optimization of single bankassurance products already may prove very profitable for both the customer and supplier when compared to usual standardized products. Compared to usual contracts with constant leasing rates such optimized payment streams are always - and often considerably - better. In extreme cases the net present value of a leasing rate paid may be smaller than the tax benefit resulting from it; thus the net present value after taxes of both the lessor and the lessee may be positive and can be increased arbitrarily while the corresponding disadvantage of the fisc also increases unbounded (Buhl, Erhard (1991); Buhl (1994a)).

If the lessor has a larger tax rate than the lessee, then for both of them the advantage of a real estate lease increases with the share of the building costs. Conversely, if the lessor's tax rate is smaller than the one of the lessee, then the advantage of the lease increases with the share of the ground (Will et al. (1993)).
Also, due to the german corporate taxes, commercial loans without any interest and discharge payments up to contract end prove optimal compared to all other loan types (Buhl (1994b)).

For both the investor and the issuing bank or firm zerobonds are better than all straight bonds, whenever bonds are profitable for them in the after tax world at all. A life policy is better than all bonds, whenever the german tax subsidy requirements are met (Buhl et al. (1993b)).

Such examples show the competitive and business potential for combined bankassurance solutions compared to the traditional core products of the financial services providers. As one main reason for the profitability of these combined solutions the lacking neutrality and the inefficiency of the german tax system is identified, particularly the following fact is key: Interest rates contained in leases, loans, straight bonds, zerobonds and insurance products are all taxed differently at either the supplier or the customer or both. This opens up a considerable optimization potential for the "coalition" of the financial services provider and its customer in nearly all practically relevant cases. The next chapter deals with the question, how such solutions may be generated by combining knowledge based techniques with methods from distributed artificial intelligence.
3 System Support for Combined Bankassurance Products

The discussion of combined bankassurance products highlighted the complexity of obtaining solutions to financial problems that are advantageous for both, the customer and the supplier. Obviously, system support is necessary to cope with this complexity (Buhl et al. (1993a)). As described in more detail in Buhl, Will (1993), König (1993), and Mack et al. (1993) the following system support is applicable, at least in principle, for both the branches and the mobile marketing channel, if access from the customer's site - e.g. via ISDN - to the data and solution agents in the network of the financial services provider is possible.

To cope with the complexity problem first, we propose a concept of cooperating knowledge based systems as an adequate support to elaborate and offer combined bankassurance products (see e.g. Buhl, Will (1993); König (1993); König et al. (1993)). For each financial domain, e.g. bonds or loans, a knowledge based system works as an expert (a so called "domain-agent") selecting and/or configuring solutions to a given problem. While working on problem solving a domain-agent applies rules like those presented in Chapter 2 for leasing and loans in order to obtain an advantageous or even optimal solution. Implementing each domain-agent as a separately running software process (e.g. on a local area network of workstations) the performance of the problem solving process can be improved by concurrently elaborating competing solutions to the same problem (e.g. leasing vs. loan for a financing problem). Moreover, the realization of this concept simplifies maintaining and extending the knowledge bases by the experts of the respective supplying firm. Embedding the domain-agents in a decentral Multi-Database-Server-Architecture provides the necessary remote access to all required customer and product data (König (1993)).

For implementing the idea of offering combined solutions of several locally optimized products cooperation of the domain-agents is necessary. This cooperation can be adequately supported by a blackboard as a common accessible database to store customer problems and residual problems as well as the corresponding solutions (Mack et al. (1993)). A homogeneous, payment-streambased representation-form of both problems and solutions on the blackboard allows the agents to "understand" each problem. For example, the leasing-agent offers an optimized contract with an upfront-one-time-payment although the customer wishes to pay constant rates. The residual problem of financing the one-time-payment will then be written on the blackboard to be solved by other domain-agents, e.g. the loan-agent. In addition to this implicit way of cooperation of the domain-agents we provide a "combination-agent" with explicit knowledge overlapping everaldomains.  in a pecisituaton ike the  rom the example above suc knowle priori suggests a good combination of different products the combination-agent is able to decompose the complex problem into partial problems to be solved by the single domain-agents. In this sense the combination-agent initiates explicitly combined solutions and thus helps to reduce search-time. Also, this explicit knowledge may lead to a better solution than the search process.

Based on the concept presented, a first prototype was developed within the project ALLFIWIB. Four domain-agents for loans, leasing, bonds, and life insurance as well as a combination-agent and communication and control modules were implemented. Testing activities proved the general practicablity of the ideas sketched. In the simple model framework of the prototype with deterministic payments and with only a few rules even "mixed" problems starting with periods of saving, a following real estate investment and subsequent periods of financing could be solved by the system of cooperating agents. Currently we work on improving the prototype and extending the knowledge bases with e.g. the economic knowledge from the references cited below.

Once it was assumed that the use of this modeling structure would be responsibility of the high schools themselves, the compatible mathematical programming software tested for that should be available for microcomputers, the most common computational platform obtainable in that category of schools.

EVENTMAN - A BUSINESS EVENT TRACKING SYSTEM
Drago epar, Franci Mulec Joef Stefan Institute, Ljubljana, Slovenia
1. Introduction

In the paper we describe a groupware computer system for supporting the debt-recovery process in the legal department at Ljubljanska banka. A similar system is described in Kiel (1993). The benefits of such systems are also described in Opper and Weiss (1992). In Section 2, we describe the present computer-supported work process and compare it with the former manual process. The computer system considerably reduces the reaction time of employees. In Section 3 we discuss the possibilities and consequences of changing the work process, which is possible with Eventman. The work process is described by a simple queuing model with serial and parallel connections of service channels. We present some simulation results obtained by GPSS.
2. The Work Process in the Department

The department recovers different overdue liabilities from the bank's customers. It has a secretary, five lawyers and a file. The file is divided among five lawyers, so that every lawyer has his own subset of cases. The secretary receives documents and telephone cals (they will be uniquely referred to as events) from other bank departments, courts and bank customers. She finds out to which case a document belongs, to which lawyer the case belongs and on the basis of this information, she passes a document or a telephone call to a lawyer. (Figure 1).
2.1. The Manual Procedure

When the secretary received a telephone call, she examined the book of about 500 pages. She found out to which case the telephone call was related and usually also to which lawyer the case belonged. If she didn't find that information in the book, she asked the lawyers. When she

found the owner of the case, she connected the phone call to him. When the secretary received a document, she registered it in the book and the same procedure followed. Processing each event took the secretary 5 minutes on average. When a lawyer received a telephone cal, he had to walk from his desk to the cabinet, take the corresponding folder from the file, go back to his desk, look over the case documents, and then answer the phone call. Afterwards, he had to put the folder of the case back to the cabinet. When he received a document and surveyed it, he decided on the next action and put the document in the folder of the case. For this procedure, he spent 20 minutes for an event on average.
2.2. The Computer-Supported Procedure

Eventman is PC-DOS-based software for tracking events like phone calls and documents. It consists of a computer database of events and bank customers and user-friendly software, which enables its users to inquire about these events and customers. Among other information it contains information about the status of the case and the identity of the lawyer to whom the case belongs. The system helps the user by reminding him of possible actions he can take given the specific status of the case on the basis of the history of the case.

Now when a secretary receives a call or a document, she identifies the case and the appropriate lawyer by entering one or two keywords into the computer on her desk. Then she enters basic data about the event into the computer system and passes the call or the document to the lawyer. The time needed for this procedure is 3 minutes for an event on average.

When the lawyer receives the document, he usually doesn't have to walk away from his desk. He can find basic data about the case and its history on the computer on his desk. When he receives the document, he confirms this on a computer and chooses the next action. He puts the document in a folder of the case. The time needed for this procedure is 5 minutes for an event on average.

The department began using Eventman at the end of 1990. 3. Changing Work Process

We will try to answer the question of whether we could further improve the present work process. With its comprehensive history, data and and process storage and description, computer support allows each lawyer to handle any event. What would happen, if every lawyer could work on all cases? We simulated two alternatives of the system from Figure 1 with VAX GPSS which is described in Martin (1985). The first alternative resumes the present work process, where every lawyer is responsible for his subset of cases. Events come into the system randomly with respect to lawyers. The result of the simulation is the same as if the secretary randomly passed the event to one of the five lawyers without considering the length of his queue. We denote this system Random. In the second alternative, the secretary passes the event to the lawyer with the shortest queue. When there are several equally short queues, the priority sequence is 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. We denote this system Minimal. We simulated 10 workdays for each alternative. We assumed an exponential distribution of interarrival times with a mean of 324 seconds (89 events per workday). The exponential distribution has higher probability for short times. This is realistic, because many events, especialy documents, come in batches, where interarrival time is 0. We assumed an exponential distribution of service times with a mean of 3 minutes for secretary and 5 minutes for lawyer. This is also a realistic assumption, because $30 \%$ of events are telephone calls, where service times are shorter than the average. 4. Conclusion

The improvements reported in section 2 are the results of shorter response times which are the consequence of computer support of the office work. The work organization is not altered. We consider a fow shop consisting of m machines, an input device and an output device, in which one type of product is to be produced. There are no buffers in the flow shop and the transportation of items between machines is taken care of by a robot. The l-part cyclic scheduling problem consists in finding the shortest cyclic schedule for the robot, i.e. a schedule that outputs one part in each cycle, can be repeated infinitely many times and has maximum throughput rate. The problem has been solved by Sethi et al. (1992) in the case where $m \le 3$ . We present an algorithm solving the 1-part cyclic scheduling problem in polynomial time for arbitrary values of $_ m$ .Our approach is based on dynamic programming techniques.

A first constructive result concerning the 1-part cyclic scheduling problem is given in Sethi et al. (1992). Define activity $A _ { i }$ as unloading machine $M _ { i }$ and subsequently loading machine $M _ { i + 1 }$ (where the input device is $M _ { 0 }$ and the output device is $M _ { m + 1 }$ ). Call the sequence in which the activities are executed in a cyclic schedule a 1-part cycle. It is easy to see that every 1-part cycle corresponds exactly to a permutation of the activities. Conversely, it can be shown that every permutation of the activities defines a feasible 1-part cycle.
Theorem 1. (Sethi et al. (1992)) In a robotic cell with $_ m$ machines, there are exactly m! 1-part cycles.

Observe that a schedule, as opposed to a cycle, must specify loading and unloading times for each machine. Then the next question is, given a 1-part cycle, i.e. a permutation of the activities, what is the shortest schedule compatible with this cycle? We call a schedule

1-periodic if it has constant cycle time, i.e. if the time between two executions of the same activity is equal to the cycle time. Similarly, a schedule that repeats every $\mathbf { \Delta } _ { \mathbf { \mathcal { n } } }$ periods is called $\pmb { n }$ -periodic. Using max-algebra (Cunninghame-Green (1979), Cohen et al. (1985)) it is possible to derive the following theorem :
Theorem 2. There is no periodic schedule with shorter mean cycle time than a shortest 1-periodic cyclic schedule.

Hence, we may restrict the analysis to 1-periodic schedules. The next step is to identify a set of 1-part cycles that necessarily contains an optimal cycle. For this purpose we introduce the concept of pyramidal permutations (analogously to pyramidal tours for the traveling salesman problem, see Gilmore et al. (1985); it is known that for the traveling salesman problem a shortest pyramidal tour can be computed by dynamic programming techniques in $O ( n ^ { 2 } )$ time). More precisely, let $\pi = ( A _ { 0 } , A _ { i _ { 1 } } , \ldots , A _ { i _ { k } } , A _ { i _ { k + 1 } } , \ldots , A _ { i _ { m } } )$ be a 1-part cycle, i.e. a permutation of the activities.
Definition 1. $\pi$ is pyramidal if $1 \leq i _ { 1 } < . . . i _ { k } = m$ and $m > i _ { k + 1 } > . . . > i _ { m - 1 } \geq 1$
Theorem 3. The set of pyramidal 1-part cycles contains an optimal 1-part cycle.

Thus, in order to find a shortest cyclic schedule, we can restrict our attention to pyramidal permutations and to their associated shortest cyclic schedule. In general it is not trivial to find a shortest cyclic schedule associated with a given permutation. This can be done using max-algebra, but this method does not provide much insight. Since the structure of pyramidal permutations is fairly simple, one may wonder whether the shortest cycle time of a pyramidal cycle can be determined in an easier way. This is indeed the case. We have an $O ( m )$ algorithm for computing a shortest schedule corresponding to a given 1-part cycle. In fact, our algorithm also enables us to solve the recognition version of the 1-part cyclic scheduling problem by dynamic programming techniques (the recognition version simply asks whether there exists a schedule with cycle time at most $C$ , for some given $\boldsymbol { C }$ ) :
Theorem 4. The recognition version of the 1-part cyclic scheduling problem can be solved
in $O ( m ^ { 2 } )$ time.
Moreover, making use of the structure of the solution given by the recognition algorithm, and applying this algorithm repeatedly, we can solve the optimization version in polynomial time.

ON UNIFORMIZATION FOR CONTINUOUS-TIME MARKOV CHAINS
Nico M. van Dijk \* University of Amsterdam
Abstract
The method of uniformization or randomization for continuous-time Markov chains is shown to be extendable to chains with
time-inhomogeneous and unbounded
transition rates. Some approximate computational aspects are addressed also. A special application of uniformization of actual interest is included.
1. INTRODUCTION

Continuous-time Markov chains are widely applicable for modelling practical situations that evolve continuously in time with jumps or changes at specific epochs. Particularly, applications are found in telecommunications (teletraffc analysis, broadcasting), computer performance evaluation (computer networks), manufacturing (material handling systems, assembly lines), inventory theory, maintenance analysis and reliability.

In dealing with continuous-time Markov chains the technique of uniformization, motivated by results in [4], has been shown to be a powerful tool for both computational and theoretical purposes over the last decades (cf. [2], [3], [5]).An elegant survey is given in [2].

So far, however, this technique seemed to be restricted to chains of which the transition rates are time-homogeneous and uniformly bounded. Though the first condition is reasonably justified for steady state situations it is less realistic for transient analysis. Conversely, while transition rates usually remain stochastically bounded over finite time intervals, the second condition can easily be violated in practical situations. For example, it already fails for the classical $\mathbf { M } \mid \mathbf { M } \mid \infty$ - infinite server queue.

This paper aims to show that the first condition is not required while the second can be circumvented in an approximative manner. Roughly speaking the presented versions are similar in spirit to the standard case in that one can sample event epochs by a Poisson process while at these epochs events take place according to conditional jump probabilities.

The results can be of practical interest for approximative procedures in combination with random sampling such as by Monte-Carlo simulation, by finite grid approximation or by iterative numerical computation. Further research in these directions is suggested.

K. DJELLAB, G. FLEURY, M. GOURGAND, A. QUILLIOT. Laboratoire d'Informatique 63177 AUBIERE Cedex. FRANCE
Abstract : After a presentation of the problem : crew scheduling for drivers in an urban transit company, we exhibit the difficulties of this kind of optimization problem.
Afterward, an algorithm which is a coupling between a stochastic (annealing-like) algorithm and linear programming is proposed to solve it.
This algorithm is used to constitute the timetable for bus drivers of the T2C company (buses of the city of Clermont-Ferrand) and some of the obtained results are given.

To conclude, the efficiency of this approach is demonstrated by comparisons with various softwares proposed to the T2C by specialized companies. Moreover the structure of our algorithms allows to solve many other kinds of timetable problems. In any urban transit company, to answer the demand, and to improve the working conditions, and to maximize its profit (minimizing its manpower), appears highly combinatoric optimization problems. Many constraints need to be satisfied, a lot of them being sot constraints. The combinatoric of the problem is not easily reduced by these constraints. The cost function becomes usually vague and it is no more necessary to find the best solution, but only a good one.
Key words : Linear programming, Stochastic methods, Timetable.

1) Description of the problem : The crew scheduling problem is to cover the whole bus schedule the workdays remaining feasible, and the total cost becoming minimal. A task is a segment of working time on a bus, between two relief points (where a new driver can replace the previous driver of the vehicle). The moving durations (necessitated to go from a relief point to another one) are known. A workday is a feasible sequence of tasks attributed to one driver. These workdays are gathered in different grids, according to geographical or timing constraints. Each workday belongs to exactly one grid, and can be cut in two straight pieces (with a break for dinner), or not. The constraints are :

i the number of diary straights and their relative duration,   
2 duration and position of the break between two successive straights.   
3_ duration, total spread, and position of the workday,   
4_ number of workdays in each grid,   
5_ moving times between two relief points (such a break is paid and must be avoided, if possible),   
6_ mean duration of the workdays of each grid,   
7_ compatibility between grid and vehicle blocks.
1-1) The difficulties of the problem : This problem has been shown to be NP-hard [3]. Moreover,

1) the set of all possible workdays is not partitioned by any constraint.   
2) The geographically limited one straight piece workdays can be done either in the morning or in the afternoon.   
3) Some of the constraints are not strict : some of them can be "desirable". One (or even more) of the workdays can slightly violate a "strict" constraint. The dates of a non commercial task can be slightly modified, if necessary. Some of the constraints cannot be known before the whole schedule is constructed.   
4) Nevertheless, some (too rare) extreme tasks are devoted to precise grids.

As for most of these kinds of problems, the cost function is not exactly defined, and the quality of a schedule is not easy to be quantified. Therefore, it seems to be very hard to automatically create a exactly satisfying crew schedule.

1 Introduction

In the Maastricht Treaty (1991) the E.C. countries specified conditions for the transition to a monetary union. Two of these conditions that are necessary for admitting a country to the monetary union are represented by convergence in consumer price inflation and convergence in long term interest rates. In our paper [1] we develop a theoretical framework which makes it possible to analyze these aspects of convergence between E.C. countries. The analysis is done in a dynamic game context, where countries, apart from minimizing individual cost functions, minimize cooperatively a convergence function. This convergence function represents the above mentioned convergence conditions. The aspect of convergence is modeled as a dynamic constraint on the individual cost functions. In this way, the costs are modeled of E.C. countries which are involved in the proces of moving towards an Economic and Monetary union, which should be established (at least) in 1999. One important result of the paper is that the maximum degree of convergence is completely determined by the non-cooperative outcome of the game. In this extended abstract we illustrate this analysis in a theoretical example. The example shows that: (1) the goals with respect to convergence can seriously influence the outcome of the game. If these goals are set too ambitious the outcome can be that countries are not willing to cooperate anymore. (2) the costs involved to obtain convergence can differ substantially between countries.

1. Introduction

The paper focuses on a uniform treatment of a special type of one-point solutions for cooperative games, called the egalitarian non-individual contribution (ENIC-)value. The value in question is special in the sense that it is constructed in two stages: first and foremost, each player in the game is allocated some kind of a yet unspecified individual contribution and subsequently, the surplus of the total profits is equally divided among all the players. In addition to the general setting, the unspecified notion of individual contribution will be chosen to be one of the following four particular notions:

the individual worth of the player to participate in the game as a solitary player. The corresponding ENIC-value is known as the center of the imputation set, called CIS-value.   
the so-called separable (or marginal) contribution of the player to participate in the game as a member of the player set. The corresponding ENIC-value goes by the name of egalitarian non-separable contribution (ENSC-)value. (cf. Driessen and Funaki (1991)).   
the so-called average contribution of the player in the game which is obtainable as some average of marginal contributions of pairs of players including the player in question. The corresponding ENIC-value is called the egalitarian non-average contribution (ENAC-)value and has been studied in detail in Driessen and Funaki (1993).   
the so-called Banzhaf contribution of the player in the game which is interpretable as the average of all the player's marginal contributions to participate in the game anyhow. The corresponding ENIC-value is called the egalitarian non-Banzhaf contribution (ENBC-)value. The notion of Banzhaf contribution itself is closely related to the well-known Shapley value as well as the Banzhaf index for simple games.

The main goal of the paper is to provide an axiomatic characterization of the ENIC-value in general and the four particular ENIC-values as well. In fact, our goal is twofold because the player set may be considered as fixed or variable. Involving a fixed player set, the main Theorem 3.1 states that the ENIC-value is fully characterized by the classical axiom of relative invariance under strategic equivalence (RISE) and a modification of the classical axiom of equal treatment of substitutes in the game (ETP). Here the modified axiom requires equal value payoffs for players with identically individual contributions. Involving a variable player set, the main Theorem 4.1 states that the ENIC-value is fully characterized by RISE, ETP and a so-called consistency axiom in terms of reduced games. The notion of a reduced game has been used in axiomatizations of many other game theoretic solutions. Concerning the axiomatization of the ENIC-value in general, the reduced game is yet unspecified except for the player set, whereas the axiomatizations of the four particular ENIC-values do involve specified reduced games (cf. Corollary 4.2).

The paper is concern with some class of combinatorial optimization problems, namely those represented by multistage process model. A definition of multistage decision process is given as a specialized form of knowledge-based model.The different classes of decomposition algorithms based on the model are defined and analyzed in the paper. The condition for problem decomposability is given. An examples are presented.
MULTISTAGE PROCESS AS A SPECIALIZED FORM OF KNOWLEDGE BASED MODEL

The notion of a multistage decision process is widely used in optimization, but its idea has been introduced by means of examples rather than by a formal description. Let us recall the definition of multistage process given in the previous author paper.

Multistage decision (constructing) process is a process P defined as a six-touple $( \mathbb { U } , \mathbb { Y } , \mathbb { Y } _ { \mathsf { o } } , \mathbb { f } , \mathbb { Y } _ { \mathbb { N } } , \mathbb { Y } _ { \mathsf { G } } )$ where the individual elements are defined as follows: U is a decision set, Y is set of states, ${ \tt y } _ { \tt o } , { \tt Y } _ { \tt N } , { \tt Y } _ { \tt G }$ are distinguished initial state and sets of not admissible and goal states, respectively, f is a partial function f : $\texttt { U } \times \texttt { Y } \to \texttt { Y }$ defined by means of the function ${ \texttt { g } } : { \texttt { Y } } \circ \ 2 ^ { \texttt { U } }$ in the following way: $( \mathbf { u } , \mathbf { y } ) \in$ Dom $\textbf { f } \Leftrightarrow \textbf { u } \in \textbf { g } ( \mathbf { y } ) ~ ,$ .

Function f was defined as a partial function. This is so in order to deal with all the limitations concerning the control decisions in the current state in a convenient way. This is done by means of the so-called sets of possible decisions in a state y , denoted as ${ \tt u } _ { \tt p }$ (y) and defined as: $\begin{array} { r } { { \mathrm {  ~ U ~ } } _ { \bf p } \left( { \mathrm {  ~ y ~ } } \right) ~ = ~ \left\{ { \bf u } ~ \in ~ { \mathrm {  ~ U ~ } } : ~ \left( { \mathrm {  ~ u ~ } } , { \mathrm {  ~ y ~ } } \right) ~ \in ~ \mathrm { D o m } ~ { \mathrm {  ~ f ~ } } \right\} . } \end{array}$ Thus function g(y) determines the decision subset ${ \mathfrak { v } } _ { \mathfrak { p } } ( { \mathfrak { v } } )$ , for which function f is determined in the state y.

At the same time an individual process $\mathbf { P }$ is represented by a set of its trajectories. A trajectory starts from the distinguished initial state $\mathtt { Y _ { o } }$ and is assumed to end in the goal states set $\mathtt { Y } _ { \mathtt { G } ^ { \prime } }$ or in the not admissible states set $\tt { Y } _ { N } ,$ or in any state for

which the set of possible decisions ${ \mathfrak { v } } _ { \mathfrak { p } } ( { \mathfrak { v } } )$ is empty. It is assumed that no state of a trajectory, apart from the last one, may belong to the set $\mathtt { Y _ { N } }$ or have empty set of possible decsions. A trajectory that ends in the set of the goal states $\mathtt { Y } _ { \mathtt { G } }$ is an admissible one and the decision sequence determining it is an admissible decision sequence. In other cases, a trajectory is said to be a not admissible one.

The task of optimization consists in finding such an admissible decision sequence u which minimizes a certain criterion Q . Thus an optimization task is uniquely determined by the pair (P,Q) where process P represents all the task limitations.

A defined problem of optimization is such a set of optimization tasks which have a commonly determined set of data, common (parametric) definition of multistage process and common (parametric) definition of criterion functions.

In the most general case sets U and Y may be presented as a Cartesian product $\texttt { U } = \texttt { U } ^ { 1 } \times \texttt { U } ^ { 2 } \times \texttt { \ldots } \texttt { U } ^ { \texttt { m } } , \quad \texttt { Y } = \texttt { Y } ^ { 1 } \times \texttt { Y } ^ { 2 } \times \texttt { \ldots } \texttt { Y } ^ { \texttt { m } }$ . Thus a decision $\mathbf { u }$ as well as a state $\mathbf { x }$ is represented by finite sequence of values that belong to succeeding sets. There are no limitations imposed on the sets, in particular they need not be numerical ones.We will use the notions "state vector" and "control decision vector" by analogy to the classical control theory: $\mathbf { u } ~ = ~ ( \mathbf { u } ^ { 1 } , \mathbf { u } ^ { 2 } , \dots \mathbf { u } ^ { \mathrm { m } } )$ $\mathbf { x } ~ = ~ ( \mathbf { x } ^ { 1 } , \mathbf { x } ^ { 2 } , \ldots \mathbf { x } ^ { \mathrm { n } } )$ . Thus values of particular coordinates of a state as well as a control decision may be names of elements as well as some objects (e.g. finite set, sequence etc). This paper is appropriated for the processes for which at least one set is not numerical one.

Particular coordinates of the vector $\textbf { u } = \mathbf { \Omega } ( \mathbf { u } ^ { 1 } , \mathbf { u } ^ { 2 } , \ldots \mathbf { u } ^ { \mathfrak { m } } )$ represents a separate decisions that must or may be taken at the same time. The sets $\mathtt { Y } _ { \mathtt { n } } , \ \mathtt { Y } _ { \mathtt { F } }$ and ${ \tt u } _ { \tt p }$ are defined by means of logical formulae. Therefore, the complete model constitutes a specialized form of a knowledge-based system.

The presented model is generalization of of the classical model of discrete dynamic systems used in control theory. The generalization lies in the fact that both the state and decision coordinates need not be numerical ones and that the definition of the sets $\mathfrak { u } _ { \mathtt { p } } , \ \mathfrak { s } _ { \mathtt { N } } , \ \mathfrak { s } _ { \mathtt { F } }$ are given by means of logical formulae.

A lot of combinatorial problems can be formulated in terms of this model, e.g. optimization of discrete manufacturing processes (the symbols f,U,Y can be interpreted by means of manufacture terms), scheduling problems, traveling salesman problem, as well as classical problems considered within the frame of artificial intelligence.
PROPERTIES OF DECOMPOSITION ALGORITHMS

Decomposition method consists in dividing the problem into some partial problems to be solved separately. There are two main reason for application of the method: computational (due to large scale problems or due to possibility of parallel computing) and algorithmic one. The last reason is very vital for combinatorial problems when the partial problems are solved by means of different algorithms.
Properties of decomposition algorithms depend on:
- type of connections between the partial problems, - properties of the partial problems algorithms.

ON SOME EXPERT CONTROL
Tadeusz Dyduch, Sect. of Geometry and Computer Graphics, Cracow University of Technology
Expert Control is considered as a control performed by Expert System, i.e. a complicated computer program, composed of three parts:
- working database, - knowledge base, - reasoning engine.

One of the most significant feature of an expert system is ability of knowledge acquiring i.e. completing and incrementing its knowledge base. This feature, i.e. self organizing knowledge base is often utilize in support decision systems. For example, well known medical diagnosis expert systems required the rational ordering of the large amount of facts, taking into account only simple relations between parameters.
EXPERT CONTROL

Expert systems utilized in control often deal with Discrete Event Systems (DES). Expert control differs from classical control in unconventional model of control object as well as the way of choosing the decisions.

It can be applied when it is difficult to identify the physical dynamics model, or if the model is too complicated to utilize it in real time computing. A model of the controlled object is, in a matter of fact, the all knowledge base of the expert control system. Obviously, the form of the knowledge base depends on its designer. Then the form is filled up with information obtained from experts or from the other sources.
EXPERT SYSTEMS
REQUIRED STATES SET AS THE MAIN PART OF KNOWLEDGE BASE

The aim of the paper is to introduce new idea of knowledge base construction, which may be used to perform expert control of some processes. This base should be create by distinguish a set of process states, which we will call Required States set (Rs set). The RS set should have the following properties:

- direct aim (the objective) of the control can be expressed by means of this set i.e. should be equivalent to maintain a current state within the RS set or to bring it into the RS set, - this set should be easy to define as well as to identify, - for as many states as possible the following conditions should be fulfilled: a state belongs to Rs set or if it does not, there exists the suitable control to lead the process state back into the RS set.
Thus, in order to acquire the knowledge from the operator of the process (the human expert of the process control) we ask him to define:

- which are the 'good enough' states (Rs set),   
- what are the possible controls for the process to be still in the RS set.

Therefore the description of the RS set becomes the most important part of the knowledge base. If environment influence occurs, which changes the object state, (for example disturbances, dynamic processes in controlled object, or changing demands (goals)), the expert system is searching for the control sequence, which leads the current process state back into RS set. It should result in reasonable shortening of the real time calculation, while controlling. Moreover, it should simplify the design of the control system, similarly to the programming of a robot arm movement, when it is done by leading the arm by the human operator.
EXAMPLE
Let us analyze some two-person game on the chess board, as an illustration for the former discussion.

Player A has 4 identical pieces, placed at the beginning on the dark places al, a3, a5, a7. Player B has only 1 piece, placed on the chosen dark, not taken place on the board. Players move their pieces on turn. Each player moves strictly one piece to the nearest, free dark place at each turn. Player A has to move their pieces to the nearest dark places, and move it only forward. The game ends, when one of player has no legal move at his turn. This player lost the game.
In this game the players have not equal chances. The player A is called a strong side, what means that for each strategy of the player B , the player A has a chance to win the game.

G. Owen gave the definition of such games, called them as two - person games in extensive form, on the contrary to the matrix form of the game. This games can be considered as easy to formal description examples of control of DES (Discrete Event Systems). This game has 1.006.880 different states and about $\mathtt { 1 8 } ^ { 2 4 }$ different paths. Nevertheless, a man becomes an expert after 5 - 10 games played against experienced adversary, and can determine the RS set for effective playing this game. The RS set consists of such positions, where pieces of the player A lie vertically, dividing the chess board into two parts with no paths between them.

Thus one can formulae the strategy for player A to win this game (obviously this strategy exists), what seems to be hopeless before, consider the number of possibly paths. This strategy lies in bringing back the play state to the Rs set.

The effective description of the Rs set for this game was done along with description of the rules of control. In order to do it the symmetry in the set of states and possibility of states aggregation have been utilized. On the basis of RS set the whole game was optimized from the player A position, by means of analyzing and optimizing the paths beginning from the RS set.

As a result system can control the game as the A player. It contains two co - operating Mealy's automata. The first one has 4 states and describes the RS set of the game. The second automaton has 22 states, describing all the other possible paths, optimized for the side of A player. Details about this special control can be obtained from the author or from the paper Dyduch (1981).

Expert control is based on the modeling of choosing the control decisions rather then on detailed, dynamic model of the controlled object, as it take place in classical control systems. The paper shows the advantages of the special formula of expert knowledge base, which can be utilize in control of some DEs. Description of the special set of controlled object states is the main part of the base. This set is called Rs set and serves as a basis for the control and optimization.

It is difficult to find the RS set automatically, but it can be done by human expert of control. That is thanks to human mind features such as: inclination to generalization, seeking symmetry and analogy in nature, easy ordering of fragmentary and uncompleted data.

Existence of an optimal sampling frequency for LQ-controlled economic systems

Jacob Engwerda   
Department of Econometrics   
Tilburg University   
P.O. Box 90153, 5000 LE Tilburg   
The Netherlands

Abstract: In this paper we present sufficient conditions for the existence of an optimal frequency for sampling an economic system. We assume that the underlying economy is described by a linear continuous-time system containing an exogenous component, and that the policymakers want to minimize a social welfare function. This welfare function is a continuous-time quadratic tracking equation over an infinite planning horizon with positive semi-definite weighting matrices.
Introduction

It will be clear that increasing the sampling frequency of an economy brings on additional costs of data gathering, whereas the additional information that can be extracted from this data for the system will, in general, decrease on an increasing sampling frequency (since e.g. the data is corrupted by noise). Therefore, the problem arises to weigh out the advantage of an increase in the performance of the system and the additional cost of data gathering.

There is an extensive ongoing literature dealing with various problems concerning sampled data systems (see e.g. Astrom et al. (1990) and Engwerda et al. (1992) for references). Main research performed in this area has been done in the field of control engineering, in particular from a digital control point of view. However, usually, the considered systems do not contain exogenous deterministic variables, a characteristic which typically occurs in macro-economic systems. Furthermore the fact that extra sampling brings on additional costs is also a point that is rarily addressed to in this literature. Both these points motivate therefore the study of this paper: how often should a controlled economic system be sampled.

The answer to this question depends, amongst othors, on which performance criterion (c.q. goals) the policymakers are striving for. We will assume that they are looking for a policy which succeeds in tracking an a priori specified path for their target variables. Furthermore, the policy has to satisfy some additional requirements like being robust for unmodeled disturbances and staying close to some prespecified policy path (see e.g. Pitchford et al. (1977), Preston et al. (1982) and Engwerda (1990) for references). In Engwerda (1990) this economic stabilization problem is formalized as an infinite horizon quadratic tracking problem and solved in case the considered system is discrete time. We will take up this approach for sampled continuous time systems. First we formalize the continuous time control problem, and then we transform it into an equivalent discrete time problem which can be solved using the analysis of Engwerda et al. (1992). An explicit expression for the performance criterion is presented under some smooth conditions. This expression is used to draw conclusions w.r.t. the existence question of an optimal sampling frequency for the system.

1 Introduction

We investigate the problem of finding the best subclique of a given size in a complete edgeweighted graph. This problem was formulated by Späth [S 85], who reports numerical results indicating that simple exchange heuristics perform very well on the problem. On the other hand, our problem is closely related to the wellstudied clique partition problem (cf. [FSS 87], [W 86], [GW 89]), for which cutting plane algorithms appear to be quite succesfuland give tight bounds on the quality of heuristic solutions. Indeed, our problem is a partition problem where exactly one non-trivial block of a given size is allowed.

Dijkhuizen and Faigle [DF 93] developed a cutting plane algorithm for the subclique problem. Although the cutting planes could be viewed as LP-relaxations for the polytope generated by feasible (0-1)-edge-incidence vectors, the algorithm gave very poor results and typically did not even approximate the true objective function value. It is therefore a challenging problem to device an algorithm for the subclique problem that allows us to evaluate the quality of a heuristic solution by giving a good bound on the true optimum.

LP-relaxations that - in spite of added variables — are very fast to solve by any LP-solver. Our LP-formulations, moreover, allowed a Lagrangean relaxation that for each choice of parameters can be solved by a direct greedy algorithm.

It was hoped that also the heuristics could be coupled with the Lagrange relaxation in order to enhance their performance. While it turned out that this approach did not noticable improve the heuristics, we could observe that lifting the problem into higher dimensions had a substantial positive effect on the quality of the LPrelaxation. Even so, the problem is very sensitive with respect to LP-relaxations that are not chosen carefully.

8 Conclusions & Improvements

We showed that the formulation of a combinatorial optimization problem has great influence in numerical experiments. Formulations which seem more difficult in the first place can sometimes give a better approximation of the solution polytope. Lifting a formulation can yield such an improved formulation.

In the case of the maximum sub-clique problem lifting yields better results. The larger the sub-cliques, the better the heuristics performed and for large sub-cliques we were able to prove optimality in most cases.

Some other facet inducing inequalities could be added to the LP-formulation in order to make it more tight. However, the number of the facet inducing inequalities we excluded is very large. For example, the number of Z-inequalities is of the order $\pmb { n } ^ { 4 }$ . Adding all these inequalities would result in an intractably large LP-formulation. Therefore, a cutting plane approach using the third formulation should probably give some improvements.

INTRODUCTION

In a magisterial work Galor (1992) has analysed the equilibrium dynamics of a two-sector overlapping-generations model with one homogeneous capital good. In contrast to the wellknown result that the dynamics of capital accumulation is asymptotically stable if the consumption good sector is relatively more capital-intensive than the investment good sector (see Uzawa (1961) and Inada (1966) on non-overlapping-generations two-sector growth models with one homogeneous capital good), Galor (1992) detected the saddle-path property of the equilibrium dynamics which is characteristic of (also one-sector) optimal growth models and multi-sector descriptive growth models with heterogeneous capital goods.

This extented abstract reports the approach and main results of a paper (see Farmer, 1993) which analyses the equilibrium dynamics of a specific two-sector overlapping-generations economy with two heterogeneous capital goods and sectoral immobile capital services.

Because of the heterogeneity of capital the equilibrium dynamics of the capital stocks and the relative capital prices is higher dimensional than the two-dimensional equilibrium dynamics in Galor's paper.

In order to able to reduce the dimension of the equilibrium dynamics in our model and to be able to apply the fine techniques which Galor (1992) has developed Morishima's (1977) assumption of static expectations of relative capital prices is introduced. But only the additional assumption that the production elasticity of capital in the $\mathbf { x } \cdot \mathbf { \partial }$ -sector equals 0.5 makes the equilibrium dynamics two-dimensional.

Under theses assumptions the saddle-path stability properties of the capital equilibrium dynamics in the proposed model setting are precisely exhibited and the differences from Galor's results are enumerated.

1. Exact matroid parity

The main problem we consider looks for a base of exact value in an integrally weighted represented matroid subject to parity conditions: we call this problem Exact Parity Base (XPB). The problem is NP-complete since it generalizes Subset Sum [Garey & Johnson (1978). It is however solvable in random pseudo-polynomial (r.p.p.) time and algorithms for doing this are reviewed in this work. Challenging open problems are solving the corresponding optimization problem by a (random) polynomial algorithm and solving XPB in pseudo-polynomial time: this is sofar possible only for some special cases [Barahona & Pulleyblank (1987)].

We are given a matroid $( S , { \pmb { \mathscr { F } } } )$ , where $\pmb { S }$ is the ground set and $\pmb { \mathscr { F } }$ is the family of the independent sets. We assume that the matroid has even rank $\mathbf { 2 } n$ and is represented over the rationals by a matrix $\pmb { M }$ . This means that: 1) there is a one-to-one correspondence between elements of $\pmb { S }$ and columns of $\pmb { M }$ ; 2) independent sets in $\pmb { \mathscr { F } }$ correspond to sets of linearly independent columns of $M ; 3 ]$ a base of the matroid correspond to a full-rank square submatrix of $\pmb { M }$ .

We further assume that the elements of the ground set are an even number $\scriptstyle 2 m$ and are partitioned into $^ { \pmb { m } }$ pairs. Hence $M = ( a _ { 1 } \mid b _ { 1 } \mid \ldots \mid a _ { m } \mid b _ { m } )$ , where for $j = 1 , \ldots , m$ , the symbol ${ \pmb a } _ { j }$ (or $\pmb { b _ { j } }$ not only denotes a column of $\pmb { M }$ , but also the corresponding element of $\pmb { S }$ , and $\{ a _ { j } , b _ { j } \}$ indicates the $j \cdot$ -th pair of elements. A base of the form $\{ a _ { j _ { 1 } } , b _ { j _ { 1 } } , \ldots , a _ { j _ { n } } , b _ { j _ { n } } \}$ is called a parity base of $\pmb { M }$ , and is identified by the set $X = \{ j _ { 1 } , \dots , j _ { n } \} \subseteq \{ 1 , \dots , m \}$ .

Should some elements of $\pmb { M }$ be noninteger it would be immediate to obtain another $\mathbf { 2 } n \times \mathbf { 2 } m$ matrix, having integer elements, and still representing $( s , \pmb { \mathscr { F } } )$ . Therefore, in the sequel we shall assume without loss of generality that the matroid will be represented by (and identified with) an integer matrix $\pmb { M }$ . Let us first remark that multi-weighted versions.of the exact problems reviewed in this work can also be addressed and solved with r.p.p. algorithms. Another remark is that some exact versions of min-cost (integral) fow problems are solvable by r.p.p. algorithms because of the close relationship between flow networks and matching optimization theory. In fact, it is well-known [Papadimitriou $\pmb { \mathscr { k } }$ Steiglitz (1982)] that the Minimum Cost Flow problem (minimizing the cost of a flow of prescribed value between a source and a sink, in a capacitated network) can be polynomially reduced to the Uncapacitated Transportation problem (minimizing the cost of a flow between sources and sinks, in an uncapacitated, bipartite network), which in turn can be transformed (via a pseudo-polynomial reduction [Lawler (1976)]) into the Minimum Cost Perfect Matching problem (minimizing the cost of a perfect matching in a bipartite graph). These two reductions are easily seen to preserve the costs of the corresponding integral solutions, and therefore they also apply to the exact versions of the same problems provided the underlying graph is acyclic.

From a practical point of view it is very important to explore if algebraic methods of the kind surveyed here could help solving optimization problems more efficiently: an important step in this direction would be to find a r.p. algorithm for finding a parity base of maximum weight in a given represented matroid.

Introduction

Existing exchange rate theory concentrates on the two-country framework. But there is little empirical support for the validity of theoretical models such as monetary or asset market approaches to exchange rate determination. Moreover, only few papers discuss exchange rate behaviour within a multi-country framework. Therefore this paper instead focuses on the joint behaviour of five major bilateral U.S. dollar exchange rates since the breakdown of the Bretton-Woods system.

Considering the most important industrial countries the question arises, whether there exist valid long-run and/or short-run relationships among their exchange rates and, if being the case, whether plausible interpretations can be offered. Within this context it is also of an interest to evaluate aspects and influences of the Exchange Rate Mechanism of the European Monetary System (EMS).

Among others, multivariate cointegration methods are applied in this study. If a set of exchange rates is cointegrated then, although each series may be individually nonstationary (e.g. integrated of order one, I(1)), there must exist at least one linear combination which is stationary (I(0)). And this linear combination can be thought of as a long-run relationship where the exchange rate series tend to move together over time (see Engle and Granger [1987] for further details).

Empirical results and discussion

In this study we used bilateral quarterly nominal exchange rates between the United States and Germany, the United Kingdom, Japan, Switzerland and France. The empirical analysis was performed for the five-variable vector $\mathbf { x ^ { \prime } } { = } ( \mathbf { D E M } / \mathbf { U S D }$ ,GBP/USD, JPY/USD, CHF/USD, FRF/USD) and all series were put in logarithmic form. We conducted two cointegration exercises, one for the time before the inception of the exchange rate mechanism of the EMS $( 1 9 7 3 \textrm { - } 1 9 7 9 )$ and one for the period from 1979 till the end of 1991.

The empirical results, reported in table 1, indicate that there exist stationary long-run relationships between the levels of these exchange rates. For the EMS period both tests, the $\lambda _ { \operatorname* { m a x } }$ as well as the trace statistics, suggest one significant cointegration vector on the $5 \%$ level, whereas for the pre-EMS period this evidence is only supported by the trace test.

Imposing several likelihood ratio tests on the form of the cointegration vectors (table 2) for the different periods leads to further results: Since the inception of the EMS the German mark-U.S. dollar rate together with the British pound and Swiss franc rate are cointegrated and form a stationary linear combination. The exchange rate between the U.S. dollar and the EMS currency French franc adjusts to this long-run relationship but has no influence upon the form of the cointegration vector. Including Italian lira in the vector leads to the same conclusions as for the French franc, these EMS currencies adjust to the cointegration vector but have no influence on the form of $\beta$ .On the contrary the Japanese Yen-U.S. dollar rate is relatively independent from the other exchange rates. Concerning the pre-EMS period the DEM/USD-rate is the only series were both hypotheses, for weak exogeniety as well as for long-run exclusion from $\beta$ , are rejected, but further tests are inconclusive.

Dynamic simulations using forecast error variance decompositions and impulse responses (see Sims [1980]) were also applied. The results indicate that impulses in the DEM/UsD-rate are followed by similar reactions of the other series whereas this is not observed vice versa. This evidence is stronger within the EMS period than in the pre-EMS period. Since the start of the EMS a major part of the variability of forecast errors of all exchange rates except the JPY/USD-rate are explained by innovations in the DEM/USDrate (more than $40 \%$ over all forecast horizons of up to 24 steps). In the pre-EMS period own innovations in the exchange rate series account for a larger part of the variance of forecast errors.

It can be summarized that our results support the evidence of an increasing importance of the German mark-U.S. dollar rate for the other European exchange rates on the one hand and a relatively independent role of the Japanese Yen-U.S. dollar rate on the other hand.
