HUMAN CAPITAL AND INTERNATIONAL CAPITAL FLOWS
Thomas Gries, University of Göttingen, Germany

In the traditional Heckscher-Ohlin type of trade and growth theory, capital mobility is not integrated. Embodied in products, factor mobility takes place by the way of commodity trade. As a consequence, H.-O. theory implies factor price equalization. Therefore, there are only few proposition to combine Heckscher-Ohlin trade theory and international factor mobility. The first approach is proposed in a model, which is frequently called the Kemp-Jones model [Ruffin (1984)]. The reason for capital mobility in this kind of model is a deviation in productivity. This recardian type of argument can not only imply trade, but also international mobility of capital. A second incentive for capital mobility was brought up by Fischer/Frenkel (1972). In the Fischer/Frenkel approach installation costs of capital induce capital mobility. Generally, capital mobility was discussed more as a problem of monetary macroeconomics than as component of pure trade theory. In the subsequent paragraphs a different view of integrating capital mobility into H.-O. trade theory is suggested [see also Gries (1993)]. Four characteristics modifying standard neoclassical open economy growth theory are important:

- The small open economy produces with three factors of production (labor, real capital and human capital). The production process described by the foreign exchange production function [see Findlay (1973,1984)]. Real capital and human capital are accumulated over time and labor is exogenously growing. A country's economic fundamentals are characterized by the local immobile factor endowment [characteristic endowment], namely labor and human capital. Human capital is identified as the 'peoples skills'. Human capital is 'embodied' in the population, and therefore is an immobile factor.   
Making use of results well known in labor economics, human capital and real capital are poor substitutes in the production process. In a survey on human capital Hamermesh (1986) finds: "Perhapss the most consistent finding is that non production workers (presumable skilled labor) are less easily substitutable for physical capital than are production workers (unskilled labor). Indeed, a number of the studies find that nonproduction workers and physical capital are $\pmb { p } \mathrm { - }$ complements. This supports Rosens' (1968) and Griliches (1969) results on capital- skill complementary hypothesis"(Hamermesh 1986, p. 461).

- The accumulation of human capital is determined by portfolio decisions and an intertemporal optimal program. Accumulated local human capital determines the local requirements of real capital. Real capital is supplied totally elastic on world markets and employed on a 'normal' level of utilization. Real capital will never be the limiting factor for a potential momentary rise in production.

These general characterizations lead to a standard intertemporal optimization problem. From the first order conditions we obtain an extended Ramsey Rule and a steady state solution for the economy's optimal per capita wealth and human capital intensity. From these variables all major variables can be derived (e.g. income per capita, the position of specialization and comparative advantages, international capital flows and international factor price deviations).

The most interesting results are summarized as follows: A country originally can be defined by the 'characteristic parameters'. The country's 'characteristic parameters' (namely the rate of time preference, the elasticity of intertemporal substitution in consumption and the vector of portfolio parameters) determine intertemporal accumulation, portfolio decision, and eventually the country's 'characteristic endowment'. The 'characteristic endowment' determines the international position of comparative advantage, guides the direction of flows of mobile real capital and determines the incentives for a potential mobility of normally immobile factors.

a. Since we used the foreign exchange production function, every human capital intensity represents a certain sector. Therefore a country's optimal relative factor abundance defines the pattern of specialization and trade. In this respect the model is a dynamic generalized version of H.-O. theory. Trade is induced through factor endowments, which are determined by optimal accumulation and portfolio decisions.

b. The portfolio decision determines the local endowment of human capital and the potential supply of mobile real capital. If the stock of accumulated human capital is small, little real capital is needed in domestic production. For a given world interest rate the required real capital is absorbed from internal and external sources. The domestic excess supply (demand) is provided to (taken from) the world markets of real capital. As a result of optimal intertemporal and portfolio decisions a country may accumulate little human capital, and therefore will attract little real capital. The lack of domestic opportunities to invest will channel wealth accumulation to world markets. A capital outflow can be observed even for a poor country with little capital endowment.

c. As a property of a homogeneous production function, every human capital intensity implies a different marginal productivity. Different countries with different 'characteristic endowments' and different optimal human capital abundance realize different marginal rates of substitution. Therefore, the factor price equalization theorem does not hold. Steady state specialization patterns imply factor prices differentials and generate permanent incentives for the mobility of normally immobile factors like labor and human capital.

Several fields of policy implications can be suggested: Human capital accumulation: Human capital is the central element of this approach. The portfolio decision on human capital accumulation is a key component in determining a country's 'characteristic endowment', and -as a result- the country's general economic performance. Therefore, political implications are plain. All policies rising human capital accumulation will attract additional real capital for domestic production and improve the general economic situation. Among many other factors determining the portfolio decisions, the distribution of wealth and income may be an important parameter.

Capital flight: The expression capital flight is usually associated with capital moving in a direction not expected from looking at the real economic fundamentals. The outflow of capital from poor countries with poor capital endowments and expected high returns is often regarded as capital fight. In this approach the mechanism is different: If the stock of accumulated human capital is small, little real capital is needed in domestic production. Little human capital attracts only a small amount of real capital. Capital outflow can be observed even for a poor country with little capital endowment. The flight of capital indicates a lack of opportunities to invest due to missing human capital.

With respect to international transfer payments a second implication seems important: Internal or external development policies that simply increase the availability of capital without strong implication for human capital accumulation, will have little success. Simple transfers of money will not be effective as developing strategy.

Direct investments Permanent factor price differentials due to different pattern of specialization induce incentives for the mobility of normally immobile factors. The larger the difference in human capital intensity between two countries, the larger the factor price differential and the stronger the incentives for factor mobility. When investors from industrialized countries notice large returns on human capital, bundles of the general immobile human capital and complementary real capital will move via direct investment to developing countries. Human capital may become partly mobile by direct investments. An increasing international migration of labor is a signal for a partly moving labor force.

Abstract

Earlier work (Hammond, $1 9 8 8 8 ,$ b) on dynamically consistent "consequentialist" behaviour in decision trees was unable to treat zero probability events satisfactorily. Here the rational probability functions considered in Hammond (1992), as well as other non-Archimedean probabilities, are incorporated into decision trees. As before, the consequentialist axioms imply the existence of a preference ordering satisfying independence. In the case of rational probability functions, those axioms, together with continuity and a new refinement assumption, imply the maximization of a somewhat novel lexicographic expected utility preference relation. This is equivalent to maximization of expected utility in the ordering of the relevant non-Archimedean field.

1. Introduction and Outline
1.1. Consequentialism in Single Person Decision Theory

The consequentialist approach to single-person decision theory, with uncertainty described by specified objective probabilities, was expounded in Hammond (1988a, b). In fact the latter paper also deals with states of nature and subjective probabilities. Here non-Archimedean subjective probabilities will not be considered at all, but left for later work.

This consequentialist approach is based on three axioms. Of these, the first requires behaviour to be well defined for an (almost) unrestricted domain of finite decision trees with: (i) decision nodes where the agent makes a move; (ii) chance nodes at which random moves occur with specified positive probabilities; (ii) and terminal nodes which result in a single consequence within a specified domain of relevant consequences. It follows that behaviour in any such tree results in a set of probability distributions over consequences. The second axiom requires behaviour to be dynamically consistent in continuation subtrees, in the sense that behaviour at any decision node is the same in a subtree as in a full tree. And the third is the "consequentialist choice" axiom, requiring that the set of possible random consequences of behaviour in any decision tree of the domain be explicable as the choice of desirable random consequences from the set of random consequences that the tree makes feasible.

The earlier work then showed how these three consequentialist axioms imply the existence of a preference ordering (i.e., a complete and transitive weak preference relation) defined on the space of random consequences. Moreover, this ordering must satisfy Samuelson's (1952) independence axiom. In this way, two of the most important and even controversial axioms of standard decision theory become implications of apparently weaker and possibly more appealing axioms of the consequentialist reformulation. Thereafter, an extra condition of continuity of behaviour with respect to changing probabilities leads to the preference ordering having an expected utility representation.
1.2. Consequentialism in Game Theory

This paper is the second in a series whose purpose is to extend the scope of this consequentialist approach from single-person decision trees to multi-person extensive games. In fact, a decision tree is nothing more than & one person "consequentialist extensive game" of perfect and complete information. The difference from the usual notion of a game in extensive form comes about because no payoffs are specified. Instead, terminal nodes are assumed to result in pure consequences within the specified domain of consequences. Then the existence of a payoff function defined on this domain of consequences is not assumed, but becomes an important implication of consequentialism.

The main obstacle to this extension of consequentialism comes about because the earlier single person theory excludes zero probability chance moves - it is in this sense that the domain of allowable decision trees is almost rather than fully unrestricted. Such a restriction is excusable in single person decision theory where there are no good reasons for retaining zero probability events. In multi-person game theory, however, testing to see whether a particular profile of strategies for each player constitutes an equilibrium involves seeing what happens when any player deviates and then all the other players react according to their presumed equilibrium strategies. Yet these reactions are behaviour in the face of events which are supposed to have probability zero, since that is supposed to be the probability of any player deviating from equilibrium. So one is faced with the need to update probabilities in a Bayesian manner even though a zero probability event has occurred. For this reason, the zero probability restriction makes it difcult to apply consequentialist decision theory to multi-person games in a way that yields subgame perfect or other kinds of refined equilibria. The task of this work is to remove this burdensome restriction.

Not surprisingly, the zero probability problem has already led several game theorists to extend the space of ordinary probabilities in various ways. In particular, Selten (1975) and Myerson (1978) considered "trembles." Kreps and Wilson (1982), and then Blume, Brandenburger and Dekel (1991a, b) considered lexicographic hierarchies of probabilities. Myerson (1986) considered complete conditional probability systems. Finally, McLennan (1989a, b) considered logarithmic likelihood ratio functions whose values can be infinite. Hammond (1992) shows that all of these different extensions, when suitably formulated, are in fact equivalent to each other, and also to a particular space of "conditional rational probability functions."

In decision trees, it is usual to specify independent probabilities at each separate chance node. After all, in principle any causes of dependence can and should be modelled within the structure of the tree itself. Then, however, it is particularly important to be sure that the entire joint distribution of all chance moves is determined uniquely from the marginal probability distributions over the chance moves at each separate chance node of the decision tree. In the case of ordinary probabilities, this is trivial because joint probabilities are found by simply multiplying appropriate marginal probabilities. Yet Hammond (1992) also shows how the equivalent sets of extended probabilities mentioned in the previous paragraph all fail this crucial test. That is, many different joint extended probability distributions over nature's possible strategies in the decision tree can arise from the same collection of independent marginal probability distributions over nature's moves at different chance nodes. This is because such extended probabilities lack the structure of an algebraic field in which the operation of multiplication is well defined.
1.3. Consequentialism with Non-Archimedean Probabilities

So it seems necessary to work with a richer space of extended probabilities, for which multiplication and other algebraic field operations are well defined. There should also be an ordering relation rich enough to give meaning to the statements that probabilities are non-negative or positive and that they are larger or smaller. Now, within an ordered field such as the real line $\Re .$ , the Archimedean axiom states that, for any positive number $\pmb { r }$ , there is an integer $\pmb { n }$ for which $\pmb { n } \pmb { r } > 1$ Overcoming the zero probability problem seems to require some kind of non-Archimedean ordered field in which this axiom is violated. Obviously, any such field must have at least one positive "infinitesimal" element e with the property that $\pmb { n } \in < 1$ for every positive integer $\pmb { \mathcal { n } }$ , even though  is positive. It follows that any such positive infinitesimal must be smaller than any positive real number; in particular, it cannot be a real number itself.

Section 2 below therefore begins by briefly reviewing the definition and key properties of non-Archimedean ordered fields. Particular attention is paid to the elementary field $\Re ( \epsilon )$ whose use was recommended in Hammond (1992). Its members are rational functions in a single infinitesimal variable denoted by e. For any finite support in an appropriate sample space, Section 2 proceeds to consider a corresponding set of elementary non-Archimedean probabilities. In the case when the field is $\Re ( \epsilon )$ , such probabilities are called "rational probability functions" (or RPF's).

It then becomes natural to consider in Section 3 decision trees having RPF's or other non-Archimedean instead of ordinary positive probabilities attached to each chance move in the tree. Behaviour in such trees gives rise to non-Archimedean consequences — i.e., RPF's or more general non-Archimedean conditional probability distributions over the domain of relevant consequences. Within the corresponding domain of finite non-Archimedean consequentialist decision trees the previous consequentialist axioms can be applied almost without change. Most implications are also the same as in Hammond (1988a, b), since virtually all the arguments in those two papers apply to probabilities taking values in a general ordered field, and not just to those taking values in the Archimedean ordered field R. In particular, the three "consequentialist" assumptions mentioned in Section 1.1 imply the existence of a revealed preference ordering. And this ordering must satisfy Samuelson's (1952) independence axiom.

The set of preference orderings that satisfy the independence axiom on the space of relevant non-Archimedean random consequences is actually very large. Many such orderings, however, pay no attention to the interpretation of e as an infinitesimal. In addition, recall that the only motivation which has been offered for non-Archimedean probabilities is to resolve the zero probability problem mentioned in Section 1.2. Now, were zero probabilities to be allowed, the problem they create is that the usual decision criteria generate behaviour sets that are too large. Accordingly, Section 4 proposes an additional and rather natural refinement axiom. This requires that in any decision tree whose chance moves have non-Archimedean probabilities differing only infinitesimally from those in an ordinary decision tree with real probabilities, behaviour with non-Archimedean probabilities should refine that with ordinary probabilities. It is then shown how this refinement axiom implies that the strict preference relation over non-Archimedean random consequences must be refine the corresponding relation over ordinary random consequences. And, in the special case of RPF's, there must be a unique extension which can be regarded as a lexicographic hierarchy of preference orderings over ordinary random consequences.

Another part of the theory where the non-Archimedean field structure makes some difference is in the continuity condition set out in Section 5 as a necessary and sufficient condition for expected utility maximization. Within a general non-Archimedean field the construction used by Herstein and Milnor (1953) and others to determine the real values of a von Neumann-Morgenstern utility function is invalid, since it relies upon a continuity or "Archimedean" axiom. Nevertheless, the theory presented here is meant to extend the earlier standard theory of expected utility and subjective probability, so it seems reasonable to retain this Archimedean axiom for the subspace of decision trees with real valued positive probabilities. In combination with the earlier axioms concerning behaviour in decision trees, this restricted continuity axiom implies that, when probabilities are described by $\mathbf { R P F ^ { \prime } s } ,$ . all the preference orderings making up the lexicographic hierarchy described in Section 4 can be represented by the expected value of the same von Neumann-Morgenstern utility function. A particular feature of the new lexicographic expected utility criterion is that it generalizes the standard criterion presented by Blume, Brandenburger and Dekel (1991a, b). For example, it allows and even requires expected utility hierarchies of differing lengths to be compared.

Now, the expectation of any real valued utility function with respect to some non-Archimedean probability distribution is itself & member of the non-Archimedean ordered field introduced in Section 2. As Section 6 shows, the new lexicographic expected utility criterion is equivalent to maximizing non-Archimedean expected utility with respect to the ordering of the field $\Re ( \epsilon )$ in which RPF's take their values.

Finally, Section 7 gathers together all the consequentialist axioms and their implications that have been set out in previous sections. They imply the existence of a unique class of cardinally equivalent von Neumann-Morgenstern utility functions such that consequentialist behaviour must be "non-Archimedean" Bayesian rational in the sense that it maximizes the lexicographic expected utility preference criterion set out in Section 4. It is shown, that BoltzMann-like equations allow the formulation of a very general model for behavioral changes. This model takes into account spontaneous (or externally induced) behavioral changes and behavioral changes by pair interactions. As most important social pair interactions imitative and avoidance processes are distinguished. The resulting model turns out to include as special cases many theoretical concepts of the social sciences, e.the multinomial logit model, the logistic equation, the gravity model and the game dynamical equations.

They are not only given by external factors (the environment) but also by the interactions of the individuals. Variations of the individual behavior are taken into account by diffusion coefficients. The force model can e.g. be applied to group dynamics, opinion formation, and the behavior of pedestrians.

1 Motivation

The traditional approach to the intertemporal portfolio and consumption problem is to determine a portfolio that maximizes the expected value of consumption for a given utility function. However, this approach has been criticized in several ways. Empirical results revealed severe and persistent violations of the underlying von Neumann-Morgenstern-axioms of rational choice (see for example Allais and Hagen (1979)). The diversity of objectives pursued by an investor when making his portfolio decision may not be adequately capturable in single utility numbers (see for example Sen (1990)). If more than one decision maker is involved the utility function of a 'representative investor' has to be found. This leads to the problem of aggregating different utilities and it is far from obvious how that should be done.

An alternative way to solve the portfolio problem is as follows. In a first step principles are formulated reflecting the objectives pursued by investors and acceptable to the majority of decision makers involved. A second step is to prove the existence of portfolio stategies satisfying these principles. In accordance with this approach we present a portfolio decision based on two principles: absence of arbitrage and value preservation. Absence of arbitrage assures that the portfolio stategies employed are dynamically efficient. Value preservation means that the present value of consumption has to be sustained over all time periods planned. While the noarbitrage-profit principle is self-evident, the value preservation principle seems to be appropriate especially for institutional investors, like investment companies.

1 Introduction

Unit squares having their vertices at integerpoints in the Cartesian plane are called cells. A polyomino is a connected finite subset of cells in the grid. The number of cells is the area of the polyomino. The length of the boundary is called its perimeter.

Polyominoes have been studied  essentially - from two points of view. The question how to tile the plane with polyominoes is adressed (among others) in [Ber81], [Con90], [Mar91]. On the other hand several authors treat enumerative questions concerning polyominoes (cf. [Ben74], [Pol69]). The asymptotic behaviour of certain types of polyominoes has several applications to problems arising in percolation theory in statistical physic (cf. [Gutt88], [Lin88]). For a survey on recent results concerning the enumeration of polyominoes see [Del91].

A polyomino is called convex, if the intersection with any horizontal or vertical line is connected. A few years ago M.-P. Delest and G. Viennot ([Del84]) found that the number of convex polyominoes of perimeter $2 n + 8$ is given by $P _ { 2 n + 8 } = ( 2 n + 1 1 ) 4 ^ { n } - 4 { \left( 2 n + 1 \right) } { \left( { 2 n } \right) }$ The proof of this formula is not bijective and thus does not provide a possibility to generate them at random.

In this talk we present a new recursion formula for the number $P _ { n }$ of convex polyominoes of given perimeter $\pmb { n }$ .We will construct a bijection from $\{ 1 , \ldots , P _ { n } \}$ into the set of polyominoes with perimeter $\pmb { n }$ . Furthermore, we suggest a simple probabilistic algorithm with linear running time for this task.

1. INTRODUCTION

The problem of determining the convex hul of a simple polygon has received a lot of attention in the early eighties. The first linear time algorithm for this task was proposed by Sklansky (1972). Sklansky's Algorithm can be described as follows:

Start at an extreme point of the polygon. Delete all left turns while moving around the polygon in clockwise direction. After each step backtrack until the path from the starting point to the point currently considered given by the not (yet) deleted points has right turns only.

The problem with this algorithm is that the lastmentioned path may become self-intersecting and that the algorithm therefore fails in some cases. Its asset is the simplicity of its idea and that it requires only very little global information about the given simple polygon in advance - its orientation and an extreme point.

The algorithm presented in this note supplements Sklansky's algorithm in a simple way assuring that the current path from the starting point to the currently considered point is always simple and consists of right turns only.

Like Sklansky's and different from other (correct) $O ( n )$ -algorithms for computing the convex hull of a simple polygon our algorithm only requires that the simple polygon be given in clockwise orientation and that the starting point is known to be an extreme point of the convex hull. From then on the decision whether or not to delete a point is based solely on local information. Our algorithm thus can not only be regarded as being simpler than the algorithms in McCallum, Avis (1979), Ghosh, Shyamasundar (1983), Bhattacharya, Elgindy (1984), it also provides new insight into the structure of the problem.

The problem of transporting goods from a set of supply points (factories) to a set of demand points (customers) so as to minimize linear transportation costs is well known and very efficient solution methods exist. In the well-known facility location problem one also includes fixed charges for the supply points. On the other hand, in ordinary transportation problems, stochastic demand has been introduced and modelled by convex costs, yielding the Stochastic Transportation Problem, [STP], solved by for example the methods in Cooper and LeBlanc (1977) and Holmberg and Jörnsten (1984). However, the simultaneous use of these generalizations has recieved little attention until now. Only a few suggestions for solution methods can be found, LeBlanc (1977), Franca and Luna (1982). In this paper we consider generalizing this problem even further, by introducing general concave costs at the supply points, as well as convex costs at the demand points. Fixed charges are not the only cost structures that occur when producing goods at a factory. Economies of scale very often yield other concave cost functions.

Introduction

Finding faults in a technical or medical system is a well known problem where much experience was gained from several applications within the last decade (Horm, 1990). Most of them are interactively used, rulebased systems. Frequently appearing symptoms are related to hypothized faults. On the other hand there are monitoring systems which observe e.g. technical processes or human patients. Monitoring systems generate messages periodically (e.g. oil-temperature and oil-pressure in a car) or in special predefined situations (e.g door is open while driving). The increasing use of monitoring systems which leads to a large number of to be diagnosed messages demands the use of a combination of fault diagnosis and monitoring systems. However the combination of the different approaches leads to several problems. Temporary relations between symptoms have to be considered in an appropriate representation of faults.

The temporal order of symptoms is not observed in traditional "snapshot diagnosis". But ordering of symptoms can be used to differ between faults. Because of causal relations the situations Symptom "S1 before S2" can be interpreted differently from the situation "S2 before S1". • Because of the spatial range of the machine and because of the delay of some reactions faults and their related symptoms does not appear at the same moment but within an interval. The question now is to choose the range of the interval in which all symptoms have to appear.

Additional problems arise concerning the operating of the system. The symptoms of different monitors arrive like a stream of signals. They have to be interpreted continuously. Questions apply to the synchronization of the incoming signals and the diagnosis system.
When does the diagnosis has to be started ? How are symptoms treated, which appear during a diagnosis ?

Finally monitoring is not only made to enter into a log, but to recognize critical situations and react to it immediately. So there are requirements that systems should react in real-time, i.e. within a predefined interval.
Concept

The relationship between faults $F _ { i }$ and Symptoms $s _ { j }$ is often described with rules similar to the following: ${ \cal F } _ { 1 } \Leftarrow$ . The fault is defined by a set of symptoms. However there is no ordering of symptoms, nor a statement of an interval in which the symptoms have to arrive. Taking a formal-language-perspective (Hopcroft et al., 1988) the set of symptoms can be interpreted as several words. Each symptom is interpreted as a letter, and each combination of all symptoms $s _ { I } , \ldots s _ { j }$ is an accepted word of the language $F _ { I }$ . Changing from sets to languages an ordering is introduced. As formal languages have there equivalents within finite state machine (FSM), these machines can be used to analyze the incoming symptoms. E.g. the rule $F _ { 1 } \Leftarrow S _ { 1 } , S _ { 2 } , S _ { 3 }$ the language $F _ { 1 } = \{ S _ { 1 } S _ { 2 } S _ { 3 } , S _ { 1 } S _ { 3 } S _ { 2 } , . . . , S _ { 3 } S _ { 2 } S _ { 1 } \}$ and the FSM in figure 1 all represent the same relationship between faults and symptoms (Hopcroft et al., 1988, Dorn, 1992). The FSM has to be interpreted in the following way. The circle represent states and the arrow possible transitions between the states. The empty state is the starting state and the bold state is the finite state. If a symptom $s _ { j }$ arrives and an transition labeled with this symptom leads from the actual to another state, one can move to this new state. If a symptom leads to the finite state the fault is detected. The FSM in figure 1 represents all combination of sequences of three symptoms.

Combining diagnosis and monitoring systems it has to be possible to declare a time window (res e al 1991, (Nejlt al 19), a pre-defin interval in which all symptomsindii a fault have to arrive. The range of the window has to be set to the maximum expected time period where symptoms relevant to the fault will receive. The time window is started with the first incoming symptom, and is closed either by arriving a finite state within the finite automaton or if the time of the window is expired. It is no problem to put a whole FSM into one time window. Additionally time windows can be used to describe temporal constraints to parts of the FSM. If e.g. $s _ { I } , s _ { 2 }$ have to arrive within 10 seconds and ${ \pmb S } _ { 3 }$ has to arrive within 6 seconds after the FSM is started, that means $F _ { 1 } \Leftarrow S _ { 1 } , S _ { 2 } , S _ { 3 } ; S _ { 2 } < S _ { 3 } ; S _ { 1 } , S _ { 2 } \epsilon [ 0 s : 1 0 s ] , S _ { 3 } \epsilon [ 0 s : 6 s ] $ this can be described within the FSM by labeling the transitions (cf. fig. 3). When the next symptom arrives the time is compared relative to the time window. If the symptom arrives in time, one changes the state as before. If the symptom arrives out of time, the window is closed. It's important to notice that the time has to be labeled not to the state but to the transition. If a state can be reached by two ways, sometimes the transitions have different time-labels, i.e. a possible label for the state would be ambiguous (in fact in some complicate cases even the labels for the transitions are ambiguous and must be declared and corrected at run-time). E.g. in figure 3 the last symptom can either be $s _ { l }$ or ${ \pmb S } _ { 3 }$ .If $s _ { 3 }$ is the last symptom, the time interval has to be set to 6 seconds. If $s _ { I }$ is the last symptom, ${ \pmb S } _ { 3 }$ is already received in time and so the weaker interval is relevant.
Using labeled FSMs the representation of faults and their related symptoms in consideration of temporal ordering and intervals is possible. Moreover the FSMs lead to a simple implementation.
Implementation

For each fault a FSM is implemented (Hüsgens, 1993). Each FSM is represented as a graph. A diagnosis now is the attempt to find a fault (in the language perspective this is a word) in the incoming stream of symptoms (in the language perspective these are the letters). A diagnosis is successful, if the word (fault) is found, i.e. if the FSM got into the finite state. Each incoming symptom is used as a trigger. It can start a new diagnosis, i.e. it starts a new process as an instance of the FSM, or it can lead to a state transition of waiting FSMs, if it is the appropriate symptom. For that at each time several processes run in parallel each waiting for a symptom. A copy of the incoming symptom is sent as a message to every process.

In contrast to usual diagnosis systems, which open a backward window as a snapshot, our approach "looks" forward, each symptom can start a new diagnosis. Usual systems work on global knowledge (the whole window), whereas our diagnosis processes only have to work on the actual symptom. Hence they consume only a minimum of computing power. Usual systems have to work up past symptoms when starting a diagnosis, whereas our diagnosis-processes are always up to date. On the other hand the number of processes increases with the number of possible faults and with the number of incoming symptoms. Moreover faults, which are described by several unordered symptoms, lead to huge FSMs. So if faults are described by a set of symptoms, the representation by FSM seems to be inappropriate. However the concept of parallel processes can be used anyway using another data-structure (e.g. sets).
A first version of the system is implemented on a 386 PC under OS/2. It is used to control a furnace within the metal industry.

A transmission network can be viewed as a graph where the nodes are the cities and the arcs are the communication means between these cities. To avoid it, the operators often route the communication demand on two paths between the source and the sink. The second one is that new arcs may have been added to the network, with a different technology in comparison with the original arcs. The routing of a flow from one technology to another requires the working of a special appliance and causes a cost called "transition cost", which has to be added to the traditional routing cost. 1 Introduction

Heterogeneity of populations, sets of objects, supply, or demand in statistical models often is ignored or described outside and prior to statistical model analysis such that this analysis runs for fictitious independent and mean objects or on an aggregate level. The reasons are lack or complexity of appropriate models incorporating heterogeneity and comfortable results for i.i.d. variables from sampling theory. Complete heterogeneity has to include and describe two essential aspects (1) different individual behavior and (2) dependence of this behavior. For aspect (1) convolution and compounding of sufficiently flexible distributions are well-established techniques. With respect to univariate logistic distributions these techniques were used since Dubey (1969) to produce many satisfying results (Knüppel 1986). For aspect (2) multivariate extensions are self-suggesting.

But multivariate logistic distributions, derived as compounds, copulas, conditionals, extensions, or else, since Gumbel's bivariate logistic distributions (1961) are known to be rather rigid in their description of dependence structures. An exception seems to be the multivariate form of Satterthwaite/Hutchinson's bivariate logistic distribution (1978). The richness of this multivariate distribution here is analyzed with respect to its individual models and their dependencies; comparisons to contingency-type logistic distributions are given, demonstrating its appropriateness in describing heterogeneity aspect (1) and its superiority in (2).

In contrast to widespread mainframe-based architectures, decentralized corporate information systems offer adaptability in a world of changing business-constraints to support corporate goals in a flexible way. Beyond this, a goal-oriented decentralized corporate-wide system and application architecture provides competitive advantages by differentiation from architectures of competitors in the market. This paper presents an economic decision model to support information managers in selecting and designing goal-oriented system and application architectures in a changing economic world.
1 Introduction

Information technology (IT) should be applied to support a company's competitive goals [3]. The information system (IS) of a company has to be designed goal-oriented with respect to a lot of technical and business constraints. Technical constraints e.g. in the area of compatibility, heterogenity, interoperability, integrity, security or performance are understood in depth [4]. The primary challenge is to deal with business constraints. A competitive IS has to support customer needs to strengthen a company's competitive position in the market to increase a company's profitability in the short run as well as in the long run. This requires an integrated design of a company's IS and a company's organizational structures and business processes. A lot of constraints result from present and future customer needs, from competitive structures in the market and generally from the state and development of the national economy and interational markets. An IS is composed of its system architecture and its application architecture. The system architecture includes hardware, system software like operating systems and communication software, and the system topology. The application architecture on the other hand includes data, knowledge and functions relevant for a company's business activities. Conventional centralized system architectures of competing companies are very similar. They hardly provide designaltematives for a company to differentiate from competitors. Especially an integrated design of system architecture and naturally distributed organizational structures is nearly impossible. In conventional ISenvironments only the application architecture allows for differentiation between competitors to gain competitive advantages. Present available IT allows for a design of decentralized corporate IS based on computer-networks and on heterogeneous interoperable platforms with distributed applications based on the peer-to-peer-paradigm or the client-server-paradigm [1],[4]. A "good" IS allows for economical adaptations to support changing requirements in a changing world. Unfortunately, literature in areas of management science and computer science hardly provides a well-founded theoretical basis to design such good IS, that is to exploit the gained degrees of freedom moder IT provides.

As is well known by most recent public discussion social security systems of all industrial societies pass through a most dramatic change: an ever smaller working population has to support a continuously growing older population, placing an enormous financial stress on a system which was designed at a completely different demographic and economic environment. Ewa Konarzewska Gubala Department of Operations Research Oskar Lange Academy of Economics in Wroclaw 53-345 Wroclaw, ul. Komandorska 118\120, Poland

Abstract: The idea of the intelligent multiple criteria decision support system is presented. The system architecture contains an intelligent module to selection of the appropriate problem structure and multiple criteria decision making method. This architecture is implemented by a prototype system COMPROMISE.
Introduction

The managerial applications of Operations Research show two main tendencies recently: (1) in the theoretical domain - the searching for and developing "soft" approaches and methods for modelling and solving semistructured decision problems, (2) in the application area - the intensive using of information technology, mainly in Decision Support System (DSS) and Expert System (ES) framework to implement OR "soft" approaches.
Multiple Criteria Decision Support Systems

Multiple Criteria Decision Support Systems (MCDSS) are considered as specific class of DSSs employing various Multiple Criteria Decision Making (MCDM) methods. These systems interactively assist the decision maker in evaluating and comparing decision alternatives by making use of objective and subjective data, models and knowledge. MCDSSs cover a wide range of semistructured decision problems characterised by the multiplicity of the conflicting objectives and by the need of an active presence of decision maker during the decision process.

The typical architecture of DSS is composed of a Data Base, a Model Base, a Dialogue Base and the software managing the above bases. According to Jelassi (1987) MCDSSs typology the most popular are systems of first generation, i.e. stand-alone systems including only one MCDM method and a more or less rudimentary user interface. To this kind of systems belong, e.g.: ADBASE (Steuer 1983-89), ELECTRE III, IV ( Skalka et al. 1984-86), ELECTRE I, IS (Roy, Skalka, 1985--87), VIMDA (Korhonen, Laakso 1987), BIPOLAR (Konarzewska 1988-89), ARIADNE (Goicoechea, Fu Li, 1989), ELECCALC (Kiss et al., 1991) etc...

The next step towards the idea of the integrated DSS components has been made by the including a Model Base with a variety of models to the system architecture and full integration with the Data Management System. There are some good examples of these systems: MIRACLE (Bernabeu, Winkels 1981), DIDAS (Lewandowski et al., 1985), PREFCALC (Jacquet-Lagreze, Jelassi, 1983- 87), BARG (Bronisz et al., 1989).
The use of Expert Systems technology

Recently, there has been increasing interest in integrating the decision analysis and ES technology. An excellent survey on this subject is provided by White (1990). Ozernoy and Bordetski (1992) review several recent applications of ES for MCDM sorting them into three groups:

Rule-based MCDM Expert Systems, e.g. EXTRA (Pasche, 1991) Systems for MCDM methods' selection, e.g. ADVISOR (Ozernoy, 1991) •Negotiation and Group Decision Support Systems, e.g. NEGOPLAN (Matwin et al., 1989).

The DSS using an ES technology referred as the Knowledge-based DSS or Intelligent Decision Support System (IDSS) introduces a new aspect of decision support - an ability of "problem recognition". This is an important modelling feature at least for two reasons:

(1) It makes possible the mixing of algorithmic and heuristic methods in solving the ill structured problems: (2) It makes possible support the user in the choice phase as well as in the problem formulation or intelligence phase (according to Simon paradigm).

The last one is exceptionally important in our opinion. In presence of variety MCDM models and methods, the conceiving problem structure and its solution concept are the crucial aspects of MCDM modelling. Usually, one assumes that this stage is done out of DSS. The intelligent support based on the MCDM expert knowledge and on the rich model base seems to be prospective mission for ES technology in MCDSSs.
COMPROMISE: Intelligent Multiple Criteria Decision Support System

General description. COMPROMISE is an integrated, interactive and intelligent MCDSS that works in IBM PC environment. It has been designed and developed in 1990 (version 1.0) and 1991 (version 2.0) by E. Konarzewska-Gubala, J. Majchrzak, M. Nowinski, M. Rymarczyk and L. Waretak from OR Department of Wroclaw Academy of Economics. (The project was supported by Polish Scientific Commiee-KBN in framework of Program 10.VI.6: Computer optimisation and its managerial applications, co-ordinated by Prof. W. Bukietynski.)

The support provided by the system concerns three major phases of decision making process: (1) Problem identification (intelligence). This step involves the intelligent user interface in order   
to identify user problem and to suggest him/her the relevant model of quantitative analysis. (2) Problem analysis (design). At this step the pre-determinate model of user problem is   
constructed and the analysis is called for. () Decision searching (choice). In this phase the final decision is developed interactively   
using the possible results of the analysis.

DSS architecture. COMPROMISE is composed of seven subsystems. Phase (1) is performed by knowledge based subsystem EXPERT. Steps (2) and (3) are supported by the specific COMPROMISE subsysteMS: ND-MOLP, F-MOLP, BIPOLAR, ELECTRE, PROMET and FILTR They contain the Model Base of system COMPROMIS (MOLP and BIPOLAR can be used as independent stand-alone systems). The following models and methods have been included: •ND-MOLP (Non Dominated solutions of MultiObjective Linear Programming) contains ADBASE method (quotation of original, licensed software "ADBASE: MOLP-Computer Package" by Steuer, 1989)
• F-MOLP (Final solutions of MOLP) contains MOLP models with different scalarisation functions: weighted, fractional, lexicographic and distance (Konarzewska, 1980)
•FILTER contains the "filtering" procedures of non dominated solution sets in singling decision problems; procedures are developed by Steuer as an integrated part of "ADBASE..." package.
• BIPOLAR contains the model BIPOLAR developed and implemented (Konarzewska, 1989) as a stand-alone MCDSS for discrete alternatives evaluations using the bipolar reference system

• ELEKTRA contains the modified ELECTRE IV method based on preference credibility structure in discrete decision problems (version presented in Skalka et al., 1986) • PROMET contains the PROMETHEE I and II methods of discrete decision analysis using the generalised criterion concept (version presented in Brans et al., 1986)

The Knowledge Base (in subsystem EXPERT) is oriented to the selection of MCDM model and method from the library of Model Base (if it is possible). Its construction is founded on the binary tree. The execution of programs on parallel multiprocessor systems requires the optimal allocation of program graph into the graph of the system. The word "flexibility" or "flexible" is used much more often today than it was a decade ago. In banking and finance, investors' preference for flexibility translates into the notion of liquidity, or the ease in which assets can be transformed. In operations management, flexible manufacturing systems replace the function and product-specific machines of the past. In the labour markets, employers are giving flexi-time and flexible hours to attract better skilled workers. In turn, a multi-skilled worker can have more job opportunities. However, the meaning of flexibility is not easy to grasp. In many situations the word is used haphazardly, often in the absence of a better one. Over-use has led to confusion and poor understanding. In spite of its wide application, flexibility is neither necessary nor sufficient. As a result, it has not been successfully unified or classified. Instead of attempting to develop yet another formal definition, this paper distills common characteristics from the ways in which it is used in different disciplines. In this framework, the arc between "flexibility" and "robustness" represents the two types of flexibility observed by Gupta and Buzacott (1988), Mandelbaum (1978), Eppink (1978), and Ansoff (1968). They see two fundamental ways of responding to change. Active or action flexibility is the ability to respond by changing or reacting.Passive or state flexibility, on the other hand, exists when there is no need to react because of immunity, insensitivity, or tolerance. This second type of flexibility is better known as robustness.

Flexibility, whether active or passive, is closely associated with uncertainty. Merkhofer (1975) states that the value of flexibility is related to the the value of information in decision analysis. Flexibility is needed when you have less than perfect information. The more flexibility you have, the greater is the value of your information gathering. Similarly, the more information you expect to obtain, the more valuable flexibility is to you. Flexibility is desirable when you are uncertain about what actions to take. Flexibility provides a way of coping with uncertainty though not necessarily reducing it. The above framework provides a basis for the development of operational measures and decision criteria. Several measures have already been proposed in the literature, most notably in doctoral theses on this subject. The most common ones are introduced here.

The most popular by far is the size of choice set or the number of choices. This can be directly deduced from the inherent meaning of flexibility. It is countable, simple, and feasible. However, it gives no indication of the degree of differentiation among the choices or their attractiveness. Furthermore, the number of choices depends on the partitioning of the choice set as well as the stage in the decision process.
Some commentators see flexibility as the ease of transition from one state to another. Ease is a function of cost and time, reflecting the freedom of choice. Unfortunately, it is not self-evident

CONCLUSIONS

Flexibility is widely believed to be desirable and useful. Nonetheless without a clear definition, it remains elusive. The conceptual framework presented here organises concepts of flexibility into related themes and thereby provides a basis for the development of operational measures and decision criteria. 1 Introduction

Pyramidal classification of multidimensional data allows the construction of overlapping clusters. The pyramidal representation is a natural extension of the hierarchical classification. The graphical representaion of indexed hierarchies by dendrograms is well-known. For the graphical representation of indexed pyramids a similar procedure can be used. Milligan (1979) has shown that the most used agglomerative hierarchical techniques single and complete linkage generate hierarchical structures with monotonically increasing distance values so the resulting dendrogram is free of inversions. Transferring this agglomerative techniques to the pyramidal classification it can be shown that only the complete linkage technique generates pyramidal structures with monotonically increasing distance values. Using the single linkage technique inversions are possible in the graphical representation. For the existence of an inversion a necessary and sufficient condition is formulated.

3 Agglomerative Clustering Techniques

The agglomerative hierarchical and pyramidal techniques produce a complete sequence of non-overlapping resp. overlapping cluster solutions. They all operate in essentially the same way, proceeding sequentially from the stage in which each object is considered to be single class to the final stage in which there is a single group containing all $_ n$ objects. At each stage in the procedure two groups considered to be the most similar are joined together. Once the classes are joined together they are never separated later in the process. The index of a joined class corresponds to the value of the dissimilarity index of the two classes that have formed it.

1 Introduction

For optimization problems that are NP-hard, which includes most problems arising in scheduling, there are at present no easy solutions. Classical OR-methods cannot be used, because you would need approximately $1 0 ^ { 3 6 }$ years of time for a complete enumeration in our simplest test case, whereas an acceptable response time is about an quater of an hour. As there is currently no way to solve such problems exactly, the objective of finding the global optimum has to be changed in the target to find the best result possible over a given period.

With roots going back in the late $1 9 6 0 ^ { \circ } { \mathsf { s } }$ and early $\bf { 1 9 7 0 ^ { \circ } s }$ heuristic methods have been object of intensive research in the last decade. The methods of tabu search, genetic algorithms and simulated annealing have been singled out by the Committee on the Next Decade of Operations Research (see [CONDOR88]) as "extremely promising" for future treatment of practical applications.
In our current research project P8199-PHY "Dynamische Ressourcenbelegungsplanung" (see [JAMMERNEGG91]) we are studying heuristic methods in process planning and control of flexible assembly systems.
2 Model

As a basic model, a FAS with four partially parallel assembly centres is examined. These four cells are supplied by AGV's. In contrast to many similar experiments in this field the system definition is made much more realistic. So the system is based on real products (toycars) and the influence of restrictions such as transport-times, palette-dimensions, machinebreakdowns and other stochastic events which occur in reality, are verified [GRONALT93]. SIMAN/CINEMA with Fortran subroutines is used to implement the model [SCHMID93].
Due to the existin interfaces theimplementationf the tested algorithms is easiy possibly by substituting the modeled system by the real system.
3 Heuristic Methods
In our current research project the following procedures are tested for efficiency in the field of flexible manufacturing:
Simulated Annealing

Simulated Annealing has become a very popular tool in combinatorical optimization since its introduction in 1982 (see [KIRKPATRICK82]). Osman and Potts [OSMAN89], as well as Ogbu und Smith [OGBU90] discussed the advantages and difficulties of this heuristic in production scheduling. On the basis of available comparisons the following can be said about this approach:

The solutions found by the Simulated Annealing algorithm are of very good quality. On the other hand it requires more time than most of the other popular heuristics to evaluate these solutions. The following factors are important for the success of this algorithm: acceptance-probability, perturbance technique, kind of temperature-reduction.
Tabu-Search

Important new results in the field of Tabu-Search algorithms in application to Job Shop scheduling were found by M. Widmer [WIDMER91], whose examinations also include details such as Tooling Constraints. Of no minor interest are the examinations of Taut, who proposes Tabu Search as the most efficient heuristic in complex job-shop re-scheduling problems (see [TAUT92]). The following advantages and problems of the procedure can be found:

The algorithm supplies good solutions without exception, which in most cases are found very quickly.   
The speed and the accuracy of the method can be varied by different parameter-settings   
The choice of the following factors is important: tabu-list size, solution-surroundings, number of optimization steps.
Threshold Accepting

This is one of the most recent approaches in heuristic optimization theory. Proposed in 1990 by Dueck and Scheuer [DUECK90], Threshold Accepting seems to be equivalent or even superior to the Simulated Annealing algorithm (see [ALTHOEFER91]). Until now there are no special results known about the application of Threshold Accepting in the field of production scheduling.
Genetic Algorithms

The method of Genetic Algorithms (GA) is based on the principles of Natural Selection, Inheritance and Mutation. The foundations developed by Holland et al. [HOLLAND75] have been and still are applied with success in all areas of combinatoric optimization, as, for example, Job-Shop Scheduling [DAVIS85], Travelling-Salesman problems [GREFENST85] and as classifier-systems [GOLDBERG89].
This technique is based on the principle, that certain structures can adjust better to the environment than others.

The advantage of this procedure is that very less knowledge about the respective problem-structure is required. Satisfying solutions are found even for rather bad parameter settings [GOLDBERG89].   
GA's can be used not only for solving combinatoric optimization problems but also as classification tools.
For all these heuristics the following can be said: It is possible to prove that the success of the algorithms does not depend on the choice of the initial solution.
Nevertheless experiments have shown that a good starting solution contributes greatly to the efficiency of an algorithm.
4 Results and Conclusion

Partner institutions are studying other OR-Methods (Linear Programming, mixed Priority-Rules, Neural Networks) and comparisons of the different methods show that heuristic algorithms can deal with complex problems (neural network-methods can only solve simple problems, as they need a big number of training cases), and outperform mixed priority rules, that are tested on complete grids.
A combination of priority rules and heuristic methods is currently tested, and we expect further improvement from this combined algorithm.

When credit markets are regulated by quantitative controls, shocks to this market have no implications for the rate of interest. An excess demand for credit is not reflected in the movements of the interest rate. Movements in the interest rate will solely reflect the state of liquidity preference and changes in monetary policy. When credit markets are deregulated, interest rates will respond to credit market disequilibrium. If information about the shocks are known only with a lag but interest rates are part of the current observed information set, agents face a signal extraction problem in identifying whether a movement in the rate of interest is due to a credit or monetary shock. Consider the optimization model of a business process including investment possibilities, production activities and market activities. At first we explain the decision variables and the constraints. For each activity we define a nonnegative decision variable representing the quantity of the activity. Some decision variables may be lower or upper bounded. For each investment possibility, a zero-one variable is defined. The investment should be realized if the optimal value of the zero-one variable is 1. For each element we construct a constraint to assure that the sum of the consumed and sold amount of the element is not greater than the sum of the purchased and produced amount. Here, the element is either a production element or a product.

A simple example is obtained if for each production activity the consumed quantities of the elements per unit of the production activity are known in advance. The consumed quantities can also be defined as the piecewise linear functions of decision variables [2]. If for some production activities the technological procedure must be determined by the optimization, the decision variables have to be defined in a different way. Such a phenomenon appears for example if in one phase of the production process the mixing problem arises. More decision variables are needed for a production activity if its product is a mixture. The quantity of such a production activity is defined as a sum of decision variables. The decision variable gives the quantity of the raw material consumed by the production of the mixture. We can assure the required quality of all mixtures by means of special constraints. The construction of those constraints is demonstrated on the example.

There are many possibilities for defining the objective function. If investment selection is included we can maximize the rate of return. In this case two programming problems need to be solved. The first one determines the optimal contribution without including the investment possibilities. In the second programming problem the objective function is a fraction. In the numerator we have the increase of the contribution caused by investments. Namely, from the income we subtract the variable cost, the semi fixed cost caused by investments, and the optimal objective function value of the first model. In the denominator are the invested means. If all constraints and the numerator are piecewise linear we obtain a fractional piecewise linear programming problem.

The fractional piecewise linear programming problem can be transformed into a linear mixed integer one and solved by available computer programs [4]. Using the Charnes-Cooper transformation [1], [3] we obtain a quadratic mixed integer programming problem where in addition to the linear terms, products of a zero-one variable by' the new positive variable introduced by the Charnes-Cooper transformation arise. We improve the pattern-imitation method for time-series forecasting presented in Motnikar et al. (1992) and (1993). Given a univariate time-series $z _ { 1 } , \ldots , z _ { n } ,$ , we defined its patterns $\pmb { \vec { r } } ( t ) \equiv$ $( z _ { t } , z _ { t + 1 } , \dotsc , z _ { t + s - 1 } )$ as vectors of $\pmb { s }$ consecutive observations starting at time $\pmb { t }$ , where $1 \leq t \leq$ $\pmb { n } - \pmb { s } + \pmb { 1 }$ and $\pmb { \mathscr { s } }$ is the pattern length. Using a certain similarity measure, we chose set ${ \pmb S } =$ $\{ \vec { r } ( t _ { 1 } ) , \ldots , \vec { r } ( t _ { k } ) \}$ of patterns sufficiently similar to the prototype pattern (denoted by $\pmb { \vec { p } } )$ , that is the last pattern before the forecast origin. We estimated a future value $z _ { n + l }$ , which is $\pmb { l }$ time-steps ahead of the forecast origin $\pmb { n }$ , by a linear combination of the observations following the $\pmb { k }$ patterns from $s$ , where weights ${ \pmb w } _ { j }$ are determined according to the similarity between patterns $\overrightarrow { r } ( t _ { j } )$ and $\pmb { \vec { p } }$ $( \vec { p } \equiv \vec { r } ( n - s + 1 ) )$ :

An observation $z _ { t }$ that is unusually large or small relative to the other values in a given stationary time-series is called an outlier. To define an outlier of a non-stationary time-series, we have to take into account non-stationary characteristics: trend, season, nonconstant variance and cycle. For more about time-series analysis, see Box, Jenkins (1970). Typically, outliers are of two types:

(i) The measurement is observed, recorded, or entered into the computer incorrectly. This type of outlier does not influence any other observations. It is called a Type I outlier (additive outlier). (ii) The measurement is correct, but represents a rare (chance) event. Usually, this type of outlier influences few subsequent observations. It is called a Type $\pmb { \cal I }$ outlier (innovational outlier); see Sincich, 1991.

If a time-series contains outliers, forecasts may be contaminated. In this paper, we discuss how Type I outliers influence time-series analysis by pattern-imitation depending on the outliers' positions in the data set and present an approach for their detection and handling.
ANALYSIS OF TIME-SERIES WITH OUTLIERS

The standard approach to outlier detection is based on the distribution function of time-series observations (e.g., Schmid, 1990). Since in the pattern-imitation method there are no statistical assumptions about the distribution function, we have to use a descriptive approach. We detect outliers (i) by eye; or (i) by z-score (observations that do not fall within 3 standard deviations of the time-series mean); or (ii) by a leave-one-out (LO0) test in the position of an extreme onestep-ahead forecast error. Let us review how outliers may cause difficulties in the three phases of time-series analysis.

1. Estimation of the model parameters. Model parameters are estimated automatically using a cross-validation technique. Estimates are robust; they are not very sensitive to single observations. However, after elimination of outliers, more accurate values of the parameters may be obtained.

2. Fit-quality test. Some time-series observations are chosen as a validation set and are not used as input data. We estimate them by one-step-ahead forecasts and calculate their mean absolute error (MAE); this represents fit-quality. Outliers in the validation set yield an incorrect estimate of fit-quality.

3. Forecasting future values $z _ { n + l }$ . A time-series with outliers produces a different linear combination (1) than a time-series without outliers. The difference between them strongly depends on the outliers' positions in the data set.

a) An outlier in the prototype pattern $\vec { p }$ prevents us from finding an appropriate set $s$ .   
Outlier $z _ { t _ { j } + s - 1 + l }$ infects one component of (1). (It follows a pattern ${ \vec { r } } ( t _ { j } ) \in S .$ )   
c) An outlier that eliminates a pattern from the set $s$ reduces (1) by one component. (It changes a similar pattern to a dissimilar one.)   
d)(1) is not changed when the outlier is in a pattern or follows a pattern that is outside $s$ .   
e) We cannot do anything with outliers in the prediction set. They may lead to large forecast errors.
HOW TO HANDLE OUTLIERS

Since not all outliers contaminate forecasts, we should decide whether to (i) replace an outlier with a resonable value (e.g., obtained by a one-step-ahead forecast): this is necessary in phase 3.a and recommended in phase 3.c; or

(ii) consider an outlier as a missing observation: this is necessary in phase 2 and recommended in phase 1 and 3.b; or   
(ii) do nothing: phases 3.d and 3.e.   
We present a forecasting algorithm that considers outliers. The corresponding phases are written in parenthesis.   
1: Estimate the model parameters by standard procedure ignoring outliers (1).   
2:Using a LOO test, detect suspect outliers and denote them as missing observations. Ignoring these observations, re-estimate·the model parameters.   
3: Ignoring missing observations, evaluate the fit-quality test (2).   
4: If the prototype pattern contains a missing value, replace it with a reasonable value (3.a).   
5: Compare all patterns $\vec { r } ( t )$ with prototype pattern ${ \pmb { \vec { p . } } }$ When a pattern $\vec { r } ( t )$ with a missing observation seems similar, replace the outlier with a reasonable value. Find the set $s$ of similar patterns (3.c).   
6: Calculate forecasts $\hat { z } _ { n } ( l )$ of future values. If observation $z _ { t _ { j } + s - 1 + l }$ is missing, eliminate the pattern $\vec { r } ( t _ { j } )$ from the set $s$ or replace the outlier with a reasonable value (3.b).

CONCLUSION

The majority of time-series methods use all observations to create a forecasting model. As a result, forecasts are contaminated unless we replace all outliers. However, in the pattern-imitation method, not all outliers influence forecasts. We presented different influences depending on the outliers' positions in the data set and suggested an algorithm that handles outliers. We estimate that in only $1 0 \%$ of positions outliers have significant impact on the forecasts of future values.

Peter NEUMAYER, Universität Kaiserslautern

Abstract:It is known that we can find a maximum matching in a weighted bipartite graph G in polynomial time, especially within $\mathbf { O ( n ^ { 3 } ) }$ steps, with 2n is the number of vertices. In such a problem each edge of G is weighted with a real, positive number or an integer. More generally, I consider now a weighted bipartite graph with vectorweighted edges. It is shown that the decision problem for a maximum matching in a vectorweighted graph G is NP-complete. Furthermore I apply a definition of complexity concerning counting problems in order to get a more detailed insight of the problem. I use the counting-complexity according to L.G. Valiant and show that the vectorweighted bipartite matching problem is #P-complete.

Valiant the problem of counting the number of perfect matchings (which is equivalent to the problem of calculating the permanent of a matrix ) is #P-complete. INTRODUCTION

Finding shortest path is a fundamental problem in the study of transportation and communication networks. Besides its own importance it appears as a subroutine in many other combinatorial optimization problems such as vehicle routing, network design or flows.

Classical methods (like Ford, Dijkstra) progressively construct paths from the initial node to all the other nodes of the network. These paths are permanently corrected in the sense of diminishing their lengths. At the end, not only shortest path to final node is obtained but all shortest paths from the initial node to the other ones.

In this paper the problem is reconsidered from the point of view of the existence of two parallel processors. Each of them applies Dijkstra's algorithm: the first starts from the initial node to the final one while the second "goes back" from the final node to the initial one. The processors work independently until they meet in some nodes; so, in a progressive manner, various paths between initial and final nodes are obtained by concatenation. From these paths, always the shortest is retained.

A lot of numerical experiments were made on a number of randomly generated networks. All of these have shown that the above search procedure needs much less time than Dijkstra's algorithm on a single processor.

Among several method: which solve this problem, Dijkstra's algorithm seems to be the most popular. The basic idea of the algorithm is to fan out from node s and label nodes in order of their distance from s. Each node i has a label d(i): the label is permanent once we know that it represents the shortest distance from s to i; otherwise it is temporary. DIJKSTRA'S PARALLEL ALGORITHM

Now, imagine two persons, named RED and BLUE moving simultaneously along the edges of the network. RED starts from the initial node s and applies Dijkstra's algorithm in order to find shortest paths from s to all other nodes. To achieve his mission RED successively updates the red labels dr(i), i ε G and, at every iteration, makes permanent that temporary red label with minimum value. On the other side, BLUE applies the "reverse" Dijkstra's algorithm starting from the final node t. His objective is to find shortest paths from all nodes in G to the node t. In order to do this, he iteratively updates the blue labels db(j), j e G, making permanent, at every iteration, that temporary blue label with minimum value. Clearly, RED and BLUE will meet in at least one node. Such nodes will be called joint nodes. If j is a joint node the sum dr(j) $\star$ db(j) represents the length of a path from s to t. Many such paths can be obtained, but only the shortest among them is retained together with its defining joint node.

Extended Abstract The dictum "the input data is not precise anyway" is often stated in defence of the many heuristic or approximate methods developed to solve difficult problems in mathematical programming. Difficult meaning not yielding a solution in a "reasonable" amount of time. A brief survey of the literature shows that a considerable amount of effort has been spent to investigate and devise this kind of methods in the area of integer and combinatorial programming, e.g., Garey & Johnson (1979), Cornuejols et al. (1977), Balas & Martin (1980),Ibarra & Kim (1975), Sahni (1975), Lawler (1979), Magazine & Oguz (1984).

Also, data imprecision or variation is a source of great concern in linear and nonlinear programming. It has led to many forms of sophisticated mathematical analysis especially in the case of linear programming. The most prominent among these is sensitivity analysis. Strictly speaking, it is the analysis of the effect of input data changes on an optimal solution of a linear program. All well known books on the subject have chapters on sensitivity and/or post optimality analysis, e.g., Dantzig (1963), Bazaraa & Jarvis (1977), Chavatal (1983).

In the case of nonlinear programming, similar topics are discussed under names like perturbation analysis, stability analysis, or parametric analysis. A collection of articles in a special issue of Journal of Optimization Theory and Applications (JOTA) edited by A. V. Fiacco (1986) may be seen to get an idea about these. Interval analysis may also be considered in this realm. Ratscheck & Voller (1991) provide a recent review of this subject.

More recent extensions of sensitivity analysis are multiparametric analysis, linear programming with interval objective function coefficients, and tolerance analysis as reflected in the works of Zeleny (1974), Yu & Zeleny (1976), Steuer (1981), and Wendell (1985). The basic premise in sensitivity analysis and these more recent works is that the preservation of the optimality of a solution has paramount importance and no effort should be spared to make a new one available when the existing solution loses this quality due to changes in data.

When this approach is contrasted with that of the dictum mentioned above for approximate (heuristic) solutions, the inherent paradoxicality can not be missed. Data imprecision is almost a welcome relief in cases where optimal solutions are hard to find and convenient substitutes (approximate solutions) are recomended instead. When it is relatively easier to find optimal solutions, on the other hand, a myriad of ways and means of restoring optimality against the slightest variations in the input data are suggested.
This study is an attempt at reconciling these two approaches. We consider the following problem:

The Gambler-Mover-Stayer Model (GMS) was developed as an instrument for judging the efficiency of psychotherapeutical training projects [4]. The model requires tests at the beginning and at the end of the training and one or more additional tests when training is in progress. The test results are assumed to be of ordinal level. The times of the tests are $\mathbf { t } = \mathbf { 0 }$ (the beginning of the training), $\mathbf { t } = 1$ , $\tan 2$ ,.. , $\mathbf { t } = \mathbf { T }$ (the end of the training). The sequence of test results of a person is denoted by $\bf { x _ { 0 } } , \ \bf { x _ { 1 } } , \ \dots \ \bf { x _ { T } } .$ The test results are evaluated by categorical values 1, 2, .. , C , where "1" is the best test result.

The central idea of the GMS is the differentiation of three types of pupils or patients: gamblers, (true) movers and stayers. The (true) movers form the real training group. At the beginning of the course they do not have the ability which is to be imparted, at least not in the highest degree. During the course they can improve their abilities with a certain probability, but they cannot fall off. They continually move toward the goal of the training project. Therefore they are called Movers.

In every training group we also have persons whose abilities fluctuate from time to time. At certain times they seem to have aquired a remarkable skill, but later on they seem to have lost it. For these persons a good test result at time T does not indicate the successful completion of the course. These persons do not move continually to the goal of the training program, they rather seem to gamble. Therefore they are called Gamblers. When judging the efficiency of a group training project it is of great importance, to separate the (true) movers from the gamblers.

Apart of these two groups there exists the group of Stayers, consisting of those persons, whose abilities must be constant during the complete training for two possible reasons: either a pupil or patient already has the ability which is to be imparted in the highest degree or else the person is not at all influenced by the training program.
The GMS is a Mixed Markov Model with three independent Markov chains describing the three mentioned groups of persons. It is related to the Mover-

Stayer Model well known in literature (see for instance [2]), from which however it differs by the differentiation between true movers and gamblers. Moreover the GMS generalizes the Black & White Model of Converse [1], which yields a Gambler-Stayer Model.

The paper presents and analyses a simple general model allowing valued ("fuzzy") preference coefficient expressions from a set of judges over a set of options. The main question addressed by the paper is the nature of information that can be obtained from such a construct. This information ranges from a very loose "opinion" to very strict "action definition". It is proposed that while in case of determination of opinion solutions are simple if not trivial, it is in the case of action definition that real obstacles arise. It becomes namely necessary to take into account the narrowed down tolerance of the judges as to possible divergence of the outgoing information from own preferences. This leads to the problem of simultaneous clustering - and - aggregation of preferences. This problem has not as yet found a satisfactory theoretical and algorithmic solution. The paper presents the objective function which avoids triviality of results (e.g. monotonicity with respect to cluster number), an outline of a relatively simple and quick suboptimization algorithm, and a new and natural definition of consensus for the clustering-and-aggregation problem, this definition being based upon the precepts of the algorithm used.
