Introduction

A job shop consists of a set of different machines that perform operations on jobs. Each job has a specified processing order through the machines; that is a job is an ordered list of operations, each of which is determined by the machine it requires and by its processing time. Operations cannot be interrupted (non-preemption), each machine can handle only one job at a time, and each job can be performed on only one machine at a time. The operation sequences on the machines are unknown and have to be determined so as to minimize the makespan, i.e. the time required to complete all jobs, see the different problem formulations by Blazewicz et al. (1991) and Adams et al. (1988).

As the name suggests, genetic algorithms are motivated by the theory of evolution, see Goldberg (1989) and Michalewicz (1992). They have been designed as general search strategies and optimization methods.

Roughly speaking, a genetic algorithm aims at producing near-optimal solutions by letting a set of random solutions undergo a sequence of unary and binary transformations (reproduction, crossover, mutation) governed by a selection scheme biased towards high-quality solutions.

The job shop scheduling problem is a typical representative of a binary constraint satisfaction problem (CSP), i.e., generally speaking, there is a set of variables each of which has its own domain of values. Find an assignment of values to variables such that a set of constraints on variable pairs is satisfied (see Dechter / Pearl (1988) and Meseguer (1989)). Assume that there is an upper bound on the makespan of an optimal schedule of the underlying job shop scheduling problem. Then computing heads and tails assigns to each operation an interval of possible start times. Considering variable domains as possible operation start times where the variables define the operations in a schedule then the disjunctive graph illustrates the job shop scheduling constraint satisfaction problem, hence it corresponds to the constraint graph (Montanari (1974)).

Consistency checks, or roughly speaking propagation of constraints will make implicitly defined constraints more visible and will prune the search tree in a branch and bound algorithm (cf. Pesch et al. (1993), Mackworth (1977). The better the bounds the more arc directions in the disjunctive graph can be fixed during the propagation process.
Genetic Based Learning

Genetic algorithms do not fit best for scheduling problems in order to get near-optimal solutions if no improvement heuristic, such as local search, is incorporated (cf. Davis (1985), Ulder et al. (1991) and only little work is done on genetic algorithms with respect to (job shop) scheduling, see Dorndorf / Pesch (1993), Husbands et al. (1991), and Starkweather et al. (1992). Some type of an improvement heuristic may be incorporated into the crossover operator (see Kolen / Pesch (1991), Yamada / Nakano (1992)). The strategy of Dorndorf and Pesch (1992) controls a sequence of priority rules or the machine inclusion sequence for the shifting bottleneck heuristic of Adams et al. (1988) or Balas et al. (1992) and learns to find best combinations in both cases. A different approach was followed by Storer et al. (1992). They map the original data of the underlying problem instance to slightly disturbed and genetically controlled data representing new problem instances. The latter are solved heuristically and the solution, i.e. the operations' processing orders, are considered to be solutions of the original problem.

One can use other kinds of rules which fix the order of operations on the same machine. For instance, any permutation of unscheduled operations might represent a rule (Davis (1985) and Hilliard $/$ Liepins (1988)). The approach to search a best sequence of decision rules for selecting operations is just in line with the ideas of Fisher and Thompson (1963) on probabilistic learning of sequences consisting of two priority rules, and Crowston et al (1963) on learning how to find promising linear combinations of basic priorities.

Constraint propagation in the sense of arc- or path-consistency (Van Hentenryck et al. (1992)) generally fixes only a few most often trivial arc directions even if tight upper bounds of the makespan in an optimal schedule are applied. Remedy yields to consider subproblems (e.g. one-machine or multiple-job problems). Hence, new genetic based approaches were applied, the one machine constraint propagation based genetic algorithm and a multiple job constraint propagation based genetic algorithm. Whenever a new population is generated a local decision rule in the sense of constraint propagation in order to achieve arc- and path-consistency is applied simultaneously to each subproblem with respect to some upper bound. Feasible solutions are obtained as in Yamada $/$ Nakano (1992). For details see Pesch (1993).
Computational Results

The probably 2 best known test problems for job shop scheduling (Fisher / Thompson (1963)): the ${ \bf 5 } \ { \bf * 2 0 }$ ,and the $1 0 \times 1 0$ problem the optima of which are 1165 and 930, respectively (cf. Carlier $/$ Pinson (1990), Brucker et al. (1991), Applegate / Cook (1991)) can optimally be solved by the one machine constraint propagation based genetic algorithm. Detailed computational results compared to other local search approaches (Aarts et al. (1991), Nakano and Yamada (1991, 1992), Dell'Amico / Trubian (1993), Van Laarhoven et al. (1992)) are provided in Pesch (1993).

The constraint propagation based approaches even try to avoid the use of problem specific knowledge that is not relevant for the complete problem. Introducing problem specific knowledge makes a genetic strategy a promising alternative. This knowledge might be incorporated by the application of a heuristic performing well on the particular problem, such as the shifting bottleneck procedure for the job shop problem.

For given MOP we determine an associated approximate MOP (AMOP). If $Q ^ { \star } < Q$ is determined as the set of optimal plans of certain MOP then the set $\overline { { \mathcal { Q } } }$ $Q ^ { \ast } C \overrightarrow { Q } < Q$ of ε-optimal plans of associated AMop is defined. Main questions arising in the choice of the E-optimal plans of AMoP are discussed. We introduce a definition of E-ordered criteria and suggest a decision concept for AMOP with $\varepsilon$ -ordered criteria. Definitions of ε-Pareto set and $\varepsilon \mathcal { P }$ -optimal plan are discussed. Main approaches to the choice of the $\varepsilon \rho$ -optimal plans for AMOP are based on reduction of the $\varepsilon$ -Pareto set. We consider and develope certain of these.

We ground a thesis: practically all problems of production planning and management (PPM) have to be modelled as AMOP. In connection with this main principles and particularities of the multicriterial optimization in applied models PPM are considered. We argue in favour of an examination of AMoP as problems under uncertain conditions. Their indeterminacy can be reduced or removed only in the process of the problem decision by introduction of a new information. We discusse general questions arising in practical applications of AMOP in PPM. The main of these is to research qualitative and quantitative interrelations of criteria. We discusse and examine main features of the choice of E-optimal plans in applied AMO models: a phenomenon of competitive optimal plans, exchangeability of criteria and restrictions as well as collisions appearing in a process of the final optimal plan choice by a decision making person. A problem of a vector criterion scalarization for these models is examined and a conclusion is made, that there are a few obstacles for its correct decision. The main one: it is impossible to compare different criteria, even normalized, because of insufficient and very different trustiness of an initial information.

We describe and examine optimality criteria and decision choice for three well known problems of decision making. The first one is the problem of the optimal choice of nomenclature and volumes of production in a small serial industry for a calendar period (year, quarter). It is proposed, that a capacity of an order book for the considered enterprise exceeds its available production facilities. For certain articles minimal and maximal production volumes are given as well as extreme output moments. Funds of time for the main production subdivisions are restricted , but there are certain means to increase. Given problem was traditionally modelled with the only criterion of maximal profit (or a certain equivalent one). We argue : this problem is naturally multicriterial, though the profit is the main one. We examine other criteria: minimal expence accounts for increasing of production facility, minimal expence accounts for storage of the finished production, maximal reliability of the optimal plan fulfilment by unreliable information. We discusse a question of scalarization vector criterion in this problem and argue an incorrectness of this procedure. Given criteria may have different interrelations in concrete problems, in particular they can be E-ordered. We propose an iterative method for E-optimal plans search, Rabinovitch (I988).

We discusse the following version of sceduling problem. Given small serial industry enterprise has a year plan with fixed production volumes. Moments of articles output aren't fixed, but they belong to certain time intervals (for instance, to quarters). The problem consist in the search of optimal moments of production output with precision to shorter intervals (for instance, to months or ten-day periods) with keeping a certain restrictions system. We suggest and argue the following optimality criteria: (I) maximal uniform work-load of main generalized production subdivisions, (2) maximal admitable concentration of output of the same production type articles, (3) minimal value of circulating capital appearing in consequence of incomplete production, (4) maximal reliability of the optimal plan fulfilment with unreliable information elements. Analysis of given criteria leads to conclusion, that (I) is the main of the-- se. In the neighbourhood of its optimal plans set a reduction of ε-Pareto set determined by others criteria is suggested.

A following marketing model is considered. Some firm plans to begin a new or modernized production type output in order to sale it at some new as well as traditional markets. The firm has forecasts about possible tentative prices and expectable demand volumes of its production at the each market. There are some means in order to increase production facilities. The problem consist in search for optimal prices and production volumes for the each market. The following optimality criteria can be considered: (I) maximal summary sale volume, (2) maximal summary profit, (3) minimal costs of production and marketing, (4) maximal sale volume for new markets, (5) minimal expectable summary damage caused by invasion at new markets. It can be considered several interrelations of criteria in dependence upon a strategic and tactical policy of the firm. For instance, (4) and (5) can be the most important and unordered ( or equally valuable), others are secondary and E-ordered. In a generalized marketing model we consider several production types as well as an extended restrictions and parameters collection ( including variable costs for reclame, service, modernization of production and so on). In the other variant of this model we have a dynamic process for prices and production volumes optimization for several periods of time. These models are suitable for practical applications. They can be used also as a part of a business game for managers teaching and training.

An optimal marketing strategy for heterogeneous groups of porkers
J. Roemen Department of Econometrics Tilburg University P.O. Box 90153, NL 5000 LE, Tilburg
1 Introduction

In this paper the question is dealt with, how a profit maximizing farmer should distribute the sale of groups of porkers over time, taking into consideration that each group consists of subgroups differing in growth rate, that the meat price varies in time, and that the next fattening round can only start when all animals in the current round have been delivered for slaughter.

(Des)investment problems related to a stock of a living commodity have been considered by, among others, Chavas et al. [1], Feinerman [2], Paarsch [3] and Rausser et al. [4]. However, they restrict attention to the case where for one feeding schedule the same growth function holds for all the animals being fattened. Moreover, in this paper the decision rule for the situation where the market prices for meat are mutually dependent is worked out. No attention is paid to the choice of an optimal feeding schedule.
2 Problem

Nowadays, pork is mainly produced on specialized farms. For fattening, such a farm has a number of barns which are divided into compartments. Depending on its size a compartment contains a few tens to well over one hundred animals. Because of health considerations, usually the so called "all in all out" system is followed in production. That means that a compartment is occupied by young animals at one point in time and that all of these animals have to be delivered for slaughter, before the next fattening round in this compartment can start. After entering, the young porkers are fattened for some time, untill they are fit for slaughter. Here we assume that the farmer follows a feeding schedule as advised by an agricultural experimentation station, so the feeding regime is given and fixed.

During fattening, the animals in a compartment usually show variations in the weight gain per day. As a result, the length of the period that an animal needs to reach a certain weight, differs from animal to animal. In this study we assume that the animals in a compartment receive the same feed ration, so the weight variation has to be ascribed to differences in genetic qualities. For our purpose, it suffices to distinguish two subgroups in a compartment: fast en slow growers. Within these subgroups no substantial differences in growth qualities exist.

As soon as a porker has reached a certain minimal weight, the farmer can sell it to a slaughter house. The price which he receives, is not constant in time, but varies from week to week. Generally speaking, this week's price moves within a restricted interval around last week's price. Therefore, we assume that it is a stochastic variable which only depends on the price in the preceding week. The feed price and the interest rate show variability too, but their variability is much smaller, so we treat them as deterministic.

Because of the heterogeneity of the animals in one compartment, the ${ \mathfrak { a } } _ { \mathfrak { a } } \mathfrak { l }$ in all out" system and the stochastic nature of the pork price, the farmer is confronted with the question how to distribute the delivery of fattened porkers over time.
3 Model and solution

The net financial result depends on the decisions taken by the farmer in each week of each fattening round. These rounds succeed each other uninterruptedly. Such a decision can be to sell this week a group of porkers or to postpone the sale and to continue fattening. These decisions are based on the weight of the animals, the price for pork, the expenses for feed and young pigs and the interest rate.

A porker can be sold as soon as it is fit for slaughter, i.e., when its weight is between a minimal and a maximal value. The fast growers reach this minimal weight at the age of $x _ { 1 , m i n }$ weeks, while their latest delivery date is at the age of $\pmb { x _ { 1 , m a x } }$ weeks. The sale of the slow growers can only start from $x _ { 2 , m i n } ( \geq x _ { 1 , m i n } )$ onward. The last possible week for this group to leave the farm is at the age of $\pmb { x _ { 2 , m a x } }$ weeks. As long as the porkers have not yet reached their minimal weight or when they threaten to pass the maximum, the decision of the farmer is obvious. However, as soon as a group is fit for slaughter, the farmer has to choose between the two available decisions. By ending each fattening round at the suitable moment the farmer can realize a maximal financial result. For the determination of the suitable moment cut-off prices for pork are calculated for each week in which animals are fit for slaughter. At the cut-off level for a certain week the farmer is indifferent between selling in that week or selling in the future. If the market price for pork in a week exceeds the cut-off level for that week, the farmer should sell, in the opposed case he should postpone the sale and continue fatting.

For the calculation of the cut-off prices in the relevant period we formulate a Markov decision model. Here the system under study is the stochastic process $\{ ( \underline { { { z } } } _ { t } , \underline { { { h } } } _ { t } , \underline { { { p } } } _ { t } ) , t =$ 0,1,2,.}, where $\pmb { \mathscr { z } } _ { t }$ stands for the age of an animal in week $\mathbf { \Delta } _ { t , \mathbf { \tilde { \mu } } _ { 0 } }$ for the composition of the compartment and $\underline { { \pmb { p } } } _ { \pmb { t } }$ for the price of pork. Age ranges from 0 to $\pmb { x _ { 2 , m a x } }$ weeks, while $\underbrace { h _ { t } }$ takes on the value 1 if both subgroups are in the compartment and the value 0 if the slow growers are still being fattened and the fast growers have already been delivered. The price for pork takes on discrete values. We assume that it obeys a first order Markov scheme with stationary transition probabilities. The cut-off prices can be calculated from the optimality equations using standard methods given by Ross [5] or Tijms [6]. When a group consists of two subgroups, three vectors of cut-off prices are calculated, one for the fast growers, one for the group as a whole and one for the slow growers, given that the fast growers have been delivered.
4 Conclusion

In this paper a model is formulated which can be used to derive an optimal delivery strategy for heterogeneous groups of porkers. The feed schedule is assumed to be given. The central question is how the farmer should react on the variability of the pork price. The model provides a system of cut-off prices for pork during the weeks in which animals can be sold.

Based on the early work of Black and Scholes (1973) an enormous number of models to solve various option pricing problems has been derived. In these models besides the usual frictionless market conditions (e.g. no transaction costs, borrowing and lending at a known, constant short-term interest rate $\pmb { r }$ , free short selling of securities) assumptions on the exercise characteristics of options (american, european), the dividend-behaviour in the case of stock options and the stochastic process of the underlying security have to be made. Exact valuation formulas or closedform solutions are not available at all pricing problems. In such cases numerical procedures can be used to value derivative assets. Monte Carlo methods, first suggested by Boyle (1977), offer such procedures and give approximative solutions in many pricing situations.

The "fair" option value is usually found as the unique solution of a stochastic differential equation. If it is possible to derive the fundamental equation by hedging arguments, the option's value does not depend directly on the structure of investors' preferences. This characteristic of the so-called preference-free option pricing models was used by Cox and Ross (1976) in their risk neutral valuation approach. They showed that in such cases the option value could be derived by postulating some world where preferences are given and consistent with the specified parameter values. Then the preference-free solution of the pricing problem is, for example, equal to the equilibrium solution of the option's value in a world with risk neutral investors. Thus, the value of an european option on a non-dividend paying stock can be obtained by discounting the expected maturity option's value at the risk free rate $\pmb { r }$ , e. g. in the case of an european call with exercise price $\pmb { K }$ and maturity-date $\pmb { T _ { o } }$ the actual option price $c$ is given by

Option pricing and jump processes

In the standard Black and Scholes approach stock price movements are described by a continuous diffusion process. This model can't explain large price changes in short time. An alternative to that class of stochastic processes is the pure jump process of Cox and Ross (1976). The underlying price dynamics can be written as

$$

A closed-form solution can be derived only in the case of a very restrictive formulation of the jump behaviour. Applying a generalized version of Itô's Lemma to 4, see Aase (1988), we get the following recursive formula as the basis for the stock price simulation,

$$

By 5 and the fact that a riskless hedge can be constructed with a fixed $\pmb { Y }$ , Monte Carlo methods are useful to give approximative option values in the pure jump situation.
Merton (1976) postulates a mixture of the continuous brownian motion process and the discontinuous poisson process for the stock price dynamics as

$$
\frac { d S } { S } = ( \alpha - \lambda k ) d t + \sigma d w + d q ,
$$

It can be seen by 6 and 7 that this approach allows discontinuous large price changes in short time in addition to the continuous stock price changes modelled by Black and Scholes. The jump component can be understood as the process to describe the arrival of very important, "abnormal" new information, while the continuous component models the arrival of the "usual" new information. Because this model allows such an intuitive economic interpretation, modelling stock price returns by mixed jump-diffusion processes has become very popular.

While Merton makes the additional assumption that the jump amplitudes are lognormally distributed to obtain a closed-form solution, Monte Carlo methods allow different distributions for the discontinuous part. For example, empirical stock price distributions could be used, too. Also a bernoulli process instead of the above poisson process can easily be included in this numerical approach. Such a bernoulli jump process is suggested by Ball and Touros (1985) to simplify empirical evidence on mixed stock distributions. For concrete results see Schäfer (1993). Furthermore, deterministic dividend payments can be considered without further analysis. One just has to include the dividend structure in the generating function 7. Thus, Monte Carlo methods can extend the applicability of the Merton approach in an important extent. Since it is possible to value american call options on dividend paying stocks in the pure diffusion case by simulation methods, the complex mixed jump-diffusion model needs other numerical procedures, like finite difference methods or quadratic approximations, which seem to be more efficient.
Further remarks

Monte Carlo methods provide a wide variety of applications to option pricing problems, see e.g. Boyle (1976), Hull and White (1987), Hull (1989) and Schäfer (1993). It was shown that especially the case of jump processes can be generalized in many aspects. Furthermore, Monte Carlo simulation is useful for the pricing of derivative securities with history dependent-payoff (exotic options) and in cases where the underlying stock returns are generated by complex mixtures of stochastic processes.

The empirical research of German's stock price behaviour is small. Beinert and Trautmann (1991) give some evidence upon jump-diffusion price processes. They contradict the CAPM-linked argument of Merton who assumed that the jump component represents unsystematic risk. If this assumption is not fulfilled, the hedge approach of Merton to derive a preference-free stochastic differential equation can't be applied any more. An alternative jump-diffusion model may be found in Naik/Lee (1990).

A linear integer optimization problem (IP) has the modified integer round-up property (MIRUP) if the optimal value of any instance of IP is not greater than the optimal value of the corresponding LP relaxation problem rounded up plus one.
The aim of this paper is to investigate numerically whether the one-dimensional cutting stock problem has MIRUP.

1.Introduction

This Paper is concerned with comparison of different statistical and machine learning algorithms through application of these Methods in Credit-Scoring. Some Classical statistical Methods for classification can be considered as Methods of "learning from examples" or "supervised learning". Traditionally such statistical classifition Methods have been divided into two main groups of algorithms : parametric and non-parametric, depending on using the assumptions about the distribution of Attributes within each class.
In section two the classification of some classifiers will be discussed. Section three is devoted to application and evaluation of underlined Classification algorithms in Credit-Scoring.
.Classification of Classifiers (learning algorithms)
Linear-Discriminant analyses is an example for statistical parametric learning algorithm, while Kernel and K-nearest-neighbour are known as statistical non-parametric learning algorithms.

On the other hand machine learning which is a subarea of Artificial Intelligence, covers widely different algorithmes in inductive concept learning (learning from example), such as ID3, CN2, NewID,., which can be considerd as non-parametric learning methods, because there is no assumption about the distribution of attributes within each class necessary. Much of the research has been devoted to theoretical aspect or defining paradigms. Much less effort has been done to apply machine learning to the real world problem. Our attempt is to bear them on real-world application and compare them with known classical methods.

Linear-Discriminant analysis is one of the classical statistical learning algorithms, which refers to classifying observations into two or more known classes depending on one or more quantitative variables through building the polynomial function. 2.2.1 Statistical Algorithms

Kernel method is based on estimation of the density of attributes within each class using training set of the dataset. At each data point of a class is a "Kernel funktion" assumed. Depending on the choice of scaling parameter the shape of the Kernel function changes. The choice of scaling parameter is more important than the choice of kernel function.

k-nearest-neighbour procedure is based on density estimation. The nearest k point in training dataset will be observed to classify a new data point. The class of this new point is the most frequent class among them.

As Tom Peters points out, "information is everything" to business organizations in their pursuit of competitive advantage and profitability [Peters, 1992 p. 109]. The intangible aspect of information, however, gives managerial personnel the vague task of placing value on the systems which create, collect, compile, and translate information into a source of profitability. The information systems (IS) literature has dealt with this issue from a quantitative standpoint with varying results [cf Matlin, 1979, West & Courtney, 1993]. However, when senior executives are asked to indicate how information technology expenditures are quantified, they cannot point to a hard measurable quantity that can express the value of the IS [Katz, 1993].

This points to the primary problem in measuring the IT justification behaviors of managers. The way $\boldsymbol { \Pi }$ investments are quantified is a function of the attitudes of managers who make the investment decisions. Fishbein and Azjen (1980) propose that behavior is a function of the attitudes toward a particular object and the subjective assessment of the attitudes of relevant others in the organization (subjective norm). Hence, a model of attitudes toward the uses of $\boldsymbol { \Pi }$ in the organization would be a predictor of justification behaviors.

Katz (1993) found that two major shortcomings of devising metrics for $\boldsymbol { \Pi }$ are that 1) IS management does not often recognize the strategic potential of $\boldsymbol { \Pi }$ and only focuses on cost savings within the operational realm, and 2) the measures derived to value $\boldsymbol { \Gamma }$ expenses are usually representative of narrow interests within the organization. Dos Santos (1991) found that new technology projects that provide the opportunity for the organization to invest in other riskier projects have more overall value to the organization. Therefore, to fully value the potential and existing worth of IT investment, broad reaching consequences need to be factored into the manager's viewpoint of IT uses.

If managers have a broad strategic vision of the organizational uses of IT, then their behavior of assessing IT investment should encompass a broader, more comprehensive, and hence a more accurate, stance on $\boldsymbol { \Pi }$ value. The basis for this attitude is that some individuals perceive investments in IT as purely operational, i.e. IT has no competitive value and is purely a method of cost reduction. Others view IT investments as strategic weapons which can further the goals and objectives of the organization. Therefore, this perception could be placed on a continuum which rates the attitude toward $\boldsymbol { \Pi }$ investment from low strategic value to high strategic value.

Various factors explain the IT valuation attitudes. We hypothesize that four factors are important for explaining one's overall attitude toward the strategic uses of IT; 1) potential for strategic use, 2) potential for overall organizational infrastructure, 3) potential for long term use, and 4) perceptions of control over the investment. The sum of these attitudes are the factors which determine a manager's potential for assessing a broad strategic view of the investment and mark the placement on the continuum.

The attitude that IT has a potential for strategic uses of the investment is important to the alignment of IS efforts to the overall corporate focus and thus to proper valuation of the investment. Jeffery (1989) proposes that organizations that excel at the effective uses of IT focus on three core strategies related to the strategic function: base management, growth management and development management. These three areas represent a broad view of the potential the $\mathbf { I T }$ investment and thus must be considered when placing value on the justification of the investment.

The attitude that the $\boldsymbol { \Pi }$ investment has the potential for an overall enhancement of the infrastructure of the organization is also important to the attitudes toward IT value. Cash, McFarlan, and McKenney (1992) point out that today's business environment indicates the need to form information partnerships with not only your customers and suppliers, but also your competition and the industry as a whole. This points to the need for managers to have a broad view of the impact of $\boldsymbol { \Pi }$ investment to include not just the effects on the operational value but rather the alliances that IT can help forge. Cash et al. (1992) suggest that managers should ask the question "Is your company vulnerable to new information partnering, and are there ways to forge alliances of your own to preempt them? [page 105]." This question must be considered when determining the overall value of the IT investment.

The third contributing variable to a manager's attitude toward strategic valuation of an IT investment is the perception of potential for long-term use of the investment. Dos Santos (1991) indicates that many $\boldsymbol { \Pi }$ investments vary a great deal in terms of flexibility in determining how the project proceeds over time. Hence, IT investments are unlike many others which have the bulk of the initial outlay up front. This indicates that it is important for managers to realize the long term potential of both the cost and the benefits. Justifications of $\mathbf { I T }$ expenditures must take this into account in order to maximize the strategic benefits. This should result in behaviors which view the IT investment as long term with strategic potential.

Finally, managers must be able to perceive strategic control over the investment. If managers do not perceive that the IT project must be controlled to ensure compliance with the strategic focus of the organization, then justification of the IT expense will not be accurate. Identification of key trends, events, and changes in the firms environment that might influence how the firm functions is vital. Managers making justification decisions must feel confident in their own ability to understand what trends and events are taking place (Milliken, 1990). In addition, Lederer and Sethi (1991) found that if overall business planning is strategic versus tactical, implementation problems are less severe. This indicates that managers who have a strategic control perception of the $\boldsymbol { \Pi }$ investment and factor that into the justification process should have a more accurate assessment of the return on the expense.

Overall, manager's attitudes toward the expense of $\boldsymbol { \Gamma }$ projects weigh heavily on their ability to exhibit behaviors which result in a strategic quantification of the expected return. Strategic expenses are cost justified on a regular basis in most organizations. They are however justified on the basis of a long-term orientation. This must be the orientation of IT investments and a manager's attitudes toward these investments will determine whether they are being treated as such.

This model of IT valuation provides a different perspective on assessing the means to which $\mathbf { \Pi } ^ { \mathbf { \Pi } }$ projects are justified. In the social science tradition, this model needs to be empirically tested with rigorous research methodology. This includes the development of scales which can accurately measure a manager's attitude toward $\boldsymbol { \Gamma }$ investments. As social science research indicates, attitudes are keen predictors of behavioral intentions and further the actual behaviors themselves. The justification of $\boldsymbol { \Pi }$ investments is a behavior that has a means to be measured through the attitude of the $\boldsymbol { \Pi }$ expenditure having strategic value.

The "Business System Planning"-Problem

IBM's Business Systems Planning (BSP) (cf. IBM (1980)) is the best known method for strategic IS planning which is proposed as a first step in the information engineering concept. It primarily uses matrices which show associations between processes and data classes. The elements of the BSP-matrix show the symbol C for processes creating and U for those using data classes (Fig. 1a).

The objective of BSP is determining independent subsystems in such a way that almost all symbols are positioned within the submatrices at the main diagonal of a rearranged BSPmatrix. All C-entries must reside within those submatrices in order to guarantee the assignment of a data class to the process that is creating it.
Solving the BSP-problem with mixed integer programming

As a first approach, the problem can be modelled as a (modified) quadratic assignment problem, in which each row and each column has to be assigned to a subsystem. One of the techniques for solving this type of problem is to linearize it and then to apply mixed-integer programming. With this approach one has to fix the number of subsystems; the user is allowed to specify upper or lower bounds on the size of the subsystems (cf. Knolmayer 1993).
Solving the BSP-problem with boolean linear programming

The application of the Cluster Identification Algorithm (cf. Kusiak (1987)) allows to identify the set of submatrices fulflling the constraint that all C-entries must reside within the created subsystems. These submatrices are called baseblocks because they represent the first solution to the original problem with the most and smallest subsystems possible. All other possible solutions must be unions of these baseblocks. Thus, the BSP problem can be modelled as a boolean linear model with $\frac { N ( N - 1 ) } { 2 }$ variables and $\frac { N ( N - 1 ) ( \hat { N } - 2 ) } { 2 }$ constraints:

Introduction

A broad spectrum of ideas, approaches and tools for computer-support in complex problem solving has been proposed over the last decade and widely used in the design and implementation of decision support systems (DSS). The recent developments in the decision support (DS) technology are related to integrated use of methods and tools of modelling, simulation and artificial intelligence aiming at the design of intelligent DS environments.

In the paper are summarized the results of the design and implementation of an intelligent modelling and simulation environment for complex, ll-defined problem solving support. The architecture of an integrated software system comprising data, model, knowledge bases and a knowledge-based model management system has been designed. A problem-dependent software system SIMOS PAM has been implemented in a number of policy analysis applications.
Decision Support Cycle: Phases and Procedures

Following concepts and frameworks for DSS design launched in the ${ \mathfrak { s o } } ^ { \prime } { \mathfrak { s } }$ (Sprague and Carlson (1982), Sol (1983), etc., an extended definition of DS environment has been suggested: intelligent modelling and simulation environment in complex, ill-defined problem solving support (Strezova (1986).

A framework comprising a set of procedures supporting the problem solving process has been developed. The general phases of the DS cycle according to this framework are as follows: A. Problem Statement. B. Model Development. C. Model Assessment and Selection. D. Decision Support.

The first stage of the phase B concerns the design of a general model of the problem stated and identification of sets of model variables. It is next supposed that a set of conditions, representing problem states, defines a set of modelled alternatives of the problem stated; more than one parametrization is required to describe this set of alternatives.
The phase C consists in multimeasure cross-validation, assessment and selection of the set of modelled alternatives. The stages of this phase are as follows:

simulation of the set of modelled alternatives   
1t validation: screening procedure (Walker (1986)   
$2 ^ { \mathsf { n d } }$ validation: sensitivity analysis I   
$\mathsf { \Omega } _ { 3 ^ { \mathsf { r d } } }$ validation: sensitivity analysis I (metamodellingvia regression analysis)
The phase D consists in analysis of the set of feasible alternatives via hypothesing future decision states of the problem modelled and a choice of the "best feasible" alternative for implementation.
Integrated Software Environment: Architecture and Functions
A generalized software system (GSS) intended for supporting the phases and the stages of the DS cycle has been designed. The GSS architecture consists of general purpose modules as is shown in Fig.1.
The Knowledge Base (KB) design process consists of phases and stages as follows:
ADesign (or choice) of knowledge shell. B. Knowledge acquisition phase comprising two stages:
B.1. Knowledge shell parameterizing; B.2. Parameter estimation stage. C. Inference knowledge generation.

Designed in such a way the KB is intended to support the modelling stages of the problem solving cycle. The KB provides metaknowledge used for model building, model assessment, validation, comparison and selection of feasible alternatives. The integrated software system for management of the pool of DB, MB, KB (this pool represents an extended KB), is considered as a Knowledge-Based Model Management System.
Application

Following the GSS architecture a problem dependent software system SIMOS PAM has been developed. The model shell of SIMOs PAM comprises program packages such as Discriminant Analysis, Mixed Integer Programming, GPSS, CSMP, LRA and a number of special purpose models. The knowledge shell embodies sets of deductive, numerical and testing rules, and sets of hypotheses concerning possible future states of a class of applications.
The concepts, procedures and systems developed have been implemented in policy analysis applications concerning the transition to new political and economic structures in Bulgaria.
Conclusion and Research Directions

A knowledge-based approach to the design of DS environment has been suggested and implemented. The notion "knowledge" is considered in a larger sense: data, models, algorithms, solution procedures, operators, rules, options, heuristics, etc.

A number of problems related to the design of intelligent DS environments represents a challenge for further research: model management topics (Chang, Holsapple, Whinston (1993), KB validation & verification, design of distributed intelligent DSS, techniques for combined use of methods and tools of information and Al technologies, etc.

The purpose of a real telecommunication network is to keep services on the best obtainable level. In order to do this, a network with overflows is often proposed. The idea boils down to collecting unserved parts of traffic from several lines (primary lines) and putting them together to another line which is not so busy (secondary line). A model of such network is presented which let us :

- examine general losses in a primary line,   
- describe a distribution function of busy links and losses in a secondary line,   
- fix a necessary number of links in a secondary line for chosen grade of service,   
- compare various strategies of control (e.g. different connection of streams).

But in some situations it is also important to decompose the general losses in a secondary line again into individual streams. The oryginal method (based on probability theory) enabling such a decomposition is proposed. The results are presented and compared to other methods. Although the method was proposed for a telecommunication network, it may be used for other networks with overflows when uncertain information is obtainable.
USING UNCERTAIN INFORMATION FROM A TELECOMMUNICATION NETWORK
METHODS

It is worth pointing out that the presented models are based on the measurements of a mean and a variance in an overload primary line. So parameters of a secondary line are calculated under uncertain circumstances. The model starts from an assumption of Normal distribution function of busy links in a line without losses. It is justified by the principle of maximum entropy - the most safe criterion in determining a distribution function under uncertain circumstances. The assumption was also verified by measurements in the real network.

Having a distribution function of busy links in a secondary line and knowing the parameters of each overflow we can evaluate losses of a separete overflow. First a distribution function of all the remaining overflows must be calculated. We obtain in effect only two distribution functions. Then probabilities of all possible losses from examined stream must be calculated and for each possibility of losses the event with the highest probability is accepted.
The method let us divide common losses in the most probable way. We obtain distribution function of losses (not only parameters). It is important when the losses "become overflows".

A lot of calculation were made to compare the presented method with other ones, Kuczura (1977), Manfield (1979) . The quantity results are available from the author. As far as the real network was examined, the quality results were also obtained.

Conclusions for a line without own calls :   
- a stream with greater peakedness Z (Z is the ratio: a variance to a mean of a stream) has greater losses,   
- as a number of links in a line increases, participation of a stream with greater Z in general losses :   
- increases when the peakednesses $\mathsf { z } _ { \mathbf { i } }$ of examined streams are of the same order,   
- decreases when the peakednesses $z _ { \mathrm { i } }$ of examined streams are different.
Conclusions for a line with own calls :

- own calls are serviced better than overflowed calls,   
, as the number of links in a line increases, percentage participation in general losses : - of own calls - decreases, - of overflowed calls - increases.
FINAL REMARKS

1. Th e proposed method deals with uncertainty in a telecommunication network.   
2. The proposed method let us decompose total losses and distribute them into individual streams.   
3. As a result we obtain the random variable distribution of losses from the chosen stream instead of the "pure" probability of losses.   
4. Assumptions made for the model let us use it for different networks (not only a telecommunication network).   
5. Computation times are comparable with other methods, Manfield (1979), Szmidt (1984).

Introduction

Within the interpretation step of a data analysis process—as one example—it would be helpful to rank the different variables according to their similarity to the solution. But then it is first necessary to define the "similarity to the solution" and how this can be measured appropriately.

One possible approach is the definition of a measure which describes the strength of "similarity" (or "concordance") numerically. With values varying between 0 and 1, such measure is usually called index.
It is obvious that the definition of such an index is based explicitly or implicitly on a specific data model. This fact clearly influences its applicability for a certain problem.
Typical application areas of indices can, however, be characterized as follows.

Properties of the data Having collected the data, it is useful to check whether the data actually have some common structure (as assumed) which then can be extracted by the application of a data analysis technique.

Properties of the solution Many data analysis techniques will determine a solution even if the specific data set does not fit the underlying model. An index can be used to examine how strong the solution supports the structure of the model.

Comparison of solutions As a result of the application of different analysis techniques to a single data set, a comparison of the solutions is often desirable. Because each objective function usually stresses a certain aspect of the data, an index measure can introduce an additional independent criterion.

Comparison of partitions

The underlying concept of the Rand Index had already been proposed earlier in different forms (and was several times rediscovered again; see, for example, (Hubert and Arabie, 1985) for the historical background). But Rand (Rand, 1971) was the first to formulate it for the comparison of two partitions by means of the entries of a contingency table.

The comparison is based on the observation which classes of the two partitions a pair of objects is assigned to. If the two objects are in the same class in both partitions, or in different classes in both partitions, this is considered as "similar", the other case (in the same class in one partition, in different classes in the other) as "dissimilar". Dividing the number of all unordered pairs of objects with similar classifications by $n ( n - 1 ) / 2$ , the total number of different (unordered) pairs of $\pmb { n }$ objects, a measure of similarity is defined. This index is 0, if there is no similarity (one partition consists of a single class (with all objects), the other of $\pmb { n }$ classes with one element); it is 1 if both partitions are identical.

Originally, Sokal and Michener (Sokal and Michener, 1958) have proposed their simple matching coefficient as a similarity measure for binary variables. Being interpreted as a measure for the comparison of two classifications, it corresponds to the Rand index.

Mirkin and Chernyi (Mirkin and Chernyi, 1970) have defined several axioms which should be satisfied by a measure of distance between two partitions. They show that the symmetric difference distance has these properties. In this context, they define the ratio

In the Modigliani-Miller world of perfect capital markets there is no need to manage the idiosyncratic risk of corporations. However, bankruptcy costs, the tax system and agency costs deriving from information asymmetries create a rationale to control the total risk of a bank. The objective of bank risk management thus is to optimize the risk/return position of the bank. Since a bank consists of a portfolio of different and often interdependent risks, this objective can only be achieved by incorporating risk interrelations into the analysis. We propose a practical method how the total risk of a bank including risk interrelations can be determined and how the risk/return situation of individual business units can be evaluated from the total bank perspective. For our analysis we choose a continuous time portfolio model, in which a set of random risk factors drives the bank profit. This specification alows the inclusion of many different bank risks such as interest rate risks, foreign exchange risks, credit risks and risks from derivative products into one unifying framework. The bank profit is modeled using a first order Taylor series approximation of the pricing functions of bank assets and liablities. The total bank risk is expressed in terms of the standard deviation of profits over short periods of time. We then demonstrate how banks with decentralized decision making authority nevertheless can optimize their overall risk/return trade off by using the risk contribution of their business units to the total bank risk as the relevant measure of risk. The optimization of the toal risk position can be easily incorporated into the bank's accounting system by employing business unit equity costs that are based on their contribution to the total bank risk. The proposed concept provides senior management with a simple tool to allocate the bank's capital such' that the bank's risk/return trade off is optimized and to provide business unit managers with incentives to optimize the total bank risk exposure.

Besides the optimization of the bank's risk/return trade off, the outlined framework has further promising applications in the field of risk measurement and risk management. We discuss how the concept can be used to visualize risk through scenario analysis, to monitor the bank's risk exposure, to evaluate the adequacy of the bank's equity capitalization and finally to set prices based on the bank's current risk situation. We further discuss the appropiateness of our equity cost concept to evaluate the risk adjusted performance of business unit managers or traders. It is shown that the concept provides a fair benchmark profit for performance evaluation only if the bank's total equity cost rate is the actually expected market risk premium on its assets and liabilities and if the bank portfolio is mean variance efficient. This implies that if the bank for some strategic reasons chooses an inefficient portfolio, calculatory profits or losses do not automatically indicate good or poor performance of business unit managers. While currently accounting profits are used both to guide risk taking decisions and to evaluate manager performance, sophisticated future risk management systems should use separate systems for the risk taking function and for risk adjusted performance evaluation. Since bank management wants to reward business units for both beating the market and for improving the total bank risk position, it needs two distinct incentive systems to pursue both goals.

Dually-Weighted Cross Decomposition for the Capacitated Facility Location Problem
Paul Wentges Institut für Unternehmensforschung der Hochschule St. Gallen Bodanstr. 6, 9000 St. Gallen, Switzerland
Abstract

The cross decomposition algorithm of [van Roy 1986] is generally considered to be one of the most efficient procedures for solving the capacitated facility location problem. A modified version of this algorithm, called dually-weighted cross decomposition, is presented. In contrast to the cross decomposition algorithm, this approach does not use the optimal dual solutions of the primal subproblems or the optimal solutions of the dual master problem as Lagrangean multipliers for the dual subproblems. A specially weighted average of the previously constructed multipliers is used instead. Finite convergence of this approach is proven and first promising results are discussed.

The cross decomposition algorithm of [van Roy 1986] simultaneously exploits both the primal structure (temporarily fixing the variables $_ y$ yields a normal transportation problem) and the dual structure (with relaxing the capacity constraints (3) in lagrangean fashion) of the (CFLP), i. e. combines Benders' decomposition and Dantzig-Wolfe decomposition in one single framework. The approach is motivated by the fact, that the primal subproblem can be viewed as a relaxed dual (Dantzig-Wolfe) master problem and the dual subproblem as a relaxed primal (Benders) master problem (see e.g. [van Roy 1983]).

The main steps of the algorithm can be described as follows (let $( S D _ { \mu } )$ be the Lagrangean relaxation of $( C F L P )$ with respect to the capacity constraints (3) and the Lagrangean multipliers $\mu$ b $( M D _ { k } )$ the relaxed Dantzig-Wolfe master problem: $\textstyle \operatorname* { m a x } \{ \delta : \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } f _ { j } y _ { j } ^ { t } +$ $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } c _ { i j } x _ { i j } ^ { t } - \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } ( s _ { j } y _ { j } ^ { t } - \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } x _ { i j } ^ { t } ) \mu _ { j } \geq \delta \forall t \in T _ { k } ; } \end{array}$ $\mu \geq 0 , \delta \in \mathbb { R } \}$ $( S P _ { y } )$ the transportation problem obtained when $_ y$ is fixed, and $( M P _ { k } )$ a relaxed Benders master problem; for a more detailed and explicit description of the problems see [van Roy 1986]):

Step 1: Initialize and get a dual solution $\mu ^ { 1 }$ (by solving the primal subproblem $( S P _ { y ^ { 0 } } )$ with $y ^ { 0 } \equiv 1$ ).   
Step 2: Solve the dual subproblem $( S D _ { \mu ^ { k } } )$ : Let $( x ^ { k } , y ^ { k } )$ be an optimal solution. Perform a convergence test; if the test is not fulfilled, go to step 5.   
Step 3: Solve the primal subproblem $( S P _ { y ^ { k } } )$ : Let $( \lambda ^ { k + 1 } , \nu ^ { k + 1 } , \mu ^ { k + 1 } )$ be an optimal dual solution. Perform a convergence test; if the test is not fulfilled, go to step 5 (or step 4, see below), otherwise go to step 2 and set $k : = k + 1$ .   
Step 4: Solve the primal master problem $\left( M P _ { k } \right)$ : Let $y ^ { k + 1 }$ be an optimal solution. Go to step 3 and set $k : = k + 1$ .   
Step 5: Solve the dual master problem $( M D _ { k } )$ : Let $\mu ^ { k + 1 }$ be an optimal solution. Go to step 2 and set $k : = k + 1$ .

In steps 2 and 3, cuts corresponding to the optimal solutions have to be added to the respective master problems; in each step, optimality has to be checked. If the Lagrangean dual is solved within a specified tolerance level $\tau$ (e.g. $0 . 5 \%$ ), one switches to Benders' decomposition (only usage of steps 3 and 4).

The cross decomposition algorithm solves the (CFLP) in a finite number of steps, since the convergence tests prevent the algorithm from cycling and therefore, after finitely many steps, the method amounts to Benders' decomposition, which is known to be finite (see e.g. [van Roy 1983] and [Holmberg 1990], respectively).
2. Dually-weighted cross decomposition

[Holmberg 1992] proposed a modification of the cross decomposition algorithm (mean value cross decomposition) to solve linear programming problems, where, in contrast to the cross decomposition algorithm, not the last optimal solution of one subproblem is used as input to the other and vice versa, but the arithmetic mean of all previously obtained optimal solutions of the respective subproblem. No master problems are used anymore and asymptotic convergence towards the optimum can be proven.

A somewhat similar approach is suggested here for the (CFLP). Instead of using the optimal dual solutions of the primal subproblems or the optimal solutions of the dual master problem as Lagrangean multipliers for the dual subproblems (like in cross decomposition) or taking the arithmetic mean of all these multipliers (like in mean value cross decomposition), a specially weighted average of the previously constructed multipliers is used.

In other words, lemma 3 states that every time a normal cross decomposition step gives an improvement of the lower bound, the same is true for dually-weighted cross decomposition. It is important to note that the opposite does not hold, although a normal cross decomposition step possibly yields a higher improvement of the lower bound.
3. Results

The cross decomposition and the dually-weighted cross decomposition algorithms were tested on 27 examples with 19-108 potential facilities and 65-174 customers on the road network of Switzerland. In these examples, a tolerance level $\tau$ of $0 . 5 \%$ for the duality gap $v ( M D _ { k } ) \mathrm { ~ - ~ }$ $v ( S D _ { \mu ^ { \mathrm { b e s t } , k } } )$ was used, in step 3 the dual solution $( \lambda ^ { k + 1 } , \nu ^ { k + 1 } , \mu ^ { k + 1 } )$ was altered as described in [Wentges 1993], and at most thirty iterations were carried out.

With the new dually-weighted cross decomposition algorithm better results could be achieved in almost all examples compared to ordinary cross decomposition. The Lagrangean dual could now be solved within the tolerance level $\tau$ in 19 instead of 11 examples (where only in three of these 11 examples, the tolerance level was reached earlier by ordinary cross decomposition, and in two cases, the same number of iterations was needed). In all other examples the duality gap $v ( M D _ { k } ) - v ( S D _ { \mu ^ { \mathrm { b e s t } , k } } )$ could be decreased substantially.
Remark: Weighting the Lagrangean multipliers as described above, may also be useful in other applications of Dantzig-Wolfe decomposition.

Some types of scheduling problems can be solved as edge coloring models in bipartite multigraphs. It is in particular the case for preemptive open shop scheduling. The presence of additional constraints generally transforms this polynomially solvable type of problem into a difficult one. The study of polynomially solvable special cases is therefore interesting for guiding the development of general heuristic procedures.

Among these additional constraints, the so called preassignment constraints play an important role. They can be handled by saying that in the graph model some edges have been precolored and this precoloring must be extended to the whole graph (with a given number of colors available).

In general this problem is NP-complete; however we will consider special cases where the precolored edges are simply a bicolored path or cycle. This will lead us to study several classes of (multi-)graphs for which the extension of coloring can be done easily whatever cycle or path is precolored.

A mouth in a graph consists of three elementary chains of some parity having the same end nodes (the intermediate nodes are all distinct). A mouth is even(resp. odd) if the three chains are even (resp. odd). It is a cone if at least one of the three chains has length two.
A cpi k-coloring of the edges of a multigraph G is an assignment to each edge of one color chosen in the cyclically ordered set $\left\{ 1 , \ldots , \mathbf { k } \right\}$ such that:

a) all edges in a family of p parallel edges receive $\mathtt { p }$ cyclically consecutive colors (notice that if $p > k$ the same color can occur several times)   
b) in every bundle of adjacent edges the colors form a cyclic interval.
A simple graph G is cpi-perfect if all multigraphs $\mathtt { G } ^ { \star }$ obtained by multiplying edges of G in an arbitrary way has a cpi kcoloring for any k.
Such colorings are needed in some types of cyclic scheduling.

AREA DESCRIPTION

In the forest the silvicultural and utilization process is carried out by performing a sequence of decisions, like the felling and the planting of the trees. Within these practices the forest product is yielded. The amount of the yield should stay at an approximately fixed annual level. This could be realized by so-called "normal forest". Moreover, living and growing of the trees are affected by unpredictable natural circumstances. Therefore, the forest as a system contains both, the decision making and the probabilistic features. Stochastic dynamic models are very appropriate for providing the optimal forest management decisions maximizing the sustained timber production and net revenues to the society (Hool (1966), Lembersky et al. (1975), Binkley (1980), Kao (1982), Kaya et al. (1987), Hassler et al. (1988)).

A general stochastic dynamic model used for optimal forest management is described by Zadnik (1992). The forest process is treated as a discrete multistage process since the decisions are carried out only at discrete time points t $( \mathrm { t } { = } 0 , 1 , { \ldots } , \mathrm { i } , \mathrm { i } { + } 1 , { \ldots } )$ .These time points divide the time into time intervals. We say, that in the time point $\mathbf { t } { = } \mathbf { i }$ a forest as a system occupies a state ${ \mathfrak { s } } ^ { * } ( \mathrm { i } )$ when it is described by the values of variables that define the state. The system makes a transition to a new state $\mathsf { s } ^ { \ast } ( \mathrm { i } + 1 )$ in the lapse of time interval under the influence of the decision $\mathbf { d } ( \mathbf { s } ^ { * } ( \mathbf { i } ) , \mathbf { h } )$ , where $\mathbf { h } { = } 1 , { \ldots } , \mathbf { H }$ and $\mathbf { H }$ is the number of all the possible decisions at the forest state $\mathbf { s } ^ { * } ( \mathbf { i } )$ : $\mathbf { s } ^ { * } ( \mathrm { i } + 1 ) \ = \ \mathbf { f } ( \mathbf { s } ^ { * } ( \mathrm { i } ) , \mathsf { d } ( \mathbf { s } ^ { * } ( \mathrm { i } ) , \mathrm { h } ) )$ . The forest process has a stochastic character. There exists the probability $\mathtt { p ( s ^ { * } ( i ) , s ^ { * } ( i + 1 ) , d ( s ^ { * } ( i ) , h ) ) }$ of a transition to the state $\mathbf { s } ^ { * } ( \mathbf { i } + 1 )$ during the next time interval, given that the system occupies the state ${ \mathfrak { s } } ^ { * } ( { \mathfrak { i } } )$ and that the decision $\mathbf { d } ( \mathbf { s } ^ { * } ( \mathbf { i } ) , \mathbf { h } )$ is undertaken. Each transition of the system generates the reward $\mathbf { r } ( \mathbf { s } ^ { * } ( \mathfrak { i } ) , \mathfrak { s } ^ { * } ( \mathfrak { i } + 1 ) , \mathsf { d } ( \mathfrak { s } ^ { * } ( \mathfrak { i } ) , \mathfrak { h } ) )$ associated with a net revenue from timber harvest and other revenues to the society. An optimal sequence of decisions and rewards are usually determined by the use of discrete stochastic dynamic programming (Vadnal (1976)).

Let us suppose that there are $\mathbf { N }$ states $\mathbf { s } ^ { * } ( \mathbf { i } )$ in the forest system at each time point t $( \mathrm { t } { = } 0 , 1 , { \ldots } , \mathrm { i } , \mathrm { i } { + } 1 , { \ldots } )$ , numbered from 1 to $\mathbf { N }$ , and that the probability of the transition fom the state $\mathbf { s } ^ { * } ( \mathbf { i } )$ to the state $\mathbf { s } ^ { * } ( \mathrm { i } + 1 )$ is a function only of these two states and not of any history of the system before its arrival in $\mathfrak { s } ^ { * } ( \mathrm { i } )$ . This probability is constant over time (homogeneous stationary Markov model). Under these suppositions a discrete-time Markov process (Kouba (1977), Suzuki (1984), Zadnik (1987)) can be involved in the above described forest management model. In such a model, the state of the forest $\mathbf { s } ^ { * } ( \mathbf { i } )$ is modelled using only the ratio of the various age classes of the forest. This means, that all the trees are distributed over a finite number of classes and that the trees move from one class to another independently of each other, i. e. there is no interaction among the individual trees taken into account. The last assumption is an extremely limiting one. That is why the focus of this paper is on the interaction among the individual trees, on the so-called interactive Markov model. It was proposed by Conlisk (1976), used in the studies of dynamics of social systems (Kulkarni et al. (1989), Omladi (1991), (1992)), but it has not yet been introduced to forestry.
INTERACTIVE MARKOV MODEL USED IN FOREST MANAGEMENT

All the trees (a large number of trees is assumed) of a managed forest are distributed within n mutually exclusive classes, assigned by 1,2,..,k,j,..,n. In this case, it is possible to describe the state of the forest at each time point t $( \mathrm { t } { = } 0 , 1 , \ldots , \mathrm { i } , \mathrm { i } { + } 1 , \ldots )$ in a form of a vector ${ \mathfrak { s } } ( { \mathfrak { i } } ) =$ $( \mathbf { { s _ { 1 i } } , \mathbf { { s _ { 2 i } } , \dots , \mathbf { { s _ { k i } } , \mathbf { { s _ { j i } } , \dots , \mathbf { { s _ { n i } } } } } } } )$ The probabilities $\mathbf { p _ { k j } }$ for an individual tree to move from class $\mathbf { k }$ to class $\mathbf { j }$ in the next time interval form a stochastic matrix $\mathbf { P }$ in a homogeneous stationary Markov case. Universally, the matrix $\mathbf { P } = \mathbf { \{ p _ { \mathbf { k } } \mathbf { \} } } $ is assumed not to depend on $\mathsf { s } ( \mathrm { i } )$ , that is, not to depend on the interactive behaviour of the trees: $\mathbf { s } ( \mathbf { i } { + } 1 ) = \mathbf { P s } ( \mathbf { i } )$ .

It is the interactive Markov model which includes the fact that individual trees follow not only their own development but are also influenced by the others. This model is derived from a general Markov model and concerns that the elements of $\mathbf { P }$ are functions of s(i). P is written as $\mathbf { P } [ \mathbf { s } ( \mathbf { i } ) ]$ . SOLVING DIAL-A-RIDE PROBLEMS IN PRACTICE
Doris Zepf Universität Passau Innstr. 29, D-94032 Passau

We want to represent the results of a joint work with a public transportation company. In the last years, the public transportation services were looking for alternatives for scheduled busses. As a result of decreasing demand for public transportation in the off-peak-hours, the aim was to provide more efficient means of transportation. One result of these considerations is the dial-a-ride system.

The dial-a-ride taxis have a fixed time-table, but they run only if required. The customer has to book them before. Moreover, there are fixed stops for departure, but the people are transported where they want, e.g. to their home.
The dial-a-ride system has the advantage of increasing rentability. Further it is more comfortable because of more security, decreasing travel time and easy transport etc.

Our goal is now to realize the automatic disposition of the taxis. We have to determine how many vehicles are necessary and to fix the routes the taxis have to drive, such that certain conditions are fulflled and a given objective (cost) function is as low as possible.

From the transportation company we were given time restrictions. Because of the organizational structure it was necesseary to produce good solutions within 5 minutes such that a re-optimization can be called if belatet orders arrive or the side conditions change (e.g. if not enough taxis are ready to carry out the bookings ).

Therefore we managed the problem with vehicle routing. We implemented fast heuristics that computed feasible solutions and improving procedures to improve the objective function. Moreover, to examine the quality of the solutions, we modelled the problem as a set partitioning problem. Based on this integer programming model, we compute lower bounds with cutting plane techniques.
METHODS

For the vehicle routing approach we constructed the graph in the following way. The region which is served is partitioned into a number of sections. The nodes of the underlying graph are in a one-to-one correspondence to the sections. Two nodes are connected by an edge if there is a street connecting the two corresponding sections without passing throughhh a third zone. The edge weights represent the time/distance between its endpoints.

In our special case the side constraints were the following. The maximal duration of a tour totals 15 minutes. The taxis have a maximal capacity of 4 persons. Further the comfort of the customer shall be increased, so there is a maximal delay (of 5 minutes) for him to be picked up. Because of the different departure times outward and inward demands are treated separately.

The current vehicle routing problem now has precedence constraints because every customer has to be picked up before he is delivered. On the other hand we are confronted with time windows because the customers must be picked up within a given time.

We implemented several constructing heuristics, similar to the greedy or insertion heuristics of the TSP or to the savings [1] heuristic. As improving methods we used 2-exchange and 2-Or-exchange methods inside a tour and between different tours.

In the set partitioning attempt we generate in a heuristic way feasible tours one vehicle can carry out following the time and capacity restrictions. The columns of the resulting matrix indicate which appointments each of the generated tours executes. We now have to solve the set partitioning problem

We start with the solution of the LP-relaxation $\operatorname* { m i n } \{ c ^ { T } x \mid A x = 1 , \ x \geq 0 \}$ and step by step add cutting planes to improve the lower bounds. The set partitioning polytope is a subset of both the set packing polytope and the set covering polytope. For this reason valid inequalities for the set covering or the set packing polytope are also valid for the set partitioning polytope.

We use the od cycle and cliqe inequalitis [2] of the t packing polytope as cuttig planes. Further we have found new facet inducing graphs for the set packing problem that we also separate in a heuristic way.

For the given test problems our heuristics constructed optimal or near-optimal solutions. With our cutting plane procedures we could prove the optimality of our vehicle routing heuristics in many cases.

Hans-Joachim Zwiesler Abteilung Mathematik V Universität Ulm D - 89069 Ulm, Germany
What is profitability?

In our context profitability is a measure of the future financial outcome of an insurance contract from the point of view of the insurance company. It determines how profitable it is for the company to sell a certain type of insurance product. (In the following we concentrate on life insurance as an example.)
How do we measure profitability?

Since profitability is a future-oriented view of the profit or loss of an insurance contract, it is based on the yearly expected cash-flow of an individual contract under realistic assumptions. This contrasts the current practice in Germany where the calculation of premiums (for private insurance) makes use of idealized actuarial bases which contain substantial safety loadings.

The computation of the expected cash-flow must take into account all effects for the company (required reserves, taxation, solvency margin etc.). For the valuation of the expected cash-flow several methods can be used:

The internal rate of return is the interest rate that leads to zero as discounted cash-value of the expected cash-flow. It emphasizes the point of view that losses are investments of the company whereas profits are refunds together with interest.

The year of break-even is the first year in which the accumulated expected cash-flow is nonnegative. It indicates how long it takes until the company's investment is paid back, i.e. when the product really starts to gain money for the company.

Both of these methods use only the company's perspective. They do not take into account the two other main factors, the customer and the agent. Their needs must be balanced against the company's need. For that purpose, one compares the premium and the initial commission to the cash-value of the expected cash-flow (using the risk discount rate, i.e. the minimal interest rate sought by the company). In relation to the premium, the cash-value should not .exceed a certain limit (mainly determined by competition).
On the other hand, cash-value and initial commission should be proportional (where the constant of proportionality is again mainly determined by competition).
Which of these methods is used, depends on the specific circumstances.
The use of profitability in product-design
The investigation of profitability is a main tool in the design of a new insurance product. The underlying iterative process is described in the following diagram:

One has to take into account that the same product is sold to different policy holders and that assumptions are not accurately predictable. Therefore, it is indispendable that various sets of assumptions are considered which reflect the distinct possible future scenarios. The results of that analysis can be changings in the design of the product as well as further insight into which key factors mainly influence the profitability. These have to be given particular attention, e.g. in the context of marketing strategies.
The profitability of a company

Our definition of profitability can also be applied to evaluate whether the start-up of a new company will be a profitable investment or not. Here commercial assumptions (interest, inflation, costs etc.) and expected new business are used to calculate the excepted future cash-flow of the whole company and determine its profitability.

Product profitability and company profitability are not only useful as ${ \bf \sp { u } _ { a } }$ priori evaluation tools", but can serve for controlling purposes as well. In this case, the actual cash-flow is compared to the previously predicted cash-flow. The analysis of the deviation allows conclusions on the accuracy of the assumptions. The updated assumptions give rise to a new expected cash-flow whose profitability may give rise to modifications in the product-design or the company's strategy.

Abstract. An individual's tolerance of risk can be quantified by using decision models with tuned parameters that maximally fit a set of risky choices the individual has made. A goal of this model fitting procedure is to identify parameters that correspond to stable underlying risk preferences. These preferences can be modeled as an individual difference, indicating a particular decision maker's tastes and willingness to accept risk. Using hierarchical statistical methods, we show significant improvements in the reliability of individual risk preference parameter estimates over other common methods for cumulative prospect theory. This hierarchical procedure uses population-level information (in addition to an individual's choices) to break "ties" (or near ties) in the fit quality for sets of possible risk preference parameters. By breaking these statistical ties in a sensible way, researchers can avoid overfitting choice data and thus more resiliently measure individual differences in people's risk preferences.

1. Introduction

People must often make choices among a number of different options for which the outcomes are not certain. Such choices are referred to as risky when the options are well-defined sets of outcomes and each has its respective payoff(s) and probability of fruition (Knight 1921, Edwards 1954, Luce and Raiffa 1957) clearly described. Expected value (EV) maximization stands as a benchmark solution to risky choice problems, but people's behavior does not always conform to this optimization principle. Rather, decision makers (DMs) reveal different preferences for risk, sometimes, for example, forgoing an option with a higher expectation in lieu of an option with lower variance (thus indicating risk aversion; in some cases DMs reveal the opposite preference, too, indicating risk seeking). Behavioral theories of risky decision making (Kahneman and Tversky 1979, 2000; Tversky and Kahneman 1992; Camerer 1995) have been developed to identify and highlight the structure in these choice patterns and provide psychological insights into DMs' revealed preferences. Reliable measures of risk preferences allow researchers to investigate the associations between risky choice behavior and other variables of interest and allow the incorporation of risk preferences in other contexts (e.g., Camerer 2004, Huettel et al. 2006). This paper is about measuring those subjective risk preferences and in particular developing a statistical estimation procedure that can increase the reliability and robustness of those parameter estimates, thus better capturing risk preferences and doing so consistently at the individual level.
1.1. Three Necessary Components for Measuring Risk Preferences

There are three elementary components in measuring risk preferences and these parts serve as the foundation for developing behavioral models of risky choice. These three components are lotteries, models, and statistical estimation/fitting procedures. We explain each of these components below in general terms and then provide detailed examples and a discussion of the elements in the subsequent sections of the paper.

1.1.1. Lotteries. Choices among options reveal DMs' preferences (Samuelson 1938, Varian 2006). Lotteries are used to elicit risky decisions, and these resulting choice data serve as the input for the decision models and parameter estimation procedures. Here we focus on choices from binary lotteries (Stott 2006, Rieskamp 2008, Nilsson et al. 2011; see Table A.1 in Appendix A for an example lottery and Appendix E for all the lotteries). The elicitation of certainty equivalence values is another well-established method for quantifying risk preferences (e.g., see Zeisberger et al. 2012). Binary lotteries are arguably a simpler way for DMs to make risky choices and thus elicit risk preferences. One reason to use binary lotteries is because people appear to have problems with assessing a lottery's certainty equivalent (Lichtenstein and Slovic 1971, Harrison and Rutström 2008), although this simplicity comes at the cost of requiring a DM to make many binary choices to achieve the same degree of estimation fidelity that other methods purport to have (e.g., the three decision risk measure from Tanaka et al. 2010).
