Fähigkeiten ist der Respekt, den die einzelnen Teammitglieder einander entgegenbringen müssen.

Die OF-Abteilung als ein Referat der Informationsgewinnung und -veredelung hat im Organisationsaufbau der Unternehmung eine reine Stabsfunktion. Ihr Leiter sollte, wenn man sich nicht für eine kollegiale Leitung (1 Betriebswirtschafter und 1 Formalwissenschaftler) entscheidet, ein Betriebswirtschafter sein; er müBte den Weg bestimmen. Das ergibt sich einfach daraus, daB es sich um betriebswirtschaftliche Probleme handelt, die operationsanalytisch zu klä- ren sind. Ein Betriebswirtschafter an der Spitze einer derartigen Stabsabteilung - allerdings müBte er auch mathematisch geschult sein - würde auch eher als ein Formalwissenschaftler darauf achten, dab die von der OF-Gruppe für die Geschäftsführung verfaBten SchluBberichte in einer verständlichen Sprache abgefat würden. Das ist ein sehr wichtiges Erfordernis, wenn nicht die Mühen und Arbeiten operationsanalytischer Untersuchungen wirkungslos verpuffen sollen. Der Operationsforscher mu auf jeden Fall imstande sein, ,,seine hochtechnische Sprache in die der Ausführenden zu übersetzen, eine Sprache, die klar und einfach Wert, Wirksamkeit und Kosten verschiedener zukünftiger Arbeitsrichtungen enthält" (15), und er begeht einen ernsten Fehler, wenn er das übersieht. Es ist unzureichend, der Unternehmungsleitung einige wenige Formeln als Ergebnis der vorhergegangenen Analysen anzubieten. Vielmehr muB das Resultat in die Sprache des Wirtschafters übersetzt werden, muB so formuliert sein, daB es von denen, die damit arbeiten sollen, leicht verstanden wird. Jede mathematisch-statistische Kabbalistik ist zu vermeiden (16).

Herrmann und Magee sagen sogar, daB, je erfahrener die Operationsforscher sind, sie desto mehr erkennen werden, daB die Erläuterungen von Forschungsergebnissen genauso wichtig sind wie die Konklusionen selbst (17).

Obwohl der Operationsforscher im Interesse der Sache auch die Durchführung der von ihm empfohlenen Handlungen weiterhin verfolgen wird, vielleicht auch deshalb, weil er befürchten muB, daB seine Lösungsvorschläge von den entscheidenden Personen falsch ausgelegt und in abgeänderter Form realisiert werden, so ist er doch grundsätzlich für betriebswirtschaftliche Entscheidungen unzuständig; er ist nur Berater, empfiehlt, bestimmte Wege einzuschlagen, gibt Ratschläge, trifft aber selbst keine Manahmen. Er ist kein Mann der unternehmerischen Tat, ,,denn er handelt nicht gern, wenn er der UngewiBheit gegenübersteht" (18). Man kann tatsächlich sogar behaupten, daB die Anforderungen an den Entscheidungsverantwortlichen und die Erfordernisse, die an einen Operationsforscher gestellt werden, bis zu einem gewissen Grade antagonistisch sind. Er kann aber für die Arbeit desjenigen, der die Entscheidungen trifft, der handelt, wertvolle Dienste leisten. Mehr will und soll er auch gar nicht. Er überschreitet niemals die Grenze des Wissens, das Handeln überläBt er dem Betriebswirt.

XVII. Nachwort

Je mehr Artikel, Aufsätze und Bücher man über das Gebiet der Operationsforschung liest, je tiefer man in die einschlägige Literatur eindringt, desto öfter findet man, daB die Autoren aus den verschiedenen Lagern unterschiedliche Vorstellungen vom Wesen des Betriebes haben, desto mehr verdichtet sich das Gefühl, daB letzten Endes der Betriebswirtschafter (oder müBte man nicht, um jedes MiBverständnis auszuschalten, Kaufmann sagen?) unter dem ,,Betrieb" etwas ganz anderes versteht als der Techniker und mit diesem die Mathematiker und viele Statistiker.

Für den einen ist der Betrieb die Produktionsabteilung einer Unternehmung, für den anderen weit mehr. Man kommt — so absurd das klingen mag - zu dem SchluB, daB die Bemühungen zweier Generationen von Betriebswirtschaftern nicht zu einer allgemeinen, auch von den Technikern akzeptierten Definition des Ausdruckes ,Betrieb" geführt haben und daB es nach einem halben Jahrhundert wissenschaftlicher Arbeit nötig ist, sich wieder mit der Terminologie der Grundbegriffe auseinanderzusetzen. Der anscheinend längst beigelegte Streit um den Begriff ,Betrieb" ist neu entflammt. Man hat sich wohl im betriebswirtschaftlichen Lager der Handelshochschulen und Wirtschaftsfakultäten weitgehend geeinigt, aber die neuen Schriften der von der Technik und insbesondere Betriebswissenschaft sowie von der Mathematik und Statistik kommenden Autoren fordern zu einer Prüfung der anscheinend allgemein angenommenen Terminologie heraus.

Die neuerliche Beschäftigung mit diesem Grundbegriff unserer Wissenschaft wird aber notwendig sein, denn die endgültige Antwort, d. h. die eindeutige Klärung des Begriffes, die allgemein anerkannte Definition wird auch den Schlüssel zum Methodenproblem geben.

This proceedings volume contains extended abstracts of talks presented at the 18th Symposium on Operations Research held at the University of Cologne, September 1-3, 1993.

The Symposia on Operations Research are the annual meetings of the Gesellschaft für Mathematik, Ökonometrie und Operations Research (GMÖOR), a scientific society providing a link between research and applications in the areas of applied mathematics, economics and operations research. The broad range of interests and scientific activities covered by GMÖOR and its members was demonstrated by about 250 talks presented at the 18th Symposium. As in recent years, emphasis was placed on optimization and stochastics, this year with a special focus on combinatorial optimization and discrete mathematics. We appreciate that with sections on parallel and distributed computing and on scientific computing also new fields could be integrated into the scope of the GMÖOR.
This book contains extended abstracts of most of the papers presented at the conference. Long versions and full papers of the talks are expected to appear elsewhere in refereed periodicals.

The contributions were divided into sixteen sections: (1) Theory of Optimization, (2) Computational Methods of Optimization, (3) Combinatorial Optimization and Discrete Mathematics, (4) Scientific Computing, (5) Decision Theory, (6) Mathematical Economics and Game Theory, (7) Banking, Finance and Insurance, (8) Econometrics, (9) Macroeconomics and Economic Theory, (10) Stochastics, (11) Production and Logistics, (12) System and Control Theory, (13) Routing and Scheduling, (14) Knowledge Based Systems, (15) Information Systems and (16) Parallel and Distributed Computing.

The conference was opened by the Vice Rector of the University, Professor Speth. Further opening addresses were given by the Vice Mayor of Cologne, Mrs. Canisius, and the chairman of the GMÖOR, Professor Bachem. This year, also the GMÖOR Senior Scientist Prize was awarded during the opening ceremony. The awardee was Professor Krelle, one of the founders of the predecessor organizations of GMÖOR.

The scientific program consisted of semi-plenary lectures, invited and contributed talks. In the semi-plenary lectures, twelve leading experts gave a one-hour survey on recent developments and most interesting results in their fields. Egon Balas and Joel L. Horowitz started this series with talks on the prize collection TSP and bootstrap methods in applied econometrics. They were followed by Michael Ball who spoke about the design and analysis of reliable networks and by Denis Boyssou with a talk on preference modelling. Rainer Burkard and Bernard Cornet gave talks on the Monge property and exchange economies. Bezalel Gavish surveyed recent results in the area of telecommunication and Jonathan Borwein discussed trends in convex programming. Jan Karel Lenstra spoke about local search methods in job shop scheduling and Robert A. Becker dealt with Ramsey equilibria. The series of semi-plenary talks was closed by David Shmoys and Luk van Wassenhove with talks on the role of linear programming for solving scheduling problems and on recent results in logistics.

With over 370 participants, about 250 presentations, software demonstrations, press conferences and a lot of other designated actions we were able to show that our field remains active, vital and open for new topics. We would like to thank the authors for presenting their papers and the chairmen of the sections, who helped us in attracting so many distinguished speakers from all over the world. We also thank Dr. Müller of Physica-Verlag for his continuous support and cooperation in publishing this proceedings volume and Mrs. Krupp for her patience and perseverance in preparing its final version.

The conference was generously sponsored by the Ministerium für Wissenschaft und Forschung des Landes Nordrhein-Westfalen and the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG), which allowed us to support people from abroad and which made it possible that so many authors from Eastern Europe could attend the Symposium. We are deeply indebted to both institutions.
Finally we would like to thank our university and the members of our organizational staff without whose enthusiastic and unselfish support this symposium would not have been possible.

The Scheduling Problem in High-Level Synthesis: Extended 0/1 LP Model and Solution Methods
Hans Achatz Universität Passau Lehrstuhl Rechnerstrukturen (Prof. W. Grass) D-94030 Passau, Germany

As demonstrated by the activity in this area high-level synthesis - often referred to as behavioral synthesis - is becoming an increasingly popular research topic. A main part of high-level synthesis is scheduling where each operation from a data flow graph is assigned to a control step besides several constraints. We have formulated the scheduling problem as a 0/1 LP. For the first time we have extended the model to different execution times and multifunctional function units. To decrease the computation time we have developed a method for constructing new lower bounds with the help of LP (!). The results show that computation time is superior to comparable approaches though our model is able to describe a larger set of problems.
1. INTRODUCTION

High-level synthesis tools transform a behavioral description in terms of algorithm into a RT-level structural description observing several constraints. In order to produce the data path part of a digital processor the following subtasks have to be solved: scheduling, resource allocation and resource binding. This paper is concerned with the scheduling problem as a first step in the sequence of subtasks. Scheduling is the task of assigning operations to control steps optimizing a certain objective function. Several different methods for scheduling have been published. Most of them are heuristics.

We have extended the $_ { 0 / 1 }$ formulation of Hwang (1991) and Lee (1989) combined with ideas from Gebotys (1991) to enlarge the set of scheduling problems that can be described in our model. These $0 / 1 \ \mathrm { { L P } }$ approaches are very promising with respect to the set of allowable constraints like chaining, multicycle operations, functional pipelining, mutually exclusive operations and loop folding. They also reported very short computing times to get optimal solutions for benchmark examples. However there are at least two drawbacks of these approaches, which are very important for practical applications. They cannot correctly handle multifunctional function units with different operator combinations and they require assigning operation time to operation instances in the behavior description. In practice operation time is a feature of the function unit (FU) or even better of an operation performed by a module. In the second case, different operations of a module for example "add" and "and" may be done in different execution times. The algorithm to be described has been implemented as a part of a high-level synthesis system SUSAN (System for Universal Scheduling and Allocation) (see Achatz (1993b)) transforming VHDL behavioral description into composition of formally verified RT-level modules.

3. GENERATING LOWER BOUNDS VIA LP

The efficiency of solving the $0 / 1 \bf { L P }$ is extremely dependent on good bounds. In our approach we generate lower bounds via LP. In all applications so far we did not have problems with computing times. For determination of these lower bounds we have to distinguish between time-constrained and resource-constrained scheduling. In the time-constrained model we assume that the number of csteps is given and that we want to minimize the hardware costs. If we know how many units of one type are needed at least the solution space would be reduced. In order to achieve a lower bound for the number of FU-types needed we construct a new objective function

Notice that the objective function only depends on one type of function unit. The problem is solved as LP (!). Therefore computing times are no problem. The solution expresses how many FUs of Type tk are needed at least if all other FU-types do not have any costs. The optimal value of the cost function can be rounded up because the LP solution is always a lower bound for the $0 / 1 \ \mathrm { \bf L P }$ solution. This estimation can be made for every FU-type. So we have generated lower bounds for every FU-type and therefore reduced the solution space drastically. For our experiments most of the lower bounds were also the optimal values. If there are multi-functional FUs with non disjunctive operation type sets the bounds are of course weaker, because one FUtype can replace the other. In a similar way we can compute new bounds for resource-constrained scheduling.

Introduction

Conjoint analysis has many applications (Cattin, Wittink (1982), Wittink, Cattin (1989)). Frequently, it is used in the context of new product design (Mahajan, Wind (1992)). Practical applications involve the estimation of the importance of selected product attributes (Gaul, Lutz, Aust (1993)) or the assessment of new product candidates where part worth estimates on an individual level and profiles of established products to model competition in the marketplace are taken as inputs (Page, Rosenbaum (1987)).

Recently, analytic approaches within the framework of (mixed) integer programming have been formulated (Dobson, Kalish (1993)) where in the buyers' problem, the share of choices problem, or the seller's problem the objective is to maximize welfare, market share, or profit with respect to product line decisions. Sequential and simultaneous approaches can be distinguished dependent on whether the new products of the line are determined one after the other or at the same time. All simultaneous approaches so far rely on the first choice assumption which postulates that buyers deterministically choose the product with the highest idiosynchratic, i.. individual, utility. However, stringently deterministic buying behaviour is very seldom in the marketplace and it should also be remembered that product utilities obtained by conjoint analysis will always contain a certain amount of estimation and measurement error (Elrod, Kumar (1989)). Thus, the output of approaches to product line design using the first choice assumption, where new products only need an infinitely small increase in utility over the existing products to draw their complete market shares, should be regarded with due caution. Alternatives to the first choice rule that have proven to be more successful in aggregate market share prediction are, e.g., the LOGIT-model and a generalized formulation of the BTL-model used by Pessemier et al. (1971). The latter features an additional parameter $\pmb { \alpha }$ , exponent to all product utilities, that allows to model anything between equal choice probabilities for all products $( \alpha = 0 )$ and first choice $( \pmb { \alpha } = \infty )$ . Hence, given idiosynchratic product utilities for a representative sample of the buyers, the choice model may be calibrated to reproduce as closely as possible given status quo market shares (Silk, Urban (1978)). The generalized BTLmodel has been applied successfully in SIMOPT, the in many respects most elaborate conjoint analysis based approach to sequential product line optimization to date (Green, Krieger (1991, 1992)). Concerning model specifications and data input, PROLIN, a new simultaneous approach for probabilistic line optimization - the core of which is introduced in the following - could be seen as natural extension of SIMOPT to the case of multiple products with additional consideration of fixed cost.
Model Formulation

We present a new heuristic for solving vehicle routing problems. The heuristic uses complex customer interchanges to improve the initial solution. Simulated Trading is a general improvement procedure for a wide class of combinatorial optimization problems, thus it is able to handle many different side constraints like time windows, backhauls and a heterogeneous vehicle fleet. The algorithm is well suited for parallelization. A parallel version of Simulated Trading was implemented on a cluster of workstations using PVM. The results we have obtained with sequential and parallel Simulated Trading show that the quality of our solutions is superior to all heuristics for which solution values were known. Because of the limitation of space we will explain only the basic principle of Simulated Trading with a short example and will give an outline of the algorithm. A formal and detailed description of Simulated Trading can be found in [BHM92].

The Standard Vehicle Routing Problem (SVRP) can be considered as the task to satisfy the demands $d _ { i }$ of a set of customers $\{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ with a number of vehicles under some side constraints and to minimize the total costs. The side constraints include that each customer has to be served by exactly one vehicle'which starts and ends at the depot, the total load of a vehicle may not exceed its capacity and the vehicle has to be back at the depot after a certain amount of time. The total costs usually include travel times and fixed costs for each used vehicle. Extensions of the SVRP like time windows, heterogenous vehicle fleet or multiple depots are possible.
1 The Idea of Simulated Trading
Consider the following conversation between four truck drivers: Joe: $^ { * } I$ would be glad if someone could serve my customer A otherwise I will need an extra
hour of driving time."

Jim answers: $^ { 6 } A$ is right on my way but my truck is full. I need 20 minutes additional time for customer B. If someone can satisfy these demands I will be able to insert A in my tour with only 10 minutes of extra time."
Jack says: "My truck has enough free capacity for $B$ , but if I would insert $B$ in my tour then I would violate the time window of C."
John says: "If I serve B then I would arrive at home too late. But if someone delivers my customer D then I would be able to take $B$ and would be back in time."
Joe finishes the discussion: "I'm able to serve customer $C$ with costs of 15 minutes and we have an overall improvement of $ \mathbf { \nabla } _ { 4 } 0$ minutes."

If we take a closer look at the example we can construct a directed graph - we will call it trading graph - in which every node corresponds to an insertion (buy) or deletion (sell) of a customer. The edges which represent the relations between inserted and deleted customers are weighted with the gain that is obtained by the corresponding move of the customer (savings-insertcosts). Figure 1 shows the trading graph for the above example.

Every matching which can be found in the trading graph corresponds to an interchange of customers. If the value of the matching is positive we can improve our current tourplan. Clearly not every matching leads to a feasible tourplan. Consider the matching $\{ ( ( A , 6 0 ) , ( A , 1 0 ) ) \}$ : if we would realize this move of customer $A$ from Joe to Jim then the load would exceed the capacity of Jim's truck. Thus we have to look for a maximal weighted matching under additional constraints which will be called a trading matching. The bold printed edges in figure 1 show a trading matching with an improvement of 40.
2 The Algorithm Outline
We will now take a short look at the algorithm outline of Simulated Trading:

Let $\mathcal { T } = ( T _ { 1 } , \ldots , T _ { t } )$ be a feasible tourplan   
REPEAT Sell-And-Buy phase Trading-Matching-Search phase IF Trading-Matching $M$ is found THEN Update tourplan $\tau$ according to M   
UNTIL timelimit is reached

During the Sell-And-Buy phase we buy and sell customers using weighted probabilities and build up the trading graph until a certain decision level (3-6) is reached. After that we search for a maximal weighted trading matching. If we have found a positive matching $M$ we can improve the current tourplan. To get out of local minima we allow negativ matchings and infeasibilities.

In addition to the sequential algorithm we have implemented a parallel version of Simulated Trading on a cluster of workstations using PVM. The idea of the parallelization is to distribute the tours of the current tourplan among the workstations and to start a Simulated Trading algorithm on each machine. After a certain time (1-2 seconds) we collect the improved tours and restart with a new clustering. We use a farthest customer clustering in order to map only tours on one machine which are closely related.

EXPERT SYSTEM FOR HANDLING DANGEROUS GOODS
Dariusz Barbucha, Wodzimierz Filipowicz, Piotr Jedrzejowicz Merchant Marine Academy, Gdynia, Poland
INTRODUCTION

There exist several computer data bases containing information on dangerous goods. As a rule they contain a description of the most of substances which can appear as a part of any consignment transported onboard ship, road vehicle or stored in a warehouse. Highest priority problems which may arise when handling dangerous substances are those related to the environment pollution. Strict, well defined, precautionary measures are to be observed when loading, stowing or storing any dangerous goods. In this field there are also some examples of the computer advisory systems.

Most of the chemical substances, which can bear potential risk, have been classified and described in a unique way in "International Maritime Dangerous Code" |3/. This book and chemistry expert are usually involved when handling dangerous substances. The existing decision support systems /EXIS, DANLOAD/ |2||4ll5| do not however, embrace the whole range of problems which may arise when carrying, stowing or storing dangerous goods. Some typical problems involve a reduction of risk when such substances are handled with both, time and cost constraints or efficient use of the transportation means as well as of the storage capacity. In order to obtain practical solutions to these problems knowledge of some related disciplines such as:
- chemistry, especially in terms of dangerous good physical and chemical properties identification,
- computer science, especially data and knowledge based systems, - applied mathematics to generate optimal decisions is also required.
DATA BASE
Computer systems use data or facts and process them while searching for solutions. Description of dangerous substances are widely available even on CD-Rom units.
For the purpose of this project a data format description from the IMDG Code is used. Data are grouped into fields most of which are common for all substances.

Information contained in each field provides some clues which may come useful when reasoning about properties of the substance, which directly can be found at "properties" field. Reaction with others substances are also stated there. Such information is of the highest importance when appropriate action in case of an incident is to be taken.

With reference to the properties and subsequent potential risks involved, there exist special constraints on segregation of the substances, details of which are stated at the "stowage" field. This field reflects irregularities in segregation requirements roughly stated in the general segregation table available in any guide to the transport of dangerous materials. Formula field contains encoded data, easily understandable to chemist expert or a computer with sufficient knowledge base, which can supply further information about the substance.
Other fields provide more additional data supplementary to the stated above as well as these used for proper identification of a substance.
DANGEROUS GOODS PROBLEMS

Dangerous goods or substances are those which are inherently dangerous or those which are liable to chemical reaction with others. Product of such reaction is usually risky for environment or can cause damage to the nearest surrounding. Strict precautionary measures are to be observed when handling and allocating any dangerous goods.
SEGREGATION CALCULATIONS

If transportation of different substances is potentially risky and may cause a spontaneous reaction, components involved must be properly separated. In the maritime transportation, four segregation distances have been introduced taking into account potential hazard as well as construction of the vessel.

Nine classes of hazardous goods have been introduced as a guideline for the first and rough assessment of their properties. These classes are further divided into subclasses. The table containing segregation distances between subclasses /classes/ is easily available in every guide to dangerous goods, including the IMDG Code.

In addition to the segregation requirements there might be necessary to segregate a particular substance from others in a different, individual way. Such irregularities may refer to the whole class, particular type of substance or may be expressed in treating a substance as if it were in different class. Properties of some goods may vary with respect to their flushpoint, solution etc. To arrive at a proper segregation one has to select the worst case from all possible distances.

Requirements which refer to the substance type are not always directly available. Sometimes, an expert has to be consulted. Alternatively an expert system with appropriate knowledge should be at hand. Existing DANLOAD system |4|/5/ is short of this ability. Implementation of the proper knowledge base has already been started with knowledge elicited from chemical experts.

Result of segregation calculations can be thought of as a matrix which rows and columns are marked with substances and intersection element is equal to the segregation distance between each pair of goods.
DANGEROUS SUBSTANCE TYPE IDENTIFICATION - KNOWLEDGE BASE AND KNOWLEDGEREPRESENTATION

Every program or algorithm contains knowledge about some problem. This can be expressed in forms of equations, formulas and some "common sense" restrictions. Knowledge systems are different from traditional programs and include a higher-level form of knowledge, which is usually stored in the form of rules and facts. Furthermore, traditional programs can not explain its way of reasoning. Expert systems are supposed to behave more like intelligent assistant. Whenever it reaches a conclusion, a user should be able to ask about the way it has been arrived at. Knowledge about any subject is constantly growing and changing, an expert system must be flexible enough to accept and modify its base.
In order to recognize properties of substances the presented system requires some chemical knowledge. This knowledge is used for identification of substances types /or type/.

In order to be of use, knowledge must be captured in some manner inside computer. A simple approach is to use some explicit declarative language, which sentences can be considered as more or less direct symbolic encoding of the knowledge. Of course, knowledge must be accessed, used, modified and ammended. The adopted notation should be easy to read and enable generation of explanations.
In our case available knowledge has been encoded in form of conditional sentences.
DANGEROUS SUBSTANCE TYPE IDENTIFICATION - EXPLANATORY MECHANISM

Possibility to get an explanation on how facts and rules were used to reach goals is a useful feature of any expert system. Presented system contains such mechanism, too. It is an integrated part of dangerous substance type identification unit, offering the two kinds of explanations: 1. "How" explanation providing information on which rule was directly used to reach conclusion.

This information show a chain of rules which have led to the final conclusion, therefore available when reasoning process is executed. As a result appropriate rules and related facts are shown on the screen.

2. Type explanation providing information on which rules, included in knowledge base, are related to given dangerous substance type. In this case, all rules for given substance type identification are displayed.
FINDING MINIMAL NUMBER OF SEPARATED COMPARTMENTS

Once segregation matrix has been calculated, dangerous goods are to be allocated in such a way that proper distances are observed and is space available used efficiently. Assuming that the store, ship or another transportation mean is free of any other load of hazardous substances, minimal number of the separated compartments can be generated by the graph coloring procedure |6/. Methods used for graph coloring have been adopted by assigning goods to nodes and greater that 1 segregation distance to edges between appropriate pairs of nodes. Such an assignment does inot distinguish proper segregation from the distances 2, 3 and 4, so further consideration of substances allocation to the compartments appears necessary. Structure of a warehouse or ship as well as capacity of the compartments impose additional constraints which are supposed to be taken into account in real applications. It should be stressed that worst case running time of graph coloring algorithms is bounded by exponential function on the number of input |7/. Such problems are said to belong to the NP-Complete class and their optimal solution might be unreachable within reasonable time, therefore some suboptimal solutions are proposed and assessed.

A Model- and Method Base System for Discrete Optimization Problems
Peter Becker
Wilhelm-Schickard-Institut für Informatik, Universitt Tübingen
1. Introduction

Methods of discrete optimization play an important role in the area of control and optimization of industrial processes. Due to the fact that most discrete optimization problems are NP-complete, a lot of specialized methods have been developed for them, which differ with respect to algorithmic properties, see e.g [5, 7] . For this reason a user is not always able to select the algorithm that fits his needs best.

Because of the above mentioned difficulties I propose a method base approach to support unexperienced users in the solution of discrete optimization problems. Analogous to a data base a method base is defined as a software system consisting of a method base system and a set of methods. The most important tasks of the method base system are: (1) providing an interface to other systems and applications, (2) automatic method selection based on user preferences (3) and data handling. (1) comprises the offering of a data definition and manipulation language to define new problem classes and new problems as well as providing interfaces to various optimization methods and databases. (2) means, that the method base system has to provide adequate representation methods for knowledge about method application and (3) means the persistent storage of models and problems in a database orientied fashion.

In the following the method base system $\pmb { \mathcal { M } }$ is presented, which fullflls the above mentioned requirements. Similar approaches exist for linear programming problems, see [1, 9, 12] .

M is written in C and $\mathbf { c } { \mathrm { + + } }$ and is based on the relational database system TRANsBAsE as well as the software library LEDA [8] . The concepts of $\pmb { \mathcal { M } }$ are validated by knapsack problems [2] and precedence constraint hamilton path problems [3] .
2. A short survey of M

M is an object oriented software tool for the definition of models and the solution of problems in the fild of discrete optimization.is base on a client-server concept: the server administers all objets the method base, the client may be one of the generic user interfaces to M or any program that has connected to the method base by the means of a special library. This approach has the advantage that the method base can easily be embedded in other systems. Interprocess communication between clients and server is done by remote procedure calls via networks.

Operations on the method base are performed only by sending messages to objects. An object may be a class, a problem, a method or any other instance of predefined or user defined classes. Classes can be seen as factories for instances (resp. objects) and are objects too. For the objects they create, classes possess construction plans that contain information about the attributes an object can have and the methods that are applicable to an object. Instances or objects are created by sending a constructor message to a class.A problemclass or model is a factory for problems. In this sense a model is the abstract definition of a specific problem and achieves model/data independence. New models are created by sending a constructor message to a special class named problemclasses. After doing this, attributes and methods can be defined for the instances of the new model by the means of special messages.

The objects are internally mapped to tuples of a relational database or to special file structures. The latter is especially necessary for dealing with large comlex objects.Operations are embedded in transactions.
3. Extensibility and method integration

To support complex mathematical structures like graphs or networks efficiently the method base system offers an interface for the integration of user defined data types. A user written type handler function for a new data type can be installed via a dynamic library. Whenever a message is sent to an object of a user defined type this message is forwarded to the attached type handler. The type handler calls the necessary functions that implement the message. So it is easy to integrate new data types for mathematical structures by using software libraries, e.g. LEDA. M offers a set of common discrete structures, e.g. arrays, lists, matrices, posets, graphs and others.

A method is implemented by a function of a dynamic library, by a function written in the method base language or by an external program. It is represented by objects of the class methods or derived subclasses which provide the attributes necessary for the communication between the method and the server. By that, definition of methods by standard software is easy. For example, a method xshow for the graphical representation of partial orders has been realized using the public domain graph editor EDGE [10]

5. User support and automatic selection of methods

The strongest user support is achieved by method plans. These method plans are an adaption of skeleton plans, which are an usual artificial intelligence technique for the solution of planning or configuration problems, see e.g. [11] . Like skeleton plans, method plans can be viewed as non-recursive and-or-graphs. The sinks of a method plan represent the basic solution methods for the problem e.g. optimization methods, integrity checks or transformation methods. Intermediate nodes of the method plan represent partial problems in the solution process. Such a node depends on other basic or intermediate nodes. We distinguish two types of nodes.

A planning node divides the associated problem into subproblems that have to be solved sequentially. For instance, to solve a knapsack problem we have to do the following steps: (1) Check whether the problem has been defined correctly. (2) Sort the items according to decreasing values of the profit per unit weight. This a precondition for all existing solution methods currently available. (3) Reduce the problem by a reduction method to fix the optimal value of as many variables as possible. This results in a smaller problem. (4) Solve the reduced problem with one of the existing optimization methods. (5) Transform the solution back into terms of the original problem. It seems to be adequate to represent this knowledge by an planning node.

The other type of nodes are fork nodes. These nodes represent alternative strategies in the solution proces.For instance step 4) in the solution of a knapsack problem can be achieved by applying a branch and bound algorithm, an algorithm based on dynamic programming or a polynomial approximation scheme. What to do depends on the users preferences and the input data, e.g the number of items. For this reason rules can be connected to a fork node. These rules control the expansion of the solution process by selecting at least one of the alternatives offered by the node. Selecting more than one node results in different strategies to achieve the desired goal, which may be executed in parallel.This leads to the advantage that a race between different methods (resp. strategies) can be started and we get a solution in the minimum of the running times.

The method plan concept has two advantages: (1) knowledge about the problem domain is structured in small pieces that are independent and reusable. For instance if we want to apply one of the basicoperators we go back in a predefined way from the sink to the source. Every planning node on that path gives us the operators we have to apply before resp. after the call of the basic operator. In this manner the necessary tasks for the application of any node can be easily deduced. (2) Every intermediate node represents a powerful and sophisticated operator. Application of the source node results in an automatic solution.

Beside method plans, other concepts for user support exist. It is possible to define a model as a special case of another model. Associated with this relationship are test and transformation methods. Based on this relationship between models classification hierachies can be defined. Using a classification hierarchy, it is possible to classify a problem under the control of the test methods. In this way we get the most specific models to which a problem belongs.
6. Other Features

Beyond the facilities mentioned in the above sections Moffers the following two important features: (1) Interfaces to database systems. At the moment an interface to TRANsBAsE exists. For example the statement
transbase.query(database:<database name>,sqlquery:<sql-query>)

leads to the execution of the specified query against the database named <database name>. <sq1-query> is a string that contains an arbitrary query in SQL.The result table is given as a list of lists and can further be processed. Interfaces to other database systems can be easily realized by the technique of user defined types. (2) A generic graphical interface called Mint, see [6] . This tool represents objects by graphical means. For instance buttons are offered for the applicable messages and methods. Moreover the user is supported in the definition of parameters to methods by giving explanations.
7. Summary

In this paper the method base system M has been presented. Main features of M are: (1) facilities to define models and solve problems in the area of discrete optimization in an object oriented, persistent and consistent way, (2) efficient support for complex mathematical stuctures and support for reuse of these structures in various models, (3) user support by automatic selection of methods. Due to these aspects M can be seen as one step towards a model managment system proposed in [4] .

Parallel Tabu Search for Irregular Cutting
J.Blazewicz, J.Kaczmarek, R.Walkowiak Institute of Computing Science Technical University of Pozna ul.Piotrowo 3a, 60-965 Pozna

The problem of cutting figures of various shapes out from the rectangular area is considered. The paper is devoted to the development of the earlier versions of the original method presented in [2,3]. A new approach is different from the previous one in the following points:

1. the use of an optimal algorithm for polygon placement [1],   
2. new elements of tabu search policy,   
3. parallelization of the algorithm.

The problem of two-dimensional irregular cutting consists in defining a cutting layout for a rectangular area (a material) and arbitrary given irregular figures. As the width of the material is fixed, the goal is to minimize the length of the material used. The proposed method is based (from the geometrical point of view) on the idea of allocating a polygon (a given shape) in another polygon (a part of material to be cut). The first of the two stages leads to a generation of a feasible (in the sense of geometrical constrains) solution. Elements are arranged from the left to the right starting with the biggest one. The second stage is made according to the tabu search [4] policy. Starting with the initial solution the search through the solution's space is carried out in order to improve quality of the solution. As the geometrical phase of the algorithm (repeatedly executed) is time consuming the parallelization of the original "tabu" method is proposed. The implementation of the algorithm is proposed for message-passing multi computer and the issue of dynamic load balancing is attacked.
Geometrical phase
The geometrical part of the method can be divided into three sub-problems:
generation of (non-overlapping) placements of two polygons, allocating an element in the given point of a layout, removing an element from a layout.

While the two last issues are easier, the former one is more complicated in the sense of an algorithm's complexity [1] and implementation difficulties. It has to give all mutual non-overlapping allocations of two polygons. A simpler version of the algorithm with a fixed rotation angle has been implemented. The implementation showed that errors may occur (i.e. some extra erroneous placements are reported) in the case when polygons have equal dimensions in the same direction. Some modifications made led to rejecting the bad solutions and also some proper ones (in the above case). The only possibility to get the full set of proper placements seemed to check overlapping of elements in one freely chosen position of each separated area (polygon, line, point) of the placement found by the original procedure.
Parallel tabu search

Tabu search policy applied here differs from the one which has been used earlier [2,3].New classification and additional moves (insert, exchange and slide moves) have been introduced. The optimum function is based on parameters of solution rather than the type and parameters of a move. Two factors: the length of a layout and density of element's allocation are taken into account. The candidate moves are generated and the optimal move selection is made according to a new solution's quality, a tabu condition and an aspiration level. Possible moves consist in allocation of one or more figures (elements) in selected areas (holes). As the number of possible moves may be quite big, the parallel execution of the moves has been proposed. The sub-processes are created to find new solutions, which are results of element's extraction and reallocation. The geometrical procedures of the types described above has to be executed at least once within the sub-process. Two level hierarchical structure of tasks arises.

This parallelization supplies the computation process with tasks of small granularity. The computations are centralized and highly synchronized. This introduces a limitation on a speed up of computation but makes process management easier.

In this context, it seemed interesting to consider ideas for tabu search parallelization presented by VoB[6]. The proposals differ in a number of various strategies of the search and a number of basic processes (i.e. different starting solutions) created. Multiregional and multistrategical approach is interesting in big multi processor systems or in the case of small neighborhood of tabu search. This kind of approach introduces additional issues of process' synchronization and assurance of search diversification and demands extra processing and exchange of information.
Load balancing

The problem of load balancing of the multi computer system has to be considered in connection with the dynamic nature of the algorithm. The number of tasks, task's costs vary as the application runs. Hence for such a variable workload the dynamic load balancing scheme has to be applied. In a small multicomputer system when granularity of the tasks is rough and the computation process is centralized also centralized approach for load balancing is applicable. This type of a policy (but in fact a potentially distributed one) has been used in our system. The scheme has a feature of an auction algorithm [5], where two sides sellers and buyers shows their intentions.

To activate the subprocess the main process sends the proposal message containing a cost (an estimated time of computation) of the task and a proposed maximal price for its execution. The price for service required by a processor depends on processor's workload. If the price proposed is not lower than the required one the task will run on the processor enquired. If no processor accepts the price, it is increased by the control process above the lowest value proposed by processors in previous inquiry. The proposal message is sent again.
An acceptance of next task influences the workload of a processor and price for service. As the task execution is completed both factors decrease.
Challenging issues of various parallelization schemes and load balancing in large multi computer systems for generated process give directions of further research.

1. Constraint logic programming and 0-1 constraints

Constraint logic programming has been one of the major developments in the area of declarative programming during the last years. The idea is to combine a logic programming language similar to Prolog with a constraint solver for a specific domain of computation such as linear arithmetic, Boolean algebra, finite domains or lists [BC93].

In [Boc93] we introduced a new constraint logic programming language $\mathrm { C L P } ( { \mathcal { P B } } )$ for logic programming with pseudo-Boolean constraints. Pseudo-Boolean constraints or $_ { 0 . 1 }$ constraints combine Boolean algebra with arithmetic. A pseudo-Boolean function is an integer-valued function $f : \{ 0 , 1 \} ^ { n } \to { \mathcal { Z } }$ of 0-1 variables. Any such function can be represented as a multilinear polynomial in its variables. A pseudo-Boolean constraint is an equation or inequality between pseudo-Boolean functions.

The aim of this paper is to present a constraint solver for linear pseudo-Boolean constraints of the form $a _ { 1 } x _ { 1 } + \ldots + a _ { n } x _ { n } \leq b$ , with $a _ { 1 } , \ldots , a _ { n } , b \in { \mathcal { Z } }$ and 0-1 variables $x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { n }$ The constraint solver has to provide solutions to the following typical problems in constraint logic programming:

2. Simplifying 0-1 constraints

When executing a constraint logic program, the main problem is to simplify a given constraint set $C$ and to compute a solved form $s ( C )$ . What should this solved form look like? There are the following basic requirements:

• $s ( C )$ should be equivalent to $C$ .   
• $s ( C )$ should be "simpler" than $C$ .
• $s ( C )$ should be false if $C$ is unsolvable.

Introduction

In the decision-theoretic literature, usually, a distinction is made between decisions under risk and decisions under complete ignorance. In practice, however, the case of "partial ignorance" (Luce and Raiffa (1958), p. 299) is prevailing which lies anywhere between the extreme cases of complete ignorance, with no knowledge of probabilities, and the opposite extreme of risk, with well-known quantitative probabilities.

In situations of partial probability information, the question arises of how to decide rationally. There is some empirical evidence that in practical economic situations of partial ignorance, e.g. project apraisal, decision makers use some sort of generalized mean-risk decision rule (cf. Brachinger (1991)). Modeling that kind of decision behavior presupposes a theory of risk under conditions of partial probability information.

Based on previous work on the perceived risk of gambles, the theory outlined in this paper is the first attempt to attack the problem of perceived risk under conditions of partial probability information. For a detailed exposition of that theory see Brachinger (1993).

The theory of computation and complexity deals with combinatorial problems set on finite combinatorial structures, and the algorithm complexity is measured with respect to an appropriate defined input length. At the same time, many problems can be defined on infinite structures (as infinite graphs, sets, etc.), presentable by infinite inputs. In such case the classical complexity theory becomes impracticable.

The paper proposes an approach to treatment of questions concerning the complexity of algorithms and corresponding problems, defined on infinite combinatorial structures. The introduced model can be also considered as natural framework for problems providing incremental search, where the information comes online, during the process of solving.

The main ideas are illustrated on some concrete examples. Algorithms for solving some of the problems are sketched, unsolvability of others is commented, and a comparison to the problems in the finite case is given.
MODEL

We will consider problems in the following general setting. The search problem $\Pi =$ $( I _ { \Pi } , S _ { \Pi } )$ is supposed to be defined on a combinatorial structure $s$ of arbitrary nature, presented by an input $I _ { \Pi }$ and having a set of solutions $S _ { \Pi }$ . $s$ could be a graph, a family of subsets of some ground set, etc. We assume that the problem has to be solved by some Solver $\mathcal { M }$ , that is in a position to perform various types of operations $t _ { 1 } , \ldots , t _ { k } .$ depending on the problem nature.

$\mathcal { M }$ must realize some aim a priori defined (to find some special subgraph of a graph, or a special subset in a given family of sets). In addition we suppose that $\mathcal { M }$ disposes of incomplete, local information about the ground structure, i.e. in general $\mathcal { M }$ does not know $s$ a priori, but completes the knowlege about it dynamically, during solving the problem, following some local-search-type algorithm.

This model generalizes the traditional one, where we could think that at the initial moment the known data (neighbourhood of $s$ ) includes all the structure. Such approach also allows to consider problems where $s$ is given by infinite input.

We presented the model on informal level because of its generality, but it could be precised in any concrete case, as it will be done in the next section. In some cases it would be convinient to think that the input data is received from some oracle, which has to be asked for additional information.

Supposing $\mathcal { M }$ can perform different operations, different types of complexity (eventually uncomparable each to other) correspond to them. In the classical complexity theory the most important type of complexity - the computational one, is measured with respect to the input size of the problem, but for problems with infinite inputs this is impossible. Our approach to the complexity in infinite structures is the following.

First, let us note that in the finite case, in generally, the algorithms use all the input in order to produce a solution, so that it could be said that the algorithm complexity (and correspondingly the problems' ones) is measured with respect to the volume of the data used. At the same time, it is possible for many individual problems to find the solution applying some local-search-type algorithm that manipulates only a part of the input (it is typical in cases when superfluous information is given). About the infinite case, it is clear that the problem has to be solved by algorithm using only a finite part of the infinite input. So, there are reasons to consider some data subset as an adequate characteristic of the input, if the knowlege of this subset allows to solve the problem in finite time.

Let $A _ { \Pi }$ be an algorithm such that if $\mathcal { M }$ follows it, a search problem $\Pi$ will be solved $i \pi \in I _ { \Pi }$ , $i _ { \Pi } ^ { A _ { \Pi } }$ denotes the data really used by $A _ { \Pi }$ to solve the problem (again the notion "really used" is to be precised in dependance on the concrete problem). According to our assumption about the different abilities of the Solver $\mathcal { M }$ , $A _ { \Pi }$ can be considered as a multyalgorithm, consisting of $\pmb { k }$ different algoritms $A _ { \Pi } ^ { 1 } , \dotsc , A _ { \Pi } ^ { k }$ corresponding to the various types of operations, and different types of complexity - one per each of the algorithms - can be examined. All these complexities will be measured with respect to a basic one - data complexity $\mu ( i _ { \Pi } ^ { A _ { \Pi } } )$ , that reflects in some appropriate way the volume of the used data $i _ { \Pi } ^ { A _ { \Pi } }$ defined above (in many cases it is most naturally function $\mu$ to give the number of elementary data units as numbers, graph vertices, elements of sets, etc., which are manipulated by the algorithm during its work). The complexity $\pmb { c _ { i } }$ of $A _ { \Pi } ^ { i }$ reflects the loss of operations during the work of $A _ { \Pi } ^ { i }$ It is a function that to every (natural) number $\pmb { n }$ juxtaposes the maximal (over all individual problems $\Pi _ { n }$ for which $A _ { \Pi } ^ { i }$ needs data complexity $n = \mu ( i _ { \Pi } ^ { A _ { \Pi } } ) )$ number of operations of type $\mathbf { \Delta } _ { t _ { i } } .$ , spent for solving the individual problems of $\Pi _ { n }$ .

We say that the (sub)algorithm $A _ { \Pi } ^ { i } ( 1 \leq i \leq k )$ is a polynomial one if for every individual problem $i _ { \Pi }$ the number of steps performed till obtaining the solution is bounded by a polynomial of the corresponding data complexity $\mu ( i _ { \Pi } ^ { A _ { \Pi } } )$ .The algorithm $A _ { \Pi }$ is polynomial if every $A _ { \Pi } ^ { i }$ is polynomial for $i = 1 , \ldots , k$ ,and $A _ { \Pi }$ is exponential if some of its complexities are exponential functions of the data complexity. The problem $\Pi$ is called polynomially solvable if there exists a polynomial algorithm $A _ { \Pi }$ such that the Solver $\mathcal { M }$ , performing $A _ { \Pi }$ , will realize the aim a priori set.

Such approach allows to evaluate the algorithms and problems complexity in infinite structures. Let us, however, note that if it is necessary to compare the complexities of two algorithms for one problem, it would be needed first to receive a relation for their data complexities, after to compare the corresponding complexity functions, and finally to obtain the relation between the algorithm complexities as a superposition of the above two relations.
EXAMPLES

We consider graph problems, supposing for simplicity that graphs are displaced on the plane, that the Solver $\mathcal { M }$ is able to move along the edges of the graph which are streight line segments, and that it possesses a "vision" in radius $\pmb { r }$ , can make computations, can store some data, as well as to measure passed distances. So we can talk about computational complexity, moving complexity (passed distance or number of passed edges), measuring complexity (number of performed measurings), memory complexity (the necessary memory volume). In the case of infinite graphs, we will suppose that $V$ (being an infinite set) does not contain cluster points, and that for every fixed node $v \in V$ its degree is finite. First we will consider the well known

Path Problem (PP). Given a graph G with positive weights of its edges and two fixed vertices s and $\pmb { t }$ (with known coordinates with respect to some fixed coordinate system), find a (Shortest, Longest) simple path (SPP, LPP) from $\pmb { s }$ to $\pmb { t }$ .

It is well known that on finite graphs the PP and SPP are polynomially solvable, for example by the Dijkstra's algorithm (DA) [3]; even if $G$ is a disjoint graph and s and $\pmb { t }$ belong to different connective components and there is no path between them, this can be checked in polynomial time [5]. It is known also that the LPP is NP-hard [4].

On connected infinite graphs, the PP and SPP are polynomially solvable, too. Really, DA could be applied, and in finite number of steps the target vertex will be reached. It is easy to see that the number of calculations, movings from one vertex to another, measurings (of angles or passed distances), and used memory are restricted by a polynomial of the data complexity, measured, for example, in number of visited edges.
At the same time, the LPP is unsolvable, as it easily follows from the infinity of the graph.
The SPP and LPP are both unsolvable if the weights can be positive and negative numbers, as well as if $G$ is disjoint and s and $\pmb { t }$ belong to different connective components.

Spanning Tree Problem (STP). Given a graph G with positive weights of its edges and a set $W \subseteq V$ of $k$ fixed vertices of $G$ (with known coordinates), find a (Shortest, Longest) Spanning Tree (SSTP, LSTP) for these vertices.

1 Introduction

Many problems arising in various branches of computational mathematics (in particular numerical analysis and scientific computations) have as natural domains real or complex numbers. This has motivated research derected to developing of extention of the classical theory of computation and complexity, dealing with combinatorial problems presentable over integers. The basic new conceptions, definitions and results can be found, for example, in [1]. We will mention here only that, according the new computational model, every arithmetic operation $( + , - , * , / )$ is assumed to be underlying one, performable in unique time.

A main theme in the initial research is the comparison of the results over the integers with ones over the reals, that gives deeper understanding to the basic concepts of decidability, computability, complexity, etc.

The present paper is an additional step in this direction.We consider the well known Knapsack Problem (KP) with two variables (1) $\operatorname* { m a x } \{ c _ { 1 } x + c _ { 2 } y ~ : ~ a _ { 1 } x + a _ { 2 } y \leq b .$ $x , y \in Z _ { + } \mathrm { ~ } \}$ , where $c _ { 1 } , c _ { 2 } , a _ { 1 } , a _ { 2 } , b \in R _ { + }$ . It is well known that if the coefficients are rational, the problem can be solved in polynomial time in the sense of the complexity theory over the integers [3]. The same is the case if at least one of $_ { \pmb { x } }$ and $\pmb { y }$ is not required to be nonnegative. In contrast, we have obtained that in the real data case there is no algorithm solving (1) if $\pmb { x }$ and/or $_ { y }$ may be negative (section 2). Peter Brucker, Bernd Jurisch, Andreas Krämer Universität Osnabrück Fachbereich Mathematik/Informatik Postfach 44 69 D-49069 Osnabrück Germany

In a job-shop scheduling problem we have $\pmb { n }$ jobs $J _ { 1 } , \ldots , J _ { n }$ to be processed on $_ m$ different machines $M _ { 1 } , \ldots , M _ { m }$ . Each job $J _ { i }$ consists of a number $\pmb { n _ { i } }$ of operations $O _ { i 1 } , \ldots , O _ { i n _ { i } }$ which have to be processed in this order. Operations $O _ { i j }$ can be processed only by one machine $\mu _ { i j } ( i = 1 , \ldots , n ; j = 1 , \ldots , n _ { i } )$ . Denote by $\pmb { p _ { i j } }$ the corresponding processing time. We assume that all processing times are integer numbers. There is only one machine of each type which can only process one operation at a time. Operations must be processed without preemption. Moreover, a job cannot be processed by two machines at the same time. For each machine $M _ { k }$ we have to find an ordering of all operations to be processed on $M _ { k }$ such that the maximal completion time $C _ { \bf m a x }$ of all jobs is minimal.

This problem is one of the most difficult NP-hard scheduling problems. A 10-job, $1 0 \mathrm { \ m a }$ chine problem formulated in 1963 (Muth & Thompson[1963]) has been solved only recently (Carlier & Pinson [1989]). The algorithm developed by Carlier and Pinson is a branch and bound method which is based on the disjunctive graph formulation of the job-shop problem. Other branch and bound algorithms have been developed recently (Applegate & Cook [1990], Brucker et al. [1991]).

The efficiency of all these branch and bound methods relies on the concept of immediate selection introduced by Carlier and Pinson. By immediate selection disjunctions, i.e. order relations between operations which have to be processed on the same machine, are fixed before branching. An order relation can be fixed if the reverse order relation yields a solution which does not improve the best solution found so far.

In Carlier & Pinson [1990] presented an $O ( n ^ { 2 } )$ -algorithm which usually fixes a large number of disjunctions. Recently they proposed an $O ( \operatorname* { m a x } \{ n \log n , d \} )$ -version of their algorithm (Carlier & Pinson [1993]). Here $\pmb { n }$ is the number of operations to be scheduled on the same machine and $\pmb { d }$ denotes the number of disjunctions to be fixed. The algorithm considers all pairs $( O _ { i } , O _ { j } )$ of operations to be processed on this machine and decides whether a disjunction between $O _ { i }$ and $O _ { j }$ can be fixed. Besides these conditions for pairs of operations Dewe® [1991] derived conditions for triples of operations which allow to fix additional disjunctions. We will generalize both concepts by

deriving conditions for fixing disjunctions which are based on $\pmb { r }$ -sets of operations to be processed on the same machine where $r \geq 2$ is an arbitrary integer   
simplifying the conditions given by DeweB   
describing algorithms for checking these conditions.

We will present an $O ( \operatorname* { m a x } \{ n \log n , d \} )$ -algorithm which fixes all disjunctions derived by so called cliques as the algorithm of Carlier and Pinson does. Our algorithm is based on alternative concepts. Due to these concepts the correctness proof is much simpler than the correctness proof in Carlier $\&$ Pinson [1990].

For checking 3-set conditions we present an $O ( n ^ { 2 } )$ -algorithm improving the approach of Dewe for checking 3-sets considerably. Finally we will report on the computational results we got by replacing the algorithm of Carlier and Pinson by these new algorithms in a branch and bound method presented in Brucker et al. [1991].

In our paper we will first introduce the job-shop problem. Then the typical situation in a node of the search tree of a branch and bound method is described. The method is based on the disjunctive graph formulation of this problem. There we have a set of already fixed order relations between operations to be scheduled on the same machine. Using these relations a head $\boldsymbol { r } _ { i }$ and a tail $\pmb q _ { \hat { \imath } }$ may be calculated for each operation i. Furthermore let $\pmb { U } \pmb { B }$ be an integer upper bound for the optimal solution value of the problem. Usually $\pmb { U } \pmb { B }$ is the value of the best solution found so far. If we want to improve this best solution each operation i must be finished not later than the due date $d _ { i } : = U B - q _ { i } - 1$ . Thus, operation i must be processed within the time window specified by the interval $[ r _ { i } , d _ { i } ]$ .

Then we will present two concepts for immediate selection. They use the time windows of the operations. The first concept based on so called cliques was introduced by Carlier and Pinson [1989]. Roughly speaking a clique $( J , c )$ consists of a set of operations $\pmb { J }$ (to be processed on the same machine) which must be scheduled within a certain time interval because of the operations' heads and due dates. Hence the capacity of the machine to process other operations during this interval is bounded. Thus, if the processing time of an operation $^ { c }$ exceeds this bound, it must be scheduled either before or after all operations of $\pmb { J }$ .

The second concept was introduced by DeweB [1991]. It uses so called $\pmb { r }$ -set conditions. This means that an operation $_ i$ must be scheduled before an operation $j$ if there exists a set $\pmb { J }$ of operations with $\pmb { r }$ elements $( i , j \in J )$ such that every sequence of operations of $\pmb { J }$ in which $j$ is scheduled before $_ i$ does not respect the time windows given by the heads and due dates.

Next we will describe algorithms to check the conditions induced by the two concepts. The first algorithm fixes disjunctions which may be derived from cliques. It has complexity $O ( \operatorname* { m a x } \{ n \log n , d \} )$ where $d$ is the number of disjunctions which will be fixed. This algorithm consists of two steps:

First heads and due dates of all operations to be scheduled on the same machine are improved. Therefore we calculate the earliest possible completion time $\scriptstyle { \pmb { s } } _ { c }$ of operation $^ { c }$ under the assumption that all operations respect their time windows and preemption is allowed. Then we can improve the head of operation $^ c$ to $\pmb { s _ { c } } - \pmb { p _ { c } }$ for the schedules without preemption. This needs $O ( n ^ { 2 } )$ (respectively $O ( n \log n ) )$ time for all operations to be scheduled on the same machine. The $O ( n \log n )$ -version is based on a sophisticated datastructure which enables to decrease $\pmb { n }$ different values by a constant amount in $O ( \log n )$ steps.
Then using the improved heads and tails we may fix all disjunctions induced by cliques in $O ( \operatorname* { m a x } \{ n \log n , d \} )$ time.

The second algorithm checks the conditions induced by triples, i.e. 3-sets. The idea is to calculate a lower bound for the total length of all parts of operations which must be scheduled between the head of operation $j$ and the due date of operation $_ i$ if we assume that $j$ is scheduled before i. Hence $_ i$ must be scheduled before $j$ if this lower bound exceeds the length of the interval. E.g. a very simple lower bound is ${ p } _ { \mathrm { { i } } } + { p } _ { \mathrm { { j } } }$ .We will give an $O ( n ^ { 2 } ) \cdot$ . algorithm for calculating such a bound for all pairs of operations $( O _ { i } , O _ { j } )$ to be processed on the same machine.

Finally we will report on the computational results. We implemented the different algorithms for immediate selection in a branch and bound algorithm (Brucker et al. [1991]) for solving the job-shop problem.

Of course, the number of search tree nodes did not change when we used our clique algorithm instead of Carlier and Pinson's one. But the running time was always improved by approx. $3 . 4 \%$ using our $O ( n ^ { 2 } )$ algorithm.

We also implemented the $O ( \operatorname* { m a x } \{ n \log n , d \} )$ -version to check clique conditions. We got an increase in the running time of approx. $3 5 { - } 4 0 \%$ for problems with 10 jobs, approx. $2 0 - 2 5 \%$ with 15 jobs, approx. $1 5 \mathrm { - } 2 0 \%$ with 20 jobs and approx. $1 5 \%$ with 30 jobs. Hence we may expect a better running time performance for problems with more jobs. The triple algorithm provided quite surprising results. In general it needed approx. $1 0 \mathrm { - } 1 5 \%$ search tree node less than the clique algorithm. The running time varied in a range of $\pm 1 0 \%$ of the amount given by the clique algorithm. We also found out that the triple algorithm fixes considerably more arcs than only the arcs induced by triples.

1 Introduction

Banking and insurance companies are both facing the problem of losing market shares with their core products sold via traditional marketing channels. In Germany the share of banking products sold in branches dropped from $98 \%$ in 1970 to $85 \%$ in 1987; the share of insurance products sold by the traditional exclusive agents dropped from roughly $90 \%$ to $70 \%$ in the same period and is expected to fall far below $50 \%$ at the end of the century (Krupp (1993); Schweickert (1993)). The bankassurance strategies in the financial services markets combine efforts to integrate insurance and banking products as well as the corresponding marketing channels. Suitable combined bankassurance products with provable customer advantages are one key for the success of these strategies; this is the topic of Chapter 2. The second key for success is to provide customer benefits by enabling the stationary and mobile marketing channels with the knowledge and capacity to offer and contract bankassurance products in an efficient way. Chapter 3 deals with the system support necessary for spreading knowledge and capacity in these channels; furtheron, first experiences from a prototype developed within the ALLFIWIB-project funded by the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft are sketched.
2 The Advantage of Combined Bankassurance Products

For customer decision support in the financial services field comparisons of e.g. loan interest rates offered by different banks or premiums for life policies offered from insurance companies are usual and widespread. The success of independent agents working together with a variety of financial services companies is largely based on such, often "computer-supported", comparisons of given, standardized offerings. Optimization of such offerings resulting in individual, tailored solutions for the special customer problem, however, is - due to complexity - hardly observable. In contrast to that, it turns out that such "local" optimization of single bankassurance products already may prove very profitable for both the customer and supplier when compared to usual standardized products. For both the investor and the issuing bank or firm zerobonds are better than all straight bonds, whenever bonds are profitable for them in the after tax world at all. A life policy is better than all bonds, whenever the german tax subsidy requirements are met (Buhl et al. (1993b)).

Such examples show the competitive and business potential for combined bankassurance solutions compared to the traditional core products of the financial services providers. As one main reason for the profitability of these combined solutions the lacking neutrality and the inefficiency of the german tax system is identified, particularly the following fact is key: Interest rates contained in leases, loans, straight bonds, zerobonds and insurance products are all taxed differently at either the supplier or the customer or both. This opens up a considerable optimization potential for the "coalition" of the financial services provider and its customer in nearly all practically relevant cases. The next chapter deals with the question, how such solutions may be generated by combining knowledge based techniques with methods from distributed artificial intelligence.
3 System Support for Combined Bankassurance Products

The discussion of combined bankassurance products highlighted the complexity of obtaining solutions to financial problems that are advantageous for both, the customer and the supplier. Obviously, system support is necessary to cope with this complexity (Buhl et al. (1993a)). As described in more detail in Buhl, Will (1993), König (1993), and Mack et al. (1993) the following system support is applicable, at least in principle, for both the branches and the mobile marketing channel, if access from the customer's site - e.g. via ISDN - to the data and solution agents in the network of the financial services provider is possible.

To cope with the complexity problem first, we propose a concept of cooperating knowledge based systems as an adequate support to elaborate and offer combined bankassurance products (see e.g. Buhl, Will (1993); König (1993); König et al. (1993)). For each financial domain, e.g. bonds or loans, a knowledge based system works as an expert (a so called "domain-agent") selecting and/or configuring solutions to a given problem. While working on problem solving a domain-agent applies rules like those presented in Chapter 2 for leasing and loans in order to obtain an advantageous or even optimal solution. Implementing each domain-agent as a separately running software process (e.g. on a local area network of workstations) the performance of the problem solving process can be improved by concurrently elaborating competing solutions to the same problem (e.g. leasing vs. loan for a financing problem). Moreover, the realization of this concept simplifies maintaining and extending the knowledge bases by the experts of the respective supplying firm. Embedding the domain-agents in a decentral Multi-Database-Server-Architecture provides the necessary remote access to all required customer and product data (König (1993)).

For implementing the idea of offering combined solutions of several locally optimized products cooperation of the domain-agents is necessary. This cooperation can be adequately supported by a blackboard as a common accessible database to store customer problems and residual problems as well as the corresponding solutions (Mack et al. (1993)). A homogeneous, payment-streambased representation-form of both problems and solutions on the blackboard allows the agents to "understand" each problem. For example, the leasing-agent offers an optimized contract with an upfront-one-time-payment although the customer wishes to pay constant rates. The residual problem of financing the one-time-payment will then be written on the blackboard to be solved by other domain-agents, e.g. the loan-agent. In addition to this implicit way of cooperation of the domain-agents we provide a "combination-agent" with explicit knowledge overlapping everaldomains.  in a pecisituaton ike the  rom the example above suc knowle priori suggests a good combination of different products the combination-agent is able to decompose the complex problem into partial problems to be solved by the single domain-agents. In this sense the combination-agent initiates explicitly combined solutions and thus helps to reduce search-time. Also, this explicit knowledge may lead to a better solution than the search process.

Based on the concept presented, a first prototype was developed within the project ALLFIWIB. Four domain-agents for loans, leasing, bonds, and life insurance as well as a combination-agent and communication and control modules were implemented. Testing activities proved the general practicablity of the ideas sketched. In the simple model framework of the prototype with deterministic payments and with only a few rules even "mixed" problems starting with periods of saving, a following real estate investment and subsequent periods of financing could be solved by the system of cooperating agents. Currently we work on improving the prototype and extending the knowledge bases with e.g. the economic knowledge from the references cited below.

The high schools usually have, at the beginning of each academic year, problems to define the timetables for their classes, mainly due to the restrictions in the time availability of the teachers. In view of that, it is proposed a modeling structure to help in this kind of time tabling, based on mathematical programming algorithms.

3. Discussion of the results

Once it was assumed that the use of this modeling structure would be responsibility of the high schools themselves, the compatible mathematical programming software tested for that should be available for microcomputers, the most common computational platform obtainable in that category of schools.

To select the software, it was used a survey conducted by Sharda (1992), taking into account the potential power of this type of tool with respect to manipulation of large and dense matrices, which certainly demand great amount of RAM memory as well long processing times. In view of that, it was utilized the OSL (IBM, 1991) code, incorporated to the optimization language GAMs (Brooke et al., 1992), under various microcomputer configurations.

Specifically for the most representative model processed for this study, built for a representative high school at the Sâo Paulo State, Brazil, it was generated a matrix with 7,671 rows, 34,801 columns and 93,482 non-zero elements, which required, according to the solving strategy used, an average of 20 Mb of RAM memory in a microcomputer 486 DX with a clock of 66 MHz.

The obtained results attested the efficiency of GAMS/OSL, specially regarding the linear solution. However, the search for the integer solution was not equally efficient, mainly due to the fact the algorithm used for that is based on branch-and-bound techniques.

Given the integer solution is attained from the initial linear solution (which could be got through diferent algorithms available inOSL including the very convergent ones for some classes of problems, such the interior point methods), the execution time consumed was considered satisfactory.
However, to get a greater efficiency to achieve the integer solution, the following solving strategies available for OSL were tested:
