Furthermore, there is evidence that many of the shifts that occurred within the health sector were implemented soon after independence, however after the mid-1980s due to budgetary constraints there were declines in access to health services, in particular in rural areas, which had the effect of worsening health inequities (Loewenson et al., 1991). For example, health sector spending increased rapidly from 1980 to 1982 but then stabilized, and thus declined in real terms, throughout the rest of the 1980s (Sanders and Davies, 1988). Immunization rates increased rapidly from 1980, reaching $5 0 \mathrm { - } 8 0 \%$ by 1986 but increased much more dramatically in urban areas during this time period. In addition, while the majority of Zimbabweans qualified for free health care services at the time of independence (all households with earnings less than Z\$150 per month qualified), the fact that the threshold for free health care remained fixed while nominal wages were rising meant that many Zimbabwean families no longer qualified for free health care by the mid-1980s. Fee schedules were also increased during the mid-1980s, greatly increasing the costs of some medical services, such as hospital deliveries (Loewenson et al., 1991). While the government also implemented a major expansion of health facilities and greatly expanded the size of the health work force, most of these expansions disproportionately benefited urban areas, with notable increases in inequities between urban and rural areas (Loewenson et al., 1991). By the late 1980s, economic conditions worsened throughout the country, and Zimbabwe entered into a structural adjustment program, which led formally to the reintroduction of user fees for health care nationally in 1991 (Bassett et al., 1997). If these health sector changes had much differential impact on women in our sample, we might expect children born during the early 1980s, and thus to older mothers in 1980, or children born in urban areas to have benefited more, but in fact we find evidence of the opposite effect. However, we also include a series of robustness checks to ensure that our results are not being driven by changes originating within the health sector, which we further discuss below.

The major thrust of the post-independence Robert Mugabe government was policy reforms in the social sectors, most notably the changes outlined above in the health and education sectors (Sanders and Davies, 1988). There is little evidence of other major economic policymaking in the decade immediately following independence (Jenkins, 1997).
3. Materials and methods
3.1. Data

All of the data used in this study were sourced from five rounds of Demographic and Health Survey (DHS), which are nationally representative surveys of reproductive-aged women, conducted in Zimbabwe in 1988, 1994, 1999, 2005-6 and 2010-11. The sample for the DHS is selected from a two-step process in which enumeration areas are first randomly sampled from census files and then households are randomly selected from the list of households within in each enumeration area. From each of the five surveys, we extracted data from all women who were between the ages of 9 and 20 in 1980, that is all women who were born between 1960 and 1971 in any of the surveys (i.e. women aged 28–39 in the 1999 survey and so on). Pooling across all five surveys, our sample consists of 6442 women who were aged 9–20 (treatment women were aged 9–13 and control women were aged 16–20) in 1980. We include survey fixed effects to capture potential effects from pooling data across surveys. In total, these women gave birth to 24,991 children before they were surveyed in one of the five DHS (see Table 1). The average years of education attained by women in the sample was 5.96 years; $3 2 \%$ of women had received some secondary schooling; and only $2 5 \%$ of the households were in urban areas. On average, women gave birth to their first child by the age of 19.13 years. Our treatment and control groups appear to be similar on measures of wealth and whether their household had electricity.

We collect child mortality information from the DHS birth histories, which collected data on the complete fertility history of all reproductive-aged women (i.e. the “BR” DHS recode files). These histories record every birth of the woman, the date of birth and the date of death (if the child dies prior to the date of the survey). The DHS also collects detailed data on the health services utilized by all children who were 5 years or younger at the time of the survey. In total, we have detailed health service utilization on 5419 children. Half of the sample of children were male.

To test the impact of maternal education on outcomes, we construct two measures of maternal schooling: the number of years of completed education and a binary variable that is coded 1 if a woman reports to have ever attended secondary school or 0 otherwise, which isolates the increase in education that happens specifically at the margin between primary and secondary school.

We also collect data on outcomes related to fertility, health, healthy behaviors, female empowerment as well as health utilization of children born to these women, assuming that care provided to children is influenced by the mothers’ behaviors. All variables, aside from those associated with the health services utilized by children, were collected from the individual (i.e. “IR”) DHS recode files. Data on the health services for children comes from the children (i.e. “KR” files) DHS recode files.

To capture changes in fertility and sexual behavior, we used data from the DHS’s fertility module. Women were asked about their age when they first experienced sexual intercourse. If women reported not yet experiencing sexual intercourse, we coded them 1 for being a virgin or 0 otherwise. For all women who were not virgins, we constructed a variable to measure their age at sexual debut. For all women, virgins or not, we calculated whether or not they were using a modern form of contraception. For all women, we also calculated the total number of children born to these women up until the date of the survey. Women were also asked about the ideal number of children that they wished to have, and we capture this as another measure of their fertility preferences.

The DHS also collected data on measures of women’s empowerment by asking women whether or not they had some say over important decisions within the household. For each set of decisions, women were asked if they alone, they along with their husband, or someone else in their household had say over how key decisions were made in the household. We created empowerment binary variables for each decision and counted all women who reported that they alone or they along with their husband had say over the decision process as empowered, and other women as not being empowered. We created an index using respondent answers to various questions regarding decisions to capture empowerment in a single variable. The surveys similarly asked about domestic violence and contained questions about whether it is acceptable for a man to beat his wife in the event of burning food, going out, refusing sex or arguing; we similarly created an index for attitudes toward domestic violence. For further details on these variables, please see Appendix A.

The DHS also asks female respondents to report on the services they received during all pregnancies within 5 years of the date of the survey, including the place of delivery of all children born within five years prior to the date of the survey. Finally, we used data from the DHS maternal mortality module to examine selective survival of survey respondents around the age cutoffs. The maternal mortality module, which asked respondents to report on the number and survival status of all of their siblings, was collected in 4 of the 5 DHS surveys (the module was not conducted in the 1988 survey). Respondents were first asked about the number of siblings their own mother had. Then for each sibling, respondents were asked about the sibling’s sex, whether the sibling was still alive, the age of the sibling if still alive, the year in which the sibling died if deceased, and the sibling’s age at death if deceased. To identify pregnancy-related deaths (which include maternal and non-maternal deaths) in the sample, siblings were also asked whether any female siblings who died had been pregnant when they died or whether they had died less than 2 months after giving birth. To understand the relationship between maternal education and child survival, we wish to estimate the following:

Estimating Eq. (1) via ordinary least squares (OLS) will lead to biased estimates of the parameter of interest, which in this case is $\beta$ . This is because less educated mothers might also have other (unobserved) characteristics that might also affect outcomes.

For example, less educated mothers might also be more prone to having sick children due to lack of their own health investments. In order to get around such issues of omitted variables, we use an exogenous shift in mother’s education induced by the educational reforms that began in 1980.

As stated before, we use the idea that age at the time of school expansion greatly affected whether a girl attended secondary school. While older students were allowed to re-enroll in secondary school, this was typically not common for women who were already 2 years past the age of starting secondary school (children start secondary school at age 13 or 14 in Zimbabwe). We use the age-specific nature of the expansion to argue that a woman’s age as of 1980 was an important driver of whether she received secondary schooling. While we estimate this as though this were a regression discontinuity design, we want to emphasize that an alternative take on the design is that the costs of attending school changed very non-linearly around age 13 in 1980. Hence, for people below age 13 in 1980, the costs of schooling were greatly reduced (due to school expansion and, therefore, easier access to schooling) compared to those 16 and older. These cost changes, however, are only valid for these age groups in 1980. At other times (say in 1990), these costs do not change in this manner (as evidenced by the younger ages in Fig. 1). To sum up, our strategy compares the outcomes for women who were 9–13 years old to the outcomes for women who were 16–20 when these women were sampled many years later (from 1988 to 2010). As in van der Klaauw (2002), the indicator for the age cutoff serves as an excluded instrument in a two stage least squares (2SLS) regression (van der Klaauw, 2002).

There are a few considerations to keep in mind. First, the further away from the cutoff of 13 we move on either side, the less comparable our sample becomes. This is because a person who was 2 years old at the time of independence likely experienced more than just a change in education due to independence. Hence, we select a window of people in the age group 9–20 in 1980 for our main sample, but we also test much small age bands above and below our age threshold. Second, as can be seen in Fig. 1, women who were exactly 14 or 15 years old in 1980 are partially treated (this is due to policies that allowed over-age women to re-enter school). Hence, we omit them from the main estimation strategy, but we have also included them in some specifications to test sensitivity of our results to their inclusion. Third, it is important to control for the general effects of age. Since our approach is similar in spirit to a regression discontinuity approach, we control for age trends before and after the discontinuity so as to precisely exploit the point of discontinuity.

4. Results
4.1. First stage results: Impact of policy changes on maternal education

Fig. 1 demonstrates the effects of the reforms on the educational attainment of all women in the DHS (not just those in our samples) with age of the women in 1980 presented along the $x$ -axis. There are two vertical lines in each figure at age 14 and 15, the ages that we consider partially treated. The women immediately on the left hand side of the vertical bars are considered the treatment group, and the women immediately on the right side are the control group (again we show data on all women in the DHS, not just those in our samples). The discontinuity is easily visible: women who were less than 13 in 1980 experienced a greater jump in schooling relative to those who were 16 or older in 1980. Table 2 summarizes the results of our first stage regressions: the discontinuity in education is associated with an increase in education of 1.68 years and an increased probability of attending some secondary school by 25.2 percentage points, after controlling for other variables. It is worth noting that these are very large and very rapid increases in both the number of year and probability of attending any secondary schooling. Table 2 also shows that the first stage is stronger in rural areas and among people with a low wealth index. In Appendix Fig. A1, we show that all provinces in Zimbabwe experienced increases in educational achievement and that this indeed was a country-wide expansion of schooling. We also include estimates of the impact of the educational policy on women who were 14 and 15 in 1980, and the effects are somewhat diminished, which makes sense since these women were only partially treated. In Table 2, we also demonstrate that our first stage results are also robust to the inclusion of polynomials in age in 1980 and with larger bandwidths in our sample.
4.2. Impact on child survival

Fig. 2a charts the mortality of children born to all women in our sample. We see a discontinuous decrease in the probability of child death, which appears to coincide with the timing of the increases in maternal education. Note that the figures only tell us the difference in survival by the age of the mother in 1980, whereas the regressions, due to the instrumental variable approach, tell us the increase in survival due to an extra year of education, the results of which are presented in Table 3. One extra year of maternal education was associated with a 1.7 percentage point decrease in the probability that a child was reported to have died prior to the survey. Given that on average $7 . 9 \%$ of the children in our sample were reported to have died at the time of the survey, the decrease in child mortality from one year of education represents an approximately $2 1 . 5 \%$ decrease in child deaths. Table 3 also shows that OLS estimates of this relationship tend to be severely underestimated. Additionally, Table 3 reveals that the effects on mortality by a certain age (5 years or 1 year) are largely similar, negative and statistically significant. Child deaths are heavily concentrated in the early years of life, which is consistent with known patterns of child mortality. This is important, since our primary measure of child survival includes all children ever born to the women in the DHS surveys, including children who may be teenagers or adults by the later surveys. We also test an alternative outcome – mortality by age 5 and mortality by age 1 – to rule out, for example, the rise of HIV among youth.

In Fig. 2b and Table 4 we present the disaggregated results for women according to geographic area and by low vs. high wealth index. Our findings suggest that the majority of gains in both education and child survival were concentrated among women living in rural areas and among the poorest women, our second stage estimates are only significant among rural and low-wealth index women (although sample sizes are much smaller when disaggregated), which is consistent with what is known about the rollout of the educational reforms4. This pattern appears to be true for all measures of mortality.

We conduct a number of robustness checks on our mortality results. These results are presented in Tables 5a and 5b. First, since schooling may have delayed the age of first birth for some women, we also run our tests excluding data from the 1988 survey, a time when some of the women in our sample may still be in school. Second, since our preferred specification excludes women who were exactly 14 and 15 in 1980, we also test whether including these women alters our results. Third, we test more narrow age bands (11–18 and 12–17), further tightening our sample to women who were just too old or too young to benefit from the policy. Finally, as is common in the RD literature, we test whether non-linear age trends in the data affect our results (see Table 5b, middle panel). In addition, as Table 5b shows, the results are robust to including birth year times survey year fixed effects and using age in 1980 interacted with region of residence as an instrument. Our findings are robust to all of these alternative samples and specifications.

Appendix Table A1 additionally shows that by restricting the sample to: (1) women who are more likely to have completed their fertility by the date of the survey (aged above 35), (2) by child sex, (3) by early birth order (these results are also seen in Fig. 2c) and (4) to births occurring 5 years prior to the survey to minimize issues with recall, the results are barely altered. Again, our findings are robust to all of these alternative samples and specifications.
4.3. Channels linking education to survival outcomes

Next, we explore the mechanisms through which increased education might be associated with changes in child mortality, which are grouped into broad categories and presented in Tables 6–8. We also present reduced form estimates for all of the same outcomes in Appendix Tables A2a–A2c. As an additional robustness check, we also present the results for the same outcomes in Tables 6 and 7 in Appendix Table A3 with a wider bandwidth in age (to allow for polynomials) and with polynomials of age in 1980. The first set of mechanisms that we explore is the impact of expanded access to maternal education on the fertility and sexual behavior of women, the results of which are presented in Table 6 (reduced form OLS estimates for all mechanisms we explore are also presented in Appendix Tables A2a–A2c). We find that increased secondary schooling delays age at first cohabitation, perhaps consequently age at first intercourse and also the age at first birth; an additional year of schooling delays entry into cohabitation by 0.5 years, off a base of 19 years. The delay in terms of having the first child is smaller at around 0.3 years, but it is perhaps mediated by the fact that more schooling reduces the time between marriage and first child. The middle panel of Column 2 in Table 6 shows that schooling also has an impact on the number of children born (including children that eventually die); however, this result is not statistically significant for women close to the end of their fertile cycle (35 years), though the magnitude is similar. We interpret this result with some caution since this is not robust to polynomials in age, the results of which are shown in Appendix Table A3. As seen in Fig. 3, there appears to be little evidence of a strong trend break in number of children in the reduced form.

Studies have shown that first births and births to younger mothers are of much higher mortality rates than other births (Hobcraft, 1993). Using data from 25 DHS data from the 1990s, Hobcraft estimated that the excess risk for firstborn children to teenage mothers was on the order of $4 0 \%$ (Hobcraft et al., 1985). Data from Texas, which has much lower rates of child mortality than in our sample, suggests that children who were born to women less than 18 years old had a $3 0 \%$ higher risk of being born preterm as compared to children born to mothers just a few years older (Royer, 2004). Increased age at first birth, even of a small amount, during this critical time period, could potentially be an important channel that links increased maternal education to reduced child mortality. To further investigate the impact of increased education on the age distribution of women enter cohabitation and motherhood, we investigate whether the policy was associated with the probability of giving birth by age of 16 (an age where students might be still be expected to be in high school) and age 20 (an age where most students would not be expected to be in high school). As presented in Table 6 (bottom panel), we see that the policy was associated with a lower probability of giving birth by age 16 but not age 20, which suggests that the increase in age at birth was concentrated among girls in their late teenage years.

Desired fertility, on the other hand, does seem to be strongly affected by schooling. Women with more schooling desire fewer children and, as Table 6 suggests, 0.22 children less off a base of 4.5 children. This result is robust to polynomial trends on either side of the discontinuity, and importantly, as can be seen from Fig. 3, there appears to be a real trend break around the discontinuity in the number of children desired.

We then examine outcomes such as female empowerment (see Section 2 and Appendix A on how this variable is created), opinions on domestic violence and risky behavior (smoking) in Table 7, and we find very little evidence that schooling plays an important role in affecting these outcomes. In the lower half of Table 7, we examine economic outcomes of the mother and find that asset ownership, urban location, and probability of working are higher for the more educated. We also define two dummy variables: one for being in the lowest wealth quintile and another for being in the highest wealth quintile. We find that more education is associated with a lower probability of being in the lowest wealth quintile, which is likely related to the changes in the probability of having electricity and living in a rural area. Appendix Table A3 shows that the coefficients on urban location and probability of working are robust to polynomial trends in age; however, we wish to stress some caution in reading too much into these results as the reduced form results in Fig. 4 do not show clear trend breaks in these outcomes around the cutoff. Taken together, we interpret the results of Tables 6 and 7 to suggest that schooling appears to affect fertility decisions and some economic outcomes that might be relevant for child survival. Education does not seem to affect outcomes related to the woman’s status in the household, although we admit that these are relatively noisy measures in the DHS.

It is important to also examine the impact of the reform on male schooling in order to determine if the results we observe are being driven by maternal education, paternal education or changes in marriage match quality that result after the school expansion. While it is rather difficult to completely disentangle these effects, we explore these possibilities in Fig. 5 and conclude that changes in maternal education are most likely driving our results. A few things are important to note in Fig. 5. First, the age specificity of the reform is less strict for men, both due to pre-independence higher rates of school attendance and perhaps also a higher likelihood of re-enrolling after independence. Second, there is no discontinuity in the age of men that women marry, and while the reform also affected men, the fact that age of husbands does not shift around the cutoff (note that women marry men who are on average 5 years older) suggests that husband’s education is likely not that different around the cutoff (bottom left in Fig. 5). Third, the bottom-right graph in Fig. 5 shows that, consistent with this idea, the most significant change among couples wherein the woman is below 14 or 15 in 1980 is the difference in educational attainment between husbands and wives. Women who experienced increased schooling have a smaller gap in educational attainment compared to women who were too old to take advantage of the reforms. These figures lend support to the notion that changes in maternal education around the time of the reform are the most important drivers of the educational reforms on child mortality. We also recognize that these results can be interpreted as suggesting that what might matter for outcomes is not maternal education per se but the difference in husband versus wife’s education. We cannot disentangle these effects in the current design.

The next set of outcomes we examine in Table 8 is related to the health-seeking behavior of the mother on behalf of her child. In Table 8, maternal education appears to have no statistically significant effect on institutional deliveries (which is surprising given the apparent jump visible in Fig. 6), but it has a large and statistically significant effect on delivery via cesarean section. The cesarean section rate in our sample is relatively low, but the magnitude of the result suggests that an extra year of education increases the likelihood of a cesarean section by nearly $8 5 \%$ . Interestingly, maternal education seems to have no effect on preventive health care acts such as antenatal care and full immunizations, although these rates are high in the full sample. These results are shown graphically in Fig. 6.

Using household surveys to measure health service utilization has been shown to be prone to different forms of bias, however, with no clear generalizable patterns for the bias, in particular in low and middle income countries (Miles et al., 2013). While we might expect women of higher education to more accurately report health service use, the fact that we observe little significant effects of education on any of the health service utilization variables we investigate causes us to believe recall bias didn’t have a major effect in driving our findings on health service utilization. Where reporting biases has been analyzed in the context of diarrhea, investigators found very little differences in accuracy of reported rates between mothers with primary and secondary education, the most relevant margin for this study (Boerma et al., 1991).

It is worth highlighting that we test health-seeking behaviors among the most recent births but child mortality in all births of the women in our sample. We therefore replicate our child mortality results in the sample of recent births in the bottom panel of Table 8. We find that the results are very similar in magnitude but and statistically significant at conventional levels despite diminished sample size (Table 8 uses only $2 0 \%$ of the data used in Table 3).
4.4. Robustness tests

As stated earlier, an important concern is that independence led to other changes, beyond those in the education sector—although why this would occur differentially for those just below and above 13 is perhaps a harder argument to make. Our first attempt at capturing the possibility that other reforms or changes might differentially affect those below 13 in 1980 is to examine our main child mortality outcome for women who had dropped out by age 9 and, hence, never took advantage of the reforms (we repeated this exercise for dropouts by age 10 or 11 and the results looked very similar)5. Fig. 7 shows that there is no discontinuity in child mortality around age 14 or 15 for women who dropped out of school years before independence. Hence, it seems unlikely that independence led to other reforms that had age-specific effects that could explain our results.

We also plot child mortality relative to the year of birth of the children in Fig. 8. We see that there were large declines in child mortality that began in the mid-1970s but that by 1983, child mortality rates had largely stabilized and remained relatively constant through the 2000s. There is no discontinuity in child mortality at independence itself, rather the continuation in a trend that began prior to independence. This pattern is consistent with a decline in mortality as the country transitioned out of civil war before independence and which researchers predicted in the 1980s, despite the lack of data to measure child mortality at the time. It is also consistent with evidence from the 1980s that suggested that most of the changes within the health care sector happened within the first few years after independence, but then stabilized or eventually faded out (Loewenson et al., 1991). Since the average age of first birth of the women in our sample was 19 years old, most of the births in our sample of children would have occurred after the major declines in child mortality in this figure occurred.

Given that the women in our control group were slightly older than women in the treatment group it may be that more children of control group mothers were born during a time period with higher prevailing child mortality rates, which could account for some of the differences in child mortality we observe between groups. To help rule this out, we conduct two additional analyses, which are presented in Appendix Tables A4a and A4b. First, we update our main results on child mortality on samples that exclude all children born in or prior to the years 1980 through 1985. Given that the average year of birth in our sample is in the late 1980s, unsurprisingly we don’t lose a lot of sample by excluding these additional children and our estimates remain largely unchanged, suggesting our main findings are not being driven by births that occurred during the early 1980s. Second, we also do a similar exercise but instead exclude all women whose first births occurred in or prior to the years 1980 through 1985. This is a much stricter restriction on our sample and so we face a much greater challenge in maintaining sample size, but again we find that the results are relatively consistent to our main findings and robust to this additional test.

Given that our findings suggest that the reduction in child mortality was driven primarily through a delay in the age of first birth, we further investigate the changes in fertility in our samples. At independence, contraceptive rates were relatively low in Zimbabwe, and the national family planning program had been deemed largely inefficient. Although family planning programs had existed in Zimbabwe since 1964, only about $1 4 \%$ of married women aged 15–49 were using any form of modern contraception at independence (Boohene and Dow, 1987). In 1981, the family planning programs were reorganized and integrated within the Ministry of Health and over the next few years underwent significant operational changes. They also adopted a new strategy that focused heavily on community-based distribution, information and education, as well as improvements in the supply of modern family planning programs (Boohene and Dow, 1987). By the mid-1980s, the contraceptive prevalence rate among married women had increased substantially; however, there was very little observed decline in fertility overall, suggesting that most of the increased use of contraceptives was likely being used by women to increase birth spacing (Boohene and Dow, 1987). In Table 7, we found a small effect of increased education on the use of modern contraception that was only significant at the $1 0 \%$ level. Furthermore, in Fig. 9, we chart the trends in birth spacing among the women in our sample. While there is a clear trend toward longer birth intervals among younger women, there is no discontinuity visible at the ages corresponding to the increase in education. Our findings strongly suggest that the biggest effect of increased maternal education on fertility appears to have been largely mechanical: an important shift in the age at cohabitation and of first birth. And, while education appears to have affected the desire to have fewer children, we find little effect on actual fertility, suggesting that access to contraception was unlikely to have been made available in an age-specific manner that could be undermining our results.

While it is common for regression discontinuity design based papers to show “smoothness of covariates”, this is particularly difficult to do in our case since the DHS does not collect data on a rich set of variables that were likely to be determined prior to early adolescence. Hence, almost any outcome in the DHS could have been affected by increased education.

In Fig. 10, we show that sex of the child, the religion of the mother, the number of women sampled and the year of survey are quite smooth around the point of discontinuity. Moreover, show that height of the mother (determined in early childhood) is also not affected around the discontinuity.

A related concern is that of differential mortality of the mother: if the more educated are less (or more) likely to be surveyed or less (or more) likely to die, then such sample selection could bias our results. Even though Appendix Fig. A2 shows that the histogram of ages is smooth around the cutoff, we further explore this possibility in a few different ways. First, using the module on maternal mortality in the DHS, we examine the likelihood of the female siblings of the respondent dying due to pregnancy-related reasons by age of the sister in 1980 and conditional on the sister being alive in 1980. Appendix Fig. A3 suggests that differential pregnancy-related mortality due to increased education is likely not an issue. Using data on all siblings (male or female) of the respondent in Appendix Fig. A4, we assess the probability that any individual sibling is alive in 1980 and whether any individual sibling is likely to be dead after 1980 conditional on being alive in 1980 (in other words, the top right graph of Appendix Fig. A4 shows that there does not appear to be a discontinuity in adult mortality as a result of increased education). In the bottom panel of Appendix Fig. A4, we examine whether sibling structure is differential around the cutoff and find that it is not. These figures help add evidence suggesting that what was mainly different for those just below and just above the age of 13 in 1980 was access to schooling.

5. Discussion and conclusions

A number of channels have been postulated as ways in which education might lead to changes in child mortality and other health outcomes. First, education may make people more efficient producers of health (the productive efficiency hypothesis), which could make people more adherent to treatments or make people get more health out of the same inputs. Second, education may make people more aware of different treatments, which may lead them to make different choices with regards to preventive behaviors or different treatments (the allocative efficiency hypothesis). Third, increased education might lead to higher incomes, which could directly affect health by increasing the purchasing power of individuals (income effects). Finally, there are also a number of additional pathways, which might influence one or more of these channels in less wellestablished ways, such as the propensity to marry a better partner, social networks, etc.

Our study provides causal evidence of the impact of maternal education on child mortality and explores some potential channels underlying this effect. We find a robust effect on child survival and find supporting evidence toward channels that involve fertility and economic outcomes due to increased education. We do not find support for mechanisms that involve health-seeking behavior or female empowerment. It is notable that these effects seem to have occurred in a setting where the quality of secondary education is reportedly quite poor. Our findings suggest that education may have largely had an incapacitation effect, in the sense that it mechanically delayed age at cohabitation and fertility. Had the quality of education been improved, there might have been additional effects, and it might also help to explain little changes in health-seeking behavior or other outcomes.

We note that the educational reforms in Zimbabwe differed from many of the previous natural experiments investigated that were compulsory in nature, since enrolling into secondary school was still voluntary post-Independence. Compulsory schooling and voluntary expansions to schooling will capture different local average treatment effect (LATE). In a world of compulsory schooling, it is possible that those children whose returns to schooling are the lowest are now the marginal children who are pushed (by law) into attending school. In our case, the children on the margin might be children whose returns to schooling might be high, but costs also sufficiently high, that prior to the reforms, these children did not go to school. Hence, when costs are lowered and schooling is not compulsory, those with the highest returns might select into schooling, while those with low returns, despite the lower costs, choose to stay out of school. Hence, compulsory schooling and expanded access to schooling measures capture two rather different LATEs depending on the assumptions we make about how each of the reforms change the returns to and costs of schooling.

Those familiar with Zimbabwe are undoubtedly aware of other changes that have happened in this country over the past few decades, including the rapid spread of HIV and the near collapse of the public health system (Todd et al., 2010). However, we believe our empirical approach can rule out most of these changes as potential alternative explanations due to the age-specific structure of our analysis. While another study suggested that Zimbabwean women who benefited from the same policy change were more likely to be aware of HIV and its modes of transmission, there is no evidence that these women were more or less likely to acquire HIV/AIDS.

At the time of independence, Zimbabwe was a well-off country relative to other countries in Sub-Saharan Africa; it had relatively high levels of literacy and high levels of primary education, but secondary education rates were still low. Moreover, under-5 mortality in Zimbabwe in 1980 was approximately 100 per 1000 live births, and the total fertility rate was just over 7, which would make it comparable to the rates in many African countries today. Like improving health, increasing education is also an important development priority. Millennium Development Goal (MDG) 2, a goal to achieve universal primary education, has been among the most successful MDGs: primary education enrollment in developing regions reached nearly $9 0 \%$ by 2011 (Go and Quijada, 2012). Primary education rates for girls have improved the most and are now nearly on par with those of boys, even in the poorest regions in the world. However, there has been substantially less progress with regards to secondary education, in particular in the least developed countries of Sub-Saharan Africa, where child mortality rates remain high (Mingat et al., 2010). Our findings suggest that increasing maternal secondary education might be an effective way to reduce child mortality and fertility rates in the developing world today.

All data on female empowerment were taken from the empowerment modules that has been asked in select DHS over the years. The empowerment module of questions was not asked in the 1988 survey and all of the empowerment questions were not asked in each survey. Therefore the response rate to these questions is much lower than for our other outcomes and the number of responses varies by empowerment question. For each set of decisions, women were asked if they alone, they along with their husband, or if someone else in their household had say over how key decisions were made in the household, including how to spend the respondent’s own earnings, how decisions regarding the respondent’s own health care were made, how decisions over large purchases were made, how decisions regarding purchases for daily needs were made, who decides which family members or other relatives the household would visit, how decisions regarding food purchases were made, and how decisions regarding how money were made. For all women who responded to these questions, if women reported having some say, either alone or with her husband, we coded this response as a 1 or 0 otherwise. We then created an index using these dummies to capture empowerment in a single variable. The surveys similarly ask about domestic violence, which contains questions about whether it is acceptable for a man to beat his wife in the event of burning food, going out, refusing sex, or arguing. These responses are coded as 1 if a woman agrees with such statements and we create an index out of all the responses to capture overall attitudes toward domestic violence.

Women were also asked to report about the immunization status of their children. Women are typically asked to retrieve the vaccination cards for each of their children, but it is not uncommon for many women to not be able to retrieve these cards at the time of the survey. We therefore used any report of a particular vaccine being received, whether or not it is confirmed by the vaccine card or not, as is standard practice with most studies that employ data on immunizations from the DHS. Since most children are supposed to receive these prescribed vaccines at some point during their first year, for immunizations, we restrict our sample to all children who are between 11 and 23 months old. As part of the Expanded Program on Immunizations, the specific vaccines that children are supposed to receive include the BCG vaccine for tuberculosis, three doses of the polio vaccine, three doses of the diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis vaccine (DTP), as well as the measles vaccine. Some of these vaccines, in particular polio and measles, are typically delivered through large scale immunization campaigns whereas some of the other vaccines were more likely to be delivered during routine postnatal care visits. We also construct measures as to whether or not children had received any immunization and whether or not children were fully immunized (meaning they had received all of the above mentioned vaccines).

Data on mortality of siblings comes from the maternal mortality module, which was collected, in the four most recent rounds of the DHS in Zimbabwe. Respondents were first asked about the number of siblings their own mother ever had. Then for each sibling, respondents are asked about the sibling’s sex, whether the sibling was still alive, the age of the sibling if still alive, the year in which the sibling died if deceased, and the deceased sibling’s age at death. To identify pregnancy related deaths (which includes maternal and non-maternal deaths) in the sample, siblings are also asked whether any female siblings who died had been pregnant when they died or whether they had died less than 2 months after giving birth. Any death that may have occurred when pregnant or within 2 months of delivery are considered pregnancy related deaths. Using either the age of the living sibling or the combination of years since death and age at death of the sibling the date of birth of siblings can be calculated, the DHS imputes both the year and month of birth of the women (randomly assigning women to a month within the estimated year) and their month and year of death (randomly assigning deaths by month in the estimated year) if applicable. We use these variables to estimate a year of birth, year of death (if applicable), and current age (if applicable) of all siblings born to each respondent. It is well known that there are many measurement challenges in using the sibling death data, including recall bias and selection biases. For example, data is only collected from living reproductive aged women so it would underestimate mortality in high mortality families and in families with only brother, but as our goal is estimate mortality of individuals rather than population level mortality rates, we believe this to be less of an issue. We exclude the respondent from the sibling sample since they are all by definition alive at the time of the survey. To minimize the impact of recall bias we restrict ourselves to include only sibling who was either 10 years older or 10 years younger than the respondent. Another problem with the sibling data includes age heaping in the reported years since death (e.g. 10 years is a common response), but we assume that this reported age heaping should not be differential based on age of respondent in 1980.

Paul Wentges Institut für Unternehmensforschung der Hochschule St. Gallen Bodanstr. 6, 9000 St. Gallen, Switzerland
Abstract

The cross decomposition algorithm of [van Roy 1986] is generally considered to be one of the most efficient procedures for solving the capacitated facility location problem. A modified version of this algorithm, called dually-weighted cross decomposition, is presented. In contrast to the cross decomposition algorithm, this approach does not use the optimal dual solutions of the primal subproblems or the optimal solutions of the dual master problem as Lagrangean multipliers for the dual subproblems. A specially weighted average of the previously constructed multipliers is used instead. Finite convergence of this approach is proven and first promising results are discussed.

The cross decomposition algorithm of [van Roy 1986] simultaneously exploits both the primal structure (temporarily fixing the variables $_ y$ yields a normal transportation problem) and the dual structure (with relaxing the capacity constraints (3) in lagrangean fashion) of the (CFLP), i. e. combines Benders' decomposition and Dantzig-Wolfe decomposition in one single framework. The approach is motivated by the fact, that the primal subproblem can be viewed as a relaxed dual (Dantzig-Wolfe) master problem and the dual subproblem as a relaxed primal (Benders) master problem (see e.g. [van Roy 1983]).

The main steps of the algorithm can be described as follows (let $( S D _ { \mu } )$ be the Lagrangean relaxation of $( C F L P )$ with respect to the capacity constraints (3) and the Lagrangean multipliers $\mu$ b $( M D _ { k } )$ the relaxed Dantzig-Wolfe master problem: $\textstyle \operatorname* { m a x } \{ \delta : \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } f _ { j } y _ { j } ^ { t } +$ $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } c _ { i j } x _ { i j } ^ { t } - \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n } ( s _ { j } y _ { j } ^ { t } - \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } x _ { i j } ^ { t } ) \mu _ { j } \geq \delta \forall t \in T _ { k } ; } \end{array}$ $\mu \geq 0 , \delta \in \mathbb { R } \}$ $( S P _ { y } )$ the transportation problem obtained when $_ y$ is fixed, and $( M P _ { k } )$ a relaxed Benders master problem; for a more detailed and explicit description of the problems see [van Roy 1986]):

Step 1: Initialize and get a dual solution $\mu ^ { 1 }$ (by solving the primal subproblem $( S P _ { y ^ { 0 } } )$ with $y ^ { 0 } \equiv 1$ ).   
Step 2: Solve the dual subproblem $( S D _ { \mu ^ { k } } )$ : Let $( x ^ { k } , y ^ { k } )$ be an optimal solution. Perform a convergence test; if the test is not fulfilled, go to step 5.   
Step 3: Solve the primal subproblem $( S P _ { y ^ { k } } )$ : Let $( \lambda ^ { k + 1 } , \nu ^ { k + 1 } , \mu ^ { k + 1 } )$ be an optimal dual solution. Perform a convergence test; if the test is not fulfilled, go to step 5 (or step 4, see below), otherwise go to step 2 and set $k : = k + 1$ .   
Step 4: Solve the primal master problem $\left( M P _ { k } \right)$ : Let $y ^ { k + 1 }$ be an optimal solution. Go to step 3 and set $k : = k + 1$ .

In steps 2 and 3, cuts corresponding to the optimal solutions have to be added to the respective master problems; in each step, optimality has to be checked. If the Lagrangean dual is solved within a specified tolerance level $\tau$ (e.g. $0 . 5 \%$ ), one switches to Benders' decomposition (only usage of steps 3 and 4).

The cross decomposition algorithm solves the (CFLP) in a finite number of steps, since the convergence tests prevent the algorithm from cycling and therefore, after finitely many steps, the method amounts to Benders' decomposition, which is known to be finite (see e.g. [van Roy 1983] and [Holmberg 1990], respectively).
2 Dually-weighted Cross Decomposition

[Holmberg 1992] proposed a modification of the cross decomposition algorithm (mean value cross decomposition) to solve linear programming problems, where, in contrast to the cross decomposition algorithm, not the last optimal solution of one subproblem is used as input to the other and vice versa, but the arithmetic mean of all previously obtained optimal solutions of the respective subproblem. No master problems are used anymore and asymptotic convergence towards the optimum can be proven.

A somewhat similar approach is suggested here for the (CFLP). 3 Results

The cross decomposition and the dually-weighted cross decomposition algorithms were tested on 27 examples with 19-108 potential facilities and 65-174 customers on the road network of Switzerland. In these examples, a tolerance level $\tau$ of $0 . 5 \%$ for the duality gap $v ( M D _ { k } ) \mathrm { ~ - ~ }$ $v ( S D _ { \mu ^ { \mathrm { b e s t } , k } } )$ was used, in step 3 the dual solution $( \lambda ^ { k + 1 } , \nu ^ { k + 1 } , \mu ^ { k + 1 } )$ was altered as described in [Wentges 1993], and at most thirty iterations were carried out.

With the new dually-weighted cross decomposition algorithm better results could be achieved in almost all examples compared to ordinary cross decomposition. The Lagrangean dual could now be solved within the tolerance level $\tau$ in 19 instead of 11 examples (where only in three of these 11 examples, the tolerance level was reached earlier by ordinary cross decomposition, and in two cases, the same number of iterations was needed). In all other examples the duality gap $v ( M D _ { k } ) - v ( S D _ { \mu ^ { \mathrm { b e s t } , k } } )$ could be decreased substantially.
Remark: Weighting the Lagrangean multipliers as described above, may also be useful in other applications of Dantzig-Wolfe decomposition.

This paper examines the impacts of a mandatory, universal prescription drug insurance program on health care utilization and health outcomes in a public health care system with free physician and hospital services. Using the Canadian National Population Health Survey from 1994 to 2003 and implementing a difference-in-differences estimation strategy, we find that the mandatory program substantially increased drug coverage among the general population. The program also increased medication use and general practitioner visits but had little effect on specialist visits and hospitalization. Findings from quantile regressions suggest that there was a large improvement in the health status of less healthy individuals. Further analysis by pre-policy drug insurance status and the presence of chronic conditions reveals a marked increase in the probability of taking medication and visiting a general practitioner among the previously uninsured and those with a chronic condition.

1. Introduction

Pharmaceutical drug expenditure accounts for a significant proportion of overall health spending in many OECD countries. On average, more than a sixth of total health expenditure was dedicated to pharmaceuticals across OECD countries in 2011. On a per capita basis, the United States spend the most, almost USD 1000, followed by Canada (OECD, 2013). The rising financial burden associated with prescription drugs has raised policy concerns about the optimal design of health insurance, and drug insurance in particular, to ensure access to affordable prescription drugs. For example, the Part D drug benefit was added to Medicare in the United States (The Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act of 2003). Several OECD countries, such as New Zealand, United Kingdom, the Netherlands and Germany, provide universal coverage for prescription drugs, which is integrated into the broader system of public health insurance or statutory social health insurance policies (Morgan et al., 2013).

Unlike physician and hospital services, which are universal in Canada, coverage for prescription drugs dispensed outside hospitals falls outside the Canada Health Act and provincial governments only provide public drug programs for some population groups, primarily seniors and social assistance recipients. A number of provincial and territorial governments introduced some form of catastrophic drug coverage with high deductibles for certain groups in the past decade (Daw and Morgan, 2012; Daw et al., 2013) but there has been little progress on a national pharmacare program. Most non-elderly Canadians who have drug insurance obtain it through employee benefit plans. However, a significant number of Canadians are un-insured or under-insured against the costs of prescription drugs (Kapur and Basu, 2005). About one in 10 Canadians who receive a prescription report cost-related non-adherence, and the lack of drug insurance coverage appears to be a key reason behind this phenomenon (Law et al., 2012).

How to reform Canada’s pharmaceutical drug coverage has been under active discussion in Canada since the late 1990s. A number of recommendations for a national pharmacare program have been proposed, such as expanding universal public system to include first-dollar of prescription drugs (National Forum on Health,

The national pharmaceuticals strategy report calls for further analysis on the impact and feasibility of maintaining a private payer role in a catastrophic drug coverage framework (Federal/Provincial/Territorial Ministerial Task Force, 2006). Some current discussions in this area include, e.g., Morgan et al. (2015), Daw et al. (2014) and Busby and Pedde (2014). Despite various recommendations, Canada is still the only country that does not provide universal coverage for prescription drugs among all developed countries with universal health care system.

While many Canadian citizens and politicians believe that some form of universal drug coverage is needed, empirical evidence to inform the design of such a policy in the Canadian context is limited.1 In this study, we exploit the natural experiment of a policy change in the province of Quebec, Canada to evaluate whether and how a mandatory universal drug program affects drug insurance coverage, health care utilization and health outcomes. Quebec’s experience can provide valuable insights to inform policy debates regarding the optimal design of drug insurance in Canada and internationally.

Using Canadian National Population Health Survey longitudinal data from 1994 to 2003, we find that the universal drug program increased drug insurance coverage by 33 percent and medication use by 13 percent. The latter estimate is in the middle range of those found in the Medicare Part D studies which vary from 5.9 percent (Yin et al., 2008) to 27 percent (Duggan and Scott-Morton, 2010) in drug utilization increase. To gauge the plausibility of the results, we calculated the elasticity of drug utilization. For simplicity we only take into account the reduction in co-payment rather than the whole non-linear pricing policy in the public plan. The coinsurance of the public plan is 25 percent, which implies a 75 percent reduction in out-of-pocket cost for those without insurance. The 13 percent increase in total drug utilization suggests an elasticity of approximately −0.17, which falls within the range of drug elasticity estimates from other contexts. Given that the utilization measure is total drug utilization, the elasticity for prescription drug utilization would be larger if there is substitution for non-prescription drugs because of the policy intervention.

The estimated spillover effect on GP visits is about 10 percent but the policy has no statistically significant spillover effects on specialist visits and hospitalization. This provides evidence of a complementary relationship between prescription drugs and physician visits. The estimated effect on GP visits is large relative to zero or small spillover effects found in the U.S. context (Balkrishnan et al., 2001; Kaestner and Khan, 2012). This should not be unexpected given the multi-payer system for physician services in the U.S. in contrast to the free single-payer public system in Canada. Possible explanations for the finding of no effects on hospitalization include, first, that we look at the overall hospitalization rate rather than hospitalizations linked to pharmaceutical therapy and second that the hospital sector was downsizing and restructuring nationally in this period and the pharmaceutical effect was likely modest by comparison with the variation from those other sources.

We find that health impacts of the policy are heterogeneous across the health outcome distribution, with large positive health gains concentrated among less healthy individuals. Analysis by pre-policy drug insurance status reveals that previously uninsured individuals experienced a large increase in the probability of taking any medication and visiting a general practitioner. Further analysis by the presence of chronic conditions shows that, compared to those without any chronic condition, the chronically ill experienced a much larger increase in the extensive margins of medication and general practitioner utilization.

This paper makes several important contributions to the literature. First, it uses nationally representative longitudinal data to identify the impacts of a universal mandatory drug program by exploiting a natural experiment in Canada. Many previous studies use administrative or claims data for particular drug plans or specific population groups which limits generalizability of their findings. Moreover, the mandatory nature of the policy intervention creates a large exogenous variation in insurance coverage, in contrast to previous studies that focus on small changes in copayments.

Second, this paper contributes to the literature by exploring the spillover effects of drug coverage on physician utilization and hospitalization. The limited empirical evidence of spillover effects is mixed and inconclusive. The context of universal public provision of physician and hospital services provides an extra advantage of identifying the spillover effects. Under health systems where physician and hospital services are covered by multiple insurers, such as the U.S. Medicare program, estimation of a uniform spillover effect may be complicated by the different cost-sharing structures of physician and hospital services across insurance plans.

Third, this study adds to the literature by evaluating the impact of drug insurance on health outcomes and its impact in different parts of the health outcome distribution. Going beyond mean health effects, we analyze whether the policy effect is relatively larger among individuals with low health status versus high health status. To our knowledge, no other study has evaluated this type of heterogeneous health effects.

Fourth, from a policy perspective, analysis of the drug program can help to inform the policy debate on expanding public drug coverage to universal level in Canada and internationally. The Quebec reform gives us a novel opportunity to examine the impacts of a policy that achieved universal drug coverage among the entire nonelderly population in Quebec. The mixed public and private financing structure of the Quebec program may also be useful for policymakers on general health insurance financing. For example, the individual mandate to buy prescription drug insurance in Quebec is similar to the individual mandate to obtain general health insurance of the U.S. national legislation passed in March 2010.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we provide background on previous work. Section 3 describes the institutional setting and policy change we are studying. In Section 4, we discuss our data and descriptive statistics. Empirical methods are discussed in Section 5. Section 6 gives the results of our analysis. Finally the conclusions are drawn in Section 7.
2. Literature review

There is a rich literature examining the effects of drug insurance/health insurance on utilization. It is well documented that individuals without insurance have lower levels of utilization than those with insurance; further, among individuals with insurance, those who face cost-sharing have lower utilization than those with full insurance. Zweifel and Manning (2000) and McWilliams (2009) review the evidence with respect to health insurance in general; Lexchin and Grootendorst (2004) and Goldman et al. (2007) review the evidence with respect to drug insurance. The RAND Health Insurance Experiment (HIE) estimated the price elasticity of demand for health care to be in the order of $- 0 . 2$ (Newhouse,

Closely related to our work are some recent U.S. studies that attempt to estimate the effects of the introduction of Medicare Part D on drug utilization.2 Almost all of these studies suggest large utilization effects on prescription drugs but the magnitudes vary considerably. For the elderly, Medicare Part D has been found to increase monthly drug use by 5.9 to 27 percent (Yin et al., 2008; Lichtenberg and Sun, 2007; Liu et al., 2011; Duggan and Scott-Morton, 2010) or 11 to 37 percent among the previously uninsured (Kaestner and Khan, 2012; Schneeweiss et al., 2009) or to increase drug spending by 74 percent among the previously uninsured (Zhang et al., 2009). A few studies of the Part D transition period find no utilization effects. For example, Basu et al. (2010) find no significant changes in number of prescriptions because of Medicare Part D for Medicare–Medicaid dual eligible beneficiaries.

Optimal drug insurance design should also take into account how changes in drug coverage affect non-drug health service utilization. Such spillover effects in the broader context of free to patient physician and hospital services have received less attention in the Canadian pharmacare policy discussion. In contrast to the large literature on drug utilization effects, only a few studies have investigated the spillover effects of drug insurance on physician services with mixed findings. Some evidence suggests a complementary relationship between physician services and prescription drugs (Stabile, 2001; Allin and Hurley, 2009; Winkelmann, 2004) while other evidence points to a substitutive one (Li et al., 2007). A study by Kaestner and Khan (2012) finds no evidence that drug insurance was strongly associated with use of outpatient services. The RAND HIE, which is more than 30 years old, did not find evidence of cross effects of outpatient cost sharing on inpatient services. However, patients did not have free access to physician services in the HIE. Some existing studies also demonstrate that higher cost-sharing or a copayment for prescription drugs is associated with greater use of inpatient and emergency medical services (Tamblyn et al., 2001; Hsu et al., 2006; Chandra et al., 2010; Afendulis et al., 2011). Tamblyn et al. (2001) find that emergency department visit rates increased by 14.2 per 10,000 person-months for the elderly persons after cost-sharing for prescription drugs was increased. Chandra et al. (2010) examine changes in copayments of prescription drugs and physician office visits for employees in the California public employees retirement system. They find significant “offset” effects in terms of increased hospital utilization in response to the higher copayments for prescriptions drugs and physician office visits. Afendulis et al. (2011) compare changes in the probability of hospitalization before and after the introduction of Part D in 2006 using a difference-in-difference-in-differences approach. They find that Part D reduced the hospitalization rate by 4.1 percent or 20.5 admissions per 10,000. However, other Medicare Part D studies do not find such offset effects on hospitalization (e.g., Liu et al., 2011; Kaestner and Khan, 2012). If we consider emergency department visits and hospitalizations as proxies for health, the studies reviewed above indicate that evidence on the health impact of prescription drug coverage is mixed and inconclusive.

Finally, comparatively few studies have examined the effects of prescription drug insurance on health status and functioning.3 If drug insurance causes an increase in drug and non-drug service utilization, the health impact depends on whether the increase in utilization is for effective high-value services to the patient. The existing literature on the link between drug insurance/cost sharing and health shows higher cost sharing is associated with more adverse events among the chronically ill, however, evidence on general health outcomes is rather limited (Goldman et al., 2007). The recently proposed Value-Based Insurance Design advocates that copayment rates be set based on the expected health value of the clinical services, so as to mitigate the adverse health consequences associated with cost-sharing for services or drugs (e.g., Fendrick and Chernew, 2006). By reducing patient copayments for high-value services, the value-based insurance plans can achieve improved health outcomes for a given level of health care expenditure. The current evidence suggests that reducing copayments can improve medication compliance among the chronically ill (e.g., Maciejewski et al., 2010). This line of literature also explores the effects of VBID programs on drug spending, nondrug medical spending, total spending and health service utilization (Chernew et al., 2010; Gibson et al., 2011; Choudhry et al., 2012; Nair et al., 2010). Chernew et al. (2010) find evidence that the VBID program reduced the use of nondrug health care services and offset the costs associated with increased drug use by the program. Gibson et al. (2011) find that the combination of VBID and disease management program resulted in sustained improvements in the use of medications and modest cost savings. Nair et al. (2010) examine the impact of reducing the prescription drug co-pay for diabetes and find that the policy was associated with decreases in emergency room visits, hospitalizations, physician visits and health care expenditures. In our context, if the mandatory drug program increases access to effective prescription drugs or physician services of high value to the beneficiaries, it may generate positive health gains. On the other hand, if the increased drug or physician utilization is not an effective treatment, it may not have any health impact.

In summary, many studies find consistent positive effects of drug coverage on drug utilization but the forms and magnitudes of cost sharing (e.g., copayments, coinsurance, caps and formulary restrictions) in these studies vary considerably as do the estimates. It is unclear whether these studies can inform the policy debate over a national pharmacare program in the Canadian context. Randomized experiments usually have small sample sizes and are not sometimes easily generalized to the population. Similarly, many Medicare Part D studies use data for a specific insurance plan, pharmacy chain or subgroup Medicare population. (Some exceptions include, e.g., Afendulis et al. (2011) and Kaestner et al. (2014)). These study samples and settings lack external validity and may not generalize to the rest of the population, although some of them advantageously use natural experiment research designs. In addition, enrolment in Medicare Part D is not mandatory while our study focuses on a policy design that enforces mandatory insurance coverage through legislation. Finally, to our knowledge, there are no studies that have examined the impact of drug insurance on health status in different parts of the health outcome distribution.
3. The institutional setting

Canada has a predominantly publicly financed health care system with 13 provincial and territorial health insurance plans operating under a national legislative framework. The Canada Health Act (1984) established five principles that the provincial health insurance plans must respect: public administration, universality, portability, comprehensiveness and accessibility. All provinces and territories provide universal coverage for medically necessary hospital and physician services that are free at the point of use. The majority of public funding comes from general tax revenues of federal and provincial governments. Most hospitals are private, notfor-profit organizations funded through global budget. Physicians receive payments from provincial governments. The late 1980s to early 1990s saw dramatic downsizing and restructuring in the hospital sector due to the government budget cutbacks. Hospitals were closed or consolidated into larger units. Caps and individual physician income threshold were imposed on physician expenditure in all or some provinces. All provinces except Ontario moved toward some form of regionalized governance for health care (Marchildon et al., 2006; Marchildon, 2004b). From late 1990s to early 2000s public health spending rebounded and provincial governments began to pour money back into health care. The 2003 First Ministers’ accord on health care renewal agreed on the priority areas for reforms: primary health care, home care, catastrophic drug coverage, access to diagnostic/medical equipment and information technology and an electronic health record. However, there has been little changes in the primary care sector at the system level until the early 2000s (Hutchison et al., 2001, 2011).

Outpatient prescription drugs in Canada are covered by a mix of public and private plans, in contrast to free publicly covered physician and hospital services. The federal government administers prescription drug programs for six specific population groups.4 Provincial and territorial governments provide public drug insurance to defined population subgroups, mainly for social assistance recipients, senior citizens, and residents with specific diseases that require high-cost prescription drugs.5 Eligibility and cost sharing arrangements in these public plans vary across provinces, and there have been some moves to decrease out-of-pocket payment in the past decade (Daw and Morgan, 2012).

Drug insurance coverage for the general population, i.e., the non-elderly not on social assistance, varies across provinces. Approximately 90 percent of those with private insurance obtain it through group plans associated with their employer, union or professional association (Hurley and Guindon, 2008). Public drug programs for the general population also exist in some provinces, but with high deductibles they only provide protection against catastrophic drug expenses.6 During the period of our study there were minimal changes of drug insurance policies for the general population in provinces other than Quebec.

Drug insurance in Quebec before 1997 reflected these general patterns: the public drug program covered welfare recipients, citizens aged 65 and over, and patients with certain serious illnesses. The public plan fully covered drug costs for low-income seniors and all welfare recipients; medium- and high-income seniors were subject to a $\$ 2$ copayment per prescription up to a maximum of $\$ 100$ per year. There was no public coverage for the rest of the population, who relied on private insurance or paying out-of-pocket. The Act Respecting Prescription Drug Insurance was passed in 1996 and went into effect in two stages (Gazette Officielle Du Quebec, 1996). The policy reform started with increased user fees for previously insured welfare recipients and senior citizens in August 1996. The mandatory universal drug program for every resident in Quebec was implemented on 1 January 1997. Under this program, all residents of Quebec were required by law to have drug insurance coverage. The public prescription drug insurance plan, administered by the Régie de l’assurance maladie du Québec (RAMQ), covers all Quebecers who are not eligible for a private plan. All persons under age 65 eligible for a private plan are required to join that plan and ensure coverage for their spouse and children.7 Private plans are usually available through employment or through membership in professional associations and unions. Coverage varies across private plans but all private insurers are required to provide minimum coverage standards that are equivalent to those offered by the provincial public plan. Persons who are eligible for a private plan cannot be covered by the public plan. Table I displays the policy changes for the elderly, the welfare recipients and the general population during our study period.

The public plan charges an income-dependent premium that is collected by the Ministère du Revenu du Québec (now known as Revenu Québec) through the income tax system. In addition, the public plan includes a monthly deductible and coinsurance payment. Currently, the annual premium of the public plan varies from $\$ 0$ to $\$ 579$ depending on net family income, the monthly deductible is $\$ 16.25$ , and the coinsurance is 32 percent up to a maximum out-of-pocket expenditure per month of $\$ 82.66$ .
4. Data and descriptive statistics
4.1. Data

The main data set for this analysis is the master files of the longitudinal household component of the National Population Health Survey (NPHS), a biennial nationally representative survey conducted by Statistics Canada. The target population of the NPHS includes community-based household residents in the 10 provinces, excluding populations on Indian Reserves, Canadian Forces Bases and some remote areas in Quebec and Ontario. The sample was created by first selecting households and then within each household, choosing one member 12 years of age or older to be the longitudinal respondent. It also includes 2,022 persons who were under the age of 12 in the first cycle and previously interviewed as part of the 1994/1995 National Longitudinal Survey of Children and Youth (NLSCY).8 Therefore, the NPHS longitudinal sample includes 17,276 persons from all ages in 1994/1995. The NPHS asks a series of questions related to health status, use of health services, chronic conditions and activity restrictions, and demographic and socio-economic status.

We use the 1994/1995, 1996/1997, 1998/1999, 2000/2001 and 2002/2003 cycles of NPHS for our analysis. Of the 17,276 people who were first interviewed in 1994/1995, we excluded 2,022 people who were younger than 12 years old because most of the outcome variables are only available for respondents aged 12 and older. We dropped 4,086 people older than 56 in the first cycle. This resulted in a sample of 11,168 people aged 12 to 56 in 1994/1995, who were followed for up to eight years. The data were then re-shaped as person-year data containing 55,840 observations (11,168 times five cycles). We further deleted 3,824 observations reporting welfare benefits as their income source in any of the survey cycles. We then eliminated individuals missing important health care utilization information.9 The final data set consists of an unbalanced, non-contiguous panel of 10,653 people (42,609 person-year observations), who were non-elderly not on social assistance and between the ages of 12 and 56 in 1994/1995 (20 to 64 at their last interview in 2002/2003).

There are several reasons why we exclude from our analysis the elderly and social assistance recipients who had full drug coverage before 1996.10 First, the policy change for these groups happened at a different time, August 1, 1996, which is several months earlier than the reform for the non-elderly. Second, the reform had different implications for this previously covered group: it increased user fees for them (in contrast to providing drug coverage to the non-elderly). Third, persons who turn 65 may choose to retain their private plan or join the public plan. In contrast, the non-elderly do not have this choice and are required to join a private plan if they are eligible for one. These distinct features of the elderly and social assistance recipients make it difficult to evaluate the policy impacts for them in this single paper. A full evaluation of the different policy changes for these groups is beyond the scope of this paper and can be a topic for future research.
4.2. Outcome variables

Drug insurance status is an indicator variable coded as one if a person reported having drug insurance and zero otherwise. Measures of health care utilization include drug utilization, physician visits and hospitalization. Drug utilization measures the number of distinct medications taken in the previous month.11 Note that this measure refers to both prescription and non-prescription drugs. Ideally we would separate these two, but separate measures are not available in the pre-policy cycles of the data. If the policy induces individuals to substitute prescription drugs for non-prescription drugs, our estimates would measure the net effects on total medication use and underestimate the impact of the policy on prescription drug use. Self-reported measures of medication use may introduce bias and measurement error.12 Therefore, we further look at aggregate drug expenditure from the Canadian Institute for Health Information (CIHI) to complement our analysis. We measure general practitioner (GP) visits and specialist visits separately as the number of visits with each type of physician in the previous 12 months. Finally, all of the medication and physician utilization variables were truncated at their 99.5 percentile to eliminate outliers.13 For all utilization measures, we further look at the extensive margin of utilization: whether a respondent had at least one medication or physician visit. Hospitalization measures whether a respondent had an overnight inpatient hospital stay in the previous 12 months.

Health outcome measures are the health utility index (HUI3) and self-assessed health status. The Health Utility Index Mark 3 (HUI3) is a generic measure of health status and health-related quality of life that is widely used in clinical studies, population health surveys and economic evaluations (Horsman et al., 2003). It is a function of eight attributes that can vary from no impairment to severely impaired: vision, hearing, speech, mobility, dexterity, feelings, cognition and pain. For the HUI, 1.0 represents perfect health and 0.0 represents death. The observed values range from $- 0 . 3 6 0$ to 1.000 in increments of 0.001 (negative scores reflect health states considered worse than death) (Furlong et al., 1999). For self-assessed health status, we create a dichotomous variable: excellent or very good health is coded as 1 and good, fair, or poor health is coded as 0. The use of self-assessed health status as a measure of health is common in the empirical literature and it has been found to be an independent predictor of mortality and morbidity (Idler and Benyamini, 1997).
